title: Hiking & Outdoor Equipment Stores
one_liner: Specialty retailers selling hiking, camping, and outdoor equipment and apparel to consumers pursuing outdoor recreation activities.
overview: The US hiking and outdoor equipment stores industry is contracting after years of pandemic-driven growth, now facing a 2.6% revenue decline in 2025 as consumer demand normalizes and discretionary spending tightens. With 6.3 billion dollars in 2026 revenue spread across roughly 1,382 stores and 20,834 employees, the sector is consolidating and shifting operations online while competing fiercely against Amazon, big-box retailers like Walmart and Dick's Sporting Goods, and direct-to-consumer brands. REI—the industry's largest player—laid off hundreds of employees in 2024-2025 and closed its unprofitable Experiences division, signaling industry-wide pressure. Outdoor recreation participation hit record levels at 183.2 million Americans in 2025, but customers are buying less often and spending more cautiously.

key_stats.growth: -2.6% decline in 2025; negative annual rate through early 2026
key_stats.concentration: high; Dick's Sporting Goods is the largest player, with top four firms controlling over 60% of market

how_it_makes_money: Specialty retailers generate revenue primarily through retail sales of outdoor apparel (30%), footwear (26%), and equipment like tents and backpacks (26%), with the remainder from value-added services like repairs, rentals, and in-store events. Many stores operate dual channels—physical locations in high-traffic areas paired with e-commerce sites to reach remote customers and offset rent costs.
cost_structure: Labor is the largest controllable cost, followed by rent and inventory carrying costs. Sourcing of goods has shifted to wholesalers since most retail chains no longer manufacture in-house. E-commerce operations require investment in fulfillment, website optimization, and digital marketing. Seasonal fluctuations (spring-summer peaks) force stores to carry high inventory levels through fall-winter downturns.
major_players: Dick's Sporting Goods (largest, 724 stores across US and Canada)
REI Co-op (second largest, 23 million members, ~180 stores, 3.8 billion dollars revenue, pivoting to digital and used gear resale)
Patagonia (independent, private, high-end niche with in-house manufacturing and repair focus)
Academy Sports + Outdoors (290 stores)
Local and regional independents and multi-sport shops
current_dynamics: Post-pandemic normalization is hitting hard. During 2020-2022, lockdowns and remote work drove demand for camping gear, hiking boots, and outdoor apparel, but as travel resumed and indoor activities reopened, sales stalled. Retailers faced massive inventory write-downs and margin compression. Simultaneously, Amazon is moving upmarket into premium outdoor gear with private-label tents and sleeping bags, while Walmart dominates on affordability through its national footprint. Dick's Sporting Goods is launching elevated outdoor retail concepts to compete directly with REI. Outdoor participation remains strong at 183 million Americans in 2025—but consumers are browsing online, comparing prices on Amazon, and buying less frequently. REI's January 2025 layoffs (180 full-time and 248 part-time positions) and October 2024 retail cuts signal that even the strongest incumbent cannot sustain pandemic-era unit economics. Consolidation is accelerating: smaller independent shops continue to close, and chains are pruning unprofitable store footprints while betting on e-commerce.
whats_growing: Outdoor recreation participation rose to record 183.2 million Americans in 2025, up 1.1% year-over-year, with hiking as the single most popular activity at 63.4 million participants. Specialty retail captured 46% of the hiking gear market share in 2024 because consumers still value curated selection and expert staff. Senior participation surged (+7.4% from 2024 to 2025), reaching 41.6% of ages 55+. Children ages 6-12 grew to 22.6 million outdoor participants. Resale and used-gear markets (REI Used, Patagonia's Common Threads eBay partnership) are emerging profit centers. Repair and sustainability-focused services appeal to younger, environmentally conscious customers.
whats_shrinking: Total retail sales for outdoor equipment declined 2.6% in 2025, ending a decade of near-zero growth. Equipment category sales (tents, kayaks, sleeping bags) contracted as pandemic-era excess inventory was cleared and travel demand shifted away from lengthy camping trips. Apparel sales stayed flat in 2024. Frequency of outdoor outings by Americans fell compared to pandemic peaks—people go outside less often even as total participation numbers hold up. Brick-and-mortar store counts have declined at 0.8% CAGR since 2020, with REI, Dick's, and smaller chains all trimming locations. Employment in the sector declined 0.4% annually from 2020-2025, indicating automation and tighter staffing models.
recent_developments: January 2025: REI laid off 180 full-time and 248 part-time employees and shuttered its unprofitable Experiences division (tours and classes), serving only 40,000 customers out of 23 million co-op members.
October 2024: REI cut 257 retail jobs as it restructured physical store footprint.
January 2024: REI laid off 357 employees (2.2% of workforce) amid worsening outdoor retail conditions and prior-year losses of 311 million dollars (2023) and 164.7 million dollars (2022).

2024-2025: Dick's Sporting Goods launched elevated outdoor retail concepts and House of Sport/Field House formats to compete with REI; Dick's Public Lands outdoor brand collapsed from eight stores to three.
Q4 2025: Amazon gained 0.3 points of unit share and 2.3 points of dollar share in outdoor equipment categories, driving online sales growth and premium private-label expansion.
2024-2025: Outdoor retail market overall saw 3% decline, with independent specialty retailers suffering double-digit declines.
outlook: The industry will remain under pressure through 2026-2027 as consumers normalize discretionary spending and economic uncertainty persists. Outdoor Foundation data from 2025 suggests demand will stabilize but not recover to pandemic peaks; participation is high but purchase frequency remains depressed. Market consolidation will accelerate: Dick's Sporting Goods and REI will continue closing underperforming stores while expanding e-commerce, while hundreds of smaller regional and local shops will exit. Big-box retailers (Walmart, Target, Costco) and Amazon will erode market share by capturing price-sensitive casual consumers. Specialty retailers that survive will be those that differentiate through expert staff, community events, in-house brands (REI's gear, Patagonia's vertical integration), repair/rental services, and used-gear marketplaces. Gross margins will remain compressed at 3-4% due to online price transparency and Amazon competition. Employment will continue declining as stores automate and shrink. Outdoor recreation participation itself will likely tick upward slightly through 2027, driven by seniors and children, but that tailwind will not translate to retail revenue growth unless operators can reverse per-customer spending trends.

title: Commercial Banking in the US
one_liner: Banks lend money to consumers and businesses while accepting deposits, earning the spread between what they pay depositors and charge borrowers.
overview: US commercial banking entered 2026 navigating a softer rate environment after the Fed's 100-basis-point cuts in late 2024-2025, lifting net interest margins to their highest levels since 2019. The industry dodged the regional-bank crisis that shook 2023 (SVB, Signature, First Republic failures) and is now focused on deposit competition and commercial real estate stress. With $1.5 trillion in revenue (2026), the sector is consolidating further while banks race to deploy AI at scale, moving beyond pilots into real operations.

key_stats.concentration: high - JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup collectively hold over 35% of deposits

how_it_makes_money: Banks earn net interest income by charging borrowers more on loans than they pay depositors on savings and checking accounts. They also generate fee income from depository services, overdrafts, advisory fees, and credit cards. Interest income now represents roughly 66% of revenue, with non-interest income at 34%.
cost_structure: Largest costs are deposit expenses (competing for customer funds in a high-rate environment), funding costs, credit losses on bad loans, technology infrastructure spending, and regulatory compliance. Deposit costs peaked in mid-2024 at 2.18% but fell to 3.85% by early 2025 as Fed rate cuts took hold, though costs began creeping back up through Q3 2025.
major_players: JPMorgan Chase (assets $3.64 trillion; 2025)
Bank of America (assets $2.62 trillion; 2025)
Wells Fargo (assets $1.71 trillion; 2025)
Citigroup (assets $1.76 trillion; 2025)
US Bancorp, Truist, PNC, Goldman Sachs Bank USA (secondary tier); regional consolidation ongoing post-2023 failures
current_dynamics: The industry is balancing three major pressures. First, the Fed's rate cuts (1.75 percentage points from September 2024 through Q4 2025) have compressed net interest margins even as they recovered to 3.39% by Q4 2025—highest since 2019—but the path forward is uncertain. Second, commercial real estate remains a latent risk: $1.26 trillion in CRE loans will mature by 2027, many originated at 4.3% now refinancing at 6.2%, while delinquencies hover near decade highs; banks are holding $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure. Third, deposit competition is fierce and deposit costs remain sticky—uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, suggesting clients are shopping rates. The 2023 failures (SVB in March, First Republic to JPMorgan in May, Signature in March) killed the mid-size bank consolidation wave temporarily but did not trigger systemic contagion, leaving the big four stronger relative to community banks.
whats_growing: Loan expansion accelerated to 5.9% annual growth by Q4 2025 (fastest in 11 quarters), driven by nondepository financial-institution loans, credit cards, and commercial real estate rebound. Deposit growth resumed with six consecutive quarterly increases. Net interest income improved as Fed cuts allowed deposit costs to fall faster than loan yields declined. AI deployment is ramping—47% of forward-looking banks now run AI agents in at least some areas, and 54% of Americans use mobile banking as their primary channel. M&A interest is rising as banks seek scale to justify technology spending.
whats_shrinking: Traditional branch employment dropped to 1.85 million by 2026 (down 2.2% in 2026 alone), the lowest since Q4 2019, as digital channels cannibalize walk-in traffic. Commercial and industrial loan demand is soft—many businesses deferred borrowing during high rates. Mortgage lending faces headwinds from rate sensitivity despite recent Fed cuts. The number of commercial banks fell to 3,712 in 2026 from 4,418 in 2022 (2.6% annual decline) as consolidation accelerates and smaller banks fail to compete on technology.
recent_developments: March 2023: Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failed in real-time bank run; Signature Bank shut down two days later; both were 16th and ~30th largest US banks
May 2023: First Republic Bank seized by FDIC, sold to JPMorgan Chase in fire sale; $229 billion in assets made it second-largest US bank failure ever
September 2024: Federal Reserve began rate-cutting cycle with first 0.50% cut; continued through Q4 2025 (total 1.75 percentage-point reduction)
Q4 2024–Q1 2025: Net interest margins compressed by declining deposit costs but improved loan yields; NIM bottomed and began recovery
Q4 2025: Commercial real estate lending rebounded 85% year-over-year; CBRE Lending Momentum Index jumped 13% in Q1 2025, stabilizing asset values after 2024 stress
Q4 2025: Banking industry net income reached $295.6 billion, up 10.2% from 2024; NIM hit 3.39% (highest since 2019)
outlook: The industry is entering 2026 with cautious optimism. The Fed is projected to cut rates to 3.125% by year-end 2026, likely keeping net interest income growth modest. Corporate borrowers should see lower rates, reversing the decline in commercial and industrial loans; AI and data-center spending are expected to keep debt demand relatively high. Deposit costs should continue to fall, but uninsured deposits remain volatile and sticky. The CRE maturity wall of $1.26 trillion in 2027 is the largest tail risk; expect elevated charge-offs throughout 2026, particularly among smaller and regional banks. Consolidation will accelerate as technology costs and regulatory burden push smaller players to merge or exit. Banks entering 2026 are emphasizing financial stability, client experience, and digital capabilities as competitive anchors. M&A is active but disruptive (typically 15–20 point NPS drop for 12–24 months post-deal). Overall growth should remain low single-digit; the mature industry is fighting for market share rather than expanding the pie.
themes: Commercial real estate maturity wall and stress
Deposit competition and sticky funding costs
AI scale deployment moving from pilot to operations
Consolidation wave driven by technology cost pressure
sources: S&P Global CRE maturity wall analysis (2024-2025)
Statista market share of leading US banks by assets and deposits (2024-2025)
Mordo Intelligence US Commercial Banking Market Report (2026)
one_sentence: US commercial banking is compressing margins as Fed rate cuts ease deposit costs, struggling with a looming $1.26 trillion commercial real estate maturity wall, and consolidating rapidly as smaller banks fall behind on technology and regulatory costs.

title: Portfolio Management in the US
one_liner: Portfolio managers invest client money across stocks, bonds, funds, and alternatives for a fee or commission.
overview: The US portfolio management industry generated roughly $340 billion in revenue in 2025, managing roughly $45-50 trillion in assets across mutual funds, ETFs, and alternatives. The industry is locked in a structural shift: passive ETFs and index funds now capture 55% of fund assets (2025), up from 34% a decade ago, while active equity mutual funds hemorrhaged over $1 trillion in 2025 alone. Fee compression is relentless—advisors managing $10 million portfolios now charge just 66 basis points (2026), down from higher historical rates. BlackRock reinforced its dominance with $14.04 trillion in AUM (end-2025) through strategic acquisitions (GIP, Preqin, HPS), while Vanguard ($11.6 trillion) and Fidelity ($7.1 trillion) round out the Big Three controlling about 50% of fund assets.

key_stats.profit_margin: 32-36% (2025, declining from 36.1% in 2022)
key_stats.concentration: high—top three firms (BlackRock, Vanguard, Fidelity) manage 50% of fund assets; top 15 managers control $64 trillion

how_it_makes_money: Portfolio managers charge fees based on assets under management (often 0.66% to 1.0% for wealthy clients, lower for institutional and passive products) or performance-based fees. Passive index funds and ETFs generate lower per-asset fees but compensate through scale and volume; active funds attempt to justify higher fees through outperformance but increasingly fail to do so.
cost_structure: Largest costs are employee salaries and benefits (especially for portfolio managers and analysts), technology infrastructure, regulatory compliance, and marketing. Salaries have grown faster than revenue due to competition for talent. Outsourcing of back-office and trading has partially offset wage pressures. Commission and trading costs are material for active managers.
major_players: BlackRock ($14.04 trillion AUM, 2025; acquired GIP Oct 2024, Preqin March 2025, HPS Investment Partners Dec 2024)
Vanguard ($11.6 trillion AUM, 2025; largest passive/index provider)
Fidelity Investments ($7.1 trillion AUM, 2025)
Capital Group ($1.5+ trillion, mostly American Funds active products)
Charles Schwab (over $80 billion in automated advisory via hybrid model)
JPMorgan Chase Asset Management
Goldman Sachs Asset Management
Morgan Stanley Investment Management
Lazard ($279 billion average AUM Q2 2026, up 17% YoY)
BNY Mellon Wealth Management ($2.1 trillion AUM March 2026)
current_dynamics: The industry is being reshaped by five forces. First, passive index funds and ETFs captured 55% of US mutual fund and ETF assets by 2025 (up from 53% in 2024 and 34% a decade ago), while active mutual funds faced $1+ trillion in net outflows in 2025, the steepest year of an 11-year exodus. Second, fee compression is accelerating: advisors managing $10 million portfolios charge 66 basis points (2026), and institutional clients demand even lower rates, squeezing margins. Third, alternatives and private markets are now generating over half the industry's revenue globally by 2030 projections; BlackRock's acquisition of HPS for $12 billion signals the shift toward higher-fee private credit and illiquid assets. Fourth, only 38% of active funds beat their passive peers after fees in 2025, down from 42% in 2024, forcing active managers to consolidate or specialize. Fifth, robo-advisors and hybrid advisory (human plus algorithm) now manage $1 trillion in US assets (2026), with incumbents like Vanguard Personal Advisor reaching $300 billion; this is pulling retail assets away from traditional advisors.
whats_growing: Passive ETFs and index funds (19% annual growth 2020-2024, $600+ billion inflows in 2025); private markets and alternatives ($29 trillion AUM by 2029); hybrid advisory models blending AI with human judgment; institutional demand for solutions products (target-date, liability-driven investments); BlackRock's market share through M&A; wealth preservation products for aging baby boomers; emerging-market exposure via globalization.
whats_shrinking: Active equity mutual funds (11 years of net outflows; $1+ trillion out in 2025); management fees on all assets (basis-point compression); profit margins (down 19% per AUM since 2018, another 9% decline expected by 2030); traditional advisory headcount as firms scale through technology; demand for high-fee active products among retail and institutional clients.
recent_developments: Preqin acquisition by BlackRock (March 2025) for £2.5 billion, extending data dominance in private markets
BlackRock's HPS Investment Partners acquisition ($12 billion, Dec 2024) expanding private credit footprint by 40% in private AUM
SEC report on rapid growth of active ETFs (Feb 2026): active ETFs grew 65% annually 2020-2024 vs. passive at 19%, yet still only 9% of total ETF assets
Robo-advisory market reach $1 trillion AUM in US (2026), with Vanguard Personal Advisor crossing $300 billion
Passive fund market share crosses 55% of US mutual fund and ETF assets (2025), active funds down to 45%
Moody's 2026 outlook: global AUM projected to grow 7% annually to $160 trillion by 2028; US market revenue expected flat to 2-3% growth
outlook: Through 2026-2027, the portfolio management industry will face a bifurcated market. Passive index funds will continue to claim growing share, driven by cost sensitivity and persistent active underperformance; expect passive to exceed 60% of AUM by 2027. Fee compression will persist, especially in wealth management: basis points will compress another 10-20 basis points for high-net-worth clients by 2027. Winners will be scale players like BlackRock, Vanguard, and Fidelity who can absorb margin pressure through volume and technology efficiency. Private markets will boom—institutional allocations to alternatives now routinely hit 20-30% of portfolios, up from single digits in the 2000s, and this shift will continue. Active managers with clear specializations or proven alpha will survive; generalists will consolidate or close. Technology disruption will accelerate: hybrid robo-advisory will capture 5-8% of retail AUM by 2027, and AI-driven portfolio optimization will become table stakes. Smaller independent managers with strong performance records will thrive by niche specialization, but the industry will be dominated by five to ten mega-platforms.
themes: passive-index-dominance: The structural shift from active to passive is now terminal; 55% of assets, 11-year exodus, unlikely to reverse
fee-compression-paradox: Revenue grows on market appreciation alone; margins fall as clients demand cheaper access
concentration-through-scale: BlackRock's $14T+ and M&A strategy consolidating data, private markets, and AUM in a few hands
alternatives-alpha-hunt: Institutions chasing private equity, hedge funds, and credit for returns passive equity won't deliver
margin-defense-through-tech: Robo-advisory and AI tools are the only lever left to sustain profitability as human advisory costs rise
hybrid-advisor-pivot: Pure robo failed; human-plus-algorithm now commands 50%+ of new fintech wealth flows

one_sentence: The US portfolio management industry is experiencing a permanent structural shift to low-cost passive products, squeezing margins while BlackRock consolidates dominance through acquisitions in private markets, forcing active managers to either specialize or disappear.

title: Soybean Processing
one_liner: A mature commodity processing industry converting soybeans into oil and meal, driven by a renewable diesel boom that's pushing crush volumes to record highs despite margin compression.
overview: The US soybean processing industry generated $54.1 billion in revenue in 2025, processing soybeans into oil for food and biofuels plus meal for livestock feed. Capacity is expanding aggressively to support renewable diesel production, with US crush forecast at record 2.54 billion bushels in 2025–26. However, profit margins have collapsed from historic highs of $2.00–$3.00/bushel in 2023 to a normalized $1.10–$1.50/bushel in 2025 as new plants come online and soybean meal surpluses weigh on prices.

key_stats.businesses: 143–150 processors (2025, mix of large and small operators)
key_stats.concentration: High: ADM ~36%, Bunge ~22%, top 4 account for ~65% (2021 baseline; likely similar 2025)

how_it_makes_money: Crushes soybeans to extract oil (45% of revenue) and meal (28% of revenue), plus specialty products (28%). Sells oil to food manufacturers for cooking oil and margarine, plus increasingly to renewable diesel producers. Sells meal to livestock feed manufacturers. Margins come from the difference between soybean input costs and combined oil+meal output prices.
cost_structure: Raw soybeans are ~70–75% of costs; labor ~8–10%; equipment, maintenance, storage, distribution make up remainder. High capital intensity (modern crush plants cost $200M–$300M+). Crush margins typically $1–$3 per bushel gross margin before fixed costs.
major_players: Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) – ~36% market share, multinational conglomerate
Bunge Limited – ~22% market share, global agricultural trader (acquired Viterra 2023)
Cargill Inc. – ~6% market share, privately held diversified agribusiness
Louis Dreyfus Company – international player opening Ohio facility (2024)
Ag Processing Inc. (AGP) – cooperative announcing new facility
SD Soybean Processors – new plant opened 2025
North Dakota Soybean Processors – new plant opened 2024
Others: 35–40% fragmented among smaller regional operators
current_dynamics: The renewable diesel boom is the defining force in 2025–26. The EPA's RVO mandates renewable fuel blending, creating nearly unlimited demand for soybean oil in renewable diesel production. This has triggered a 23% capacity expansion over three years, with over $6 billion invested in new crush facilities. Crush volumes hit record 2.54 billion bushels forecast for 2025–26, but the surge in meal output (as a byproduct of oil extraction) is flooding the market and crushing margins. Crush margins fell from $2–$3/bushel in 2023 to $1.10–$1.50/bushel in 2025 as four new major plants came online in North Dakota, Kansas, and elsewhere. China's 13% tariff (imposed 2018, still in place 2025) has reduced US soybean exports to China by 33% versus 2024, forcing reliance on domestic crush rather than global markets. Soybean prices themselves are volatile: peaked at $12.30/bu in early 2024, fell to $9.55 mid-August 2024, recovered to $10.30 end-of-2025, and remain around $11.60/bu in August 2026 despite oversupply concerns.
whats_growing: Soybean oil demand for renewable diesel production; crush capacity expansion (75M bushels/year online 2025, 114M in 2026); efficiency improvements (oil extraction rose from 17.9% to 19.8% over 60 years, now running above trend since 2020); new regional processing hubs in North Dakota, Kansas, and Ohio diversifying away from traditional Plains concentration; employment in new facilities.
whats_shrinking: Crush margins and per-unit profitability (down 50–60% from 2023 peak); utilization rates at existing plants (capacity expansion exceeding margin support); China soybean exports (down 33% YoY as of late 2025); domestic livestock feed demand growth (soybean meal seeing surplus pressure from crush byproducts); traditional premium products as commodity pressure increases.
recent_developments: 2024: Louis Dreyfus broke ground on new Ohio soybean-processing plant; North Dakota Soybean Processors opened Casselton facility; Incobrasa opened $250M Gilman, Illinois plant.

2025: ADM, AGP, SD Soybean Processors brought new facilities online; EPA finalized RVO mandates for 2026–27 mandating maximum-capacity renewable diesel production; 75M bushels/year new capacity came online.
August 2026: ADM announced upgrades to four soybean crush plants unlocking ~700,000 metric tons additional annual capacity; crush margins remained compressed at $1.10–$1.50/bu despite record volumes.
outlook: 2026–2027 outlook is split. Renewable diesel production is forecast to recover in 2026 after a 10% dip in 2025 (due to tax credit confusion), supporting sustained high crush volumes. New capacity additions will push U.S. crush toward 2.6–2.7 billion bushels by 2027. However, crush margins are unlikely to return to 2023 highs; industry expects a 'new normal' of $1.50–$2.00/bu as global soybean supply remains ample and South American competition intensifies. Soybean prices may drift slightly upward from current $11–$12/bu if global demand remains firm, but no supercycle expected. China trade remains chill with 13% tariffs still in place and purchases tied to bilateral trade deals (25M MT/year 2026–2028 agreed). The industry will consolidate further as smaller processors struggle with low margins; new regional players backed by government/cooperative support will survive. Long-term: soybean processing is mature with predictable low-single-digit revenue growth, but renewable fuel policy will remain a wild card for profitability.
themes: Renewable diesel boom driving record crush
China trade headwind and tariff risk
data_year: 2026 (current); 2025 most recent full year; 2024–2026 forward outlook
sources: American Soybean Association Crush Expansion Update (2025)
IBISWorld Soybean Processing Report (2021 baseline, 2026 employment data)
FarmDocDaily Illinois Soybean Processing Efficiency Study (August 2025)
one_sentence: Record soybean crushing driven by renewable diesel mandates is overwhelming the market with cheap meal and collapsing margins, forcing consolidation and efficiency plays among processors while China tariffs and global oversupply cap near-term profits.

title: Wheat, Barley & Sorghum Farming in the US
one_liner: A mature commodity industry facing margin pressure from drought, China tariff swings, and commodity price weakness despite export dependence and federal support.
overview: The US wheat, barley, and sorghum farming industry generated $16.2 billion in revenue in 2025, with growth slowing to 0.2% decline projected for 2026 as severe drought ravages the Plains and China's tariff retaliation crushes sorghum exports. Net farm income for grain farmers is under acute pressure from cost inflation and price weakness, with 2026 receipts falling 2.4% as wheat production drops to its lowest since 1965. Exports remain critical—accounting for 65-70% of revenue—but trade barriers and global competition have eroded margins to near-cycle lows.

key_stats.concentration: Low (fragmented family farms); hard red winter wheat dominates 38% of production mix

baseline_2022.growth: 5.3% (2022, bolstered by Ukraine war spike and pandemic nonperishable demand)

how_it_makes_money: Farmers grow wheat (78% of revenue), sorghum (14%), and barley (6%), selling directly to grain wholesalers, food processors, animal feed makers, and exporters. Exports account for 65-70% of revenue; domestic sales go to flour mills, breweries, and animal feed producers. Revenue is set by commodity prices, yields per acre, and planted acreage. Government subsidies provide a cushion against volatility. Profit is thin because grain is a homogeneous commodity with minimal differentiation.
cost_structure: Major costs are land, machinery (harvesters, tractors, silos), seed, fertilizer, fuel, and labor. Farms are highly capital-intensive but employ family labor; average establishment is 1.3 employees. Depreciation and maintenance of equipment are substantial. Input costs have risen sharply since 2022. Weather, pests, and irrigation are uncontrollable cost drivers.
major_players: Family farms and owner-operators (95%+ of industry); no single corporate entity dominates
Kansas and North Dakota lead in acreage (15.6% and 14.5% respectively, 2022); Plains region accounts for 39% of US wheat acreage
Downstream: Archer Daniels Midland (ADM), Bunge, grain wholesalers (Corn, Wheat & Soybean Wholesaling)
current_dynamics: The industry is in acute structural stress. Wheat production fell 29% from 2025 to 2026 (1.402B to 990M bushels), driven by the worst Plains drought since records began, with 63% of winter wheat in drought areas as of June 2026. Yield plummeted to 46.7 bu/acre from 54.9 in 2025—the lowest in over a decade. China's 44-49% tariffs imposed April 2025 decimated sorghum exports (down 97% to China by July 2025), though modest relief arrived in November 2025 when Beijing paused some tariffs. Wheat prices have crashed from the 2022 Ukraine-war spike ($219/ton baseline) to $5.00-5.12 per bushel in early 2026—a 6-year low—because global supplies are bloated and demand is soft. Farm income is collapsing: wheat receipts fell from $11.2B (2024) to $9.86B (2025) to $9.5B (2026). Subsidies, once a reliable safety net, face congressional pressure for reductions. The industry remains heavily export-dependent, making it vulnerable to currency fluctuations and geopolitical trade wars.
whats_growing: Precision agriculture adoption (genetically modified seeds, resistant traits) is slowly increasing yield per acre where conditions allow, though 2026 drought negated this edge. Domestic demand for nonperishable wheat-based products remains stable and slightly above pre-pandemic levels. Animal feed demand from livestock is gradually recovering. Barley's niche in craft beer and malt beverages is expanding at a modest single-digit rate.
whats_shrinking: Planted acreage for wheat and barley is declining as farmers shift to higher-margin crops or abandon marginal land. Sorghum exports to China evaporated (97% collapse to that market by July 2025) and have not fully recovered despite tariff relief. Total wheat production is in free fall—down 29% year-over-year in 2026. Per-capita wheat flour consumption in the US has been flat to slightly negative for years. Government subsidies for grain farming are being scrutinized and are expected to decline. Number of farms is declining at -0.2% annually; small operations are being pushed out by consolidation.
recent_developments: June 2026: USDA forecasts US winter wheat production at 1.048 billion bushels (down 25% from 2025), the lowest since 1965/66; drought devastates Plains with Kansas yields projected at 37 bu/acre vs. 51 in 2025.
April 2025: China imposes 44-49% tariffs on US sorghum, wheat, corn, and soybeans; US sorghum exports to China collapse 97% by July.
February 2026: Wheat farm price rises to $5.12/bu (up from $5.01 in January), but remains a 6-year low as global stocks swell and US ending stocks hit 6-year highs.

November 2025: China pauses 24% retaliatory tariff and rolls back duties of up to 15% on some US ag shipments, retaining 10% base levy; modest sorghum and wheat purchases resume but remain well below pre-tariff levels.
February 2026: USDA lowers net farm income forecast to $153.4B (2026), down 0.7% from 2025; wheat receipts fall $200M (2.4%) due to lower volume sold.
Mid-2025: Drought Monitor shows 63% of US winter wheat acreage in drought areas; Southern Great Plains in extreme drought, particularly panhandle regions.
outlook: The 2026-2027 outlook is bleak near-term, improving slowly thereafter. Wheat production will likely stabilize around 1.0-1.2B bushels (well below the 1.4B average of past decade) as drought persists in the Plains. Prices are expected to remain depressed at $4.80-5.20/bu through 2026 as global inventories unwind slowly. Sorghum exports to China may recover gradually if tariffs remain stable at 10%, but will not return to pre-2025 levels given substitution by Australian and Argentine suppliers. Farm income will stay under pressure: input costs are sticky high while commodity prices are structural lows, squeezing margins. The number of farms will continue to shrink as unprofitable small operations exit or consolidate. Government subsidies may decline if Congress prioritizes deficit reduction, removing a key profit buffer. Yield per acre will rebound when drought breaks, but planted acreage will remain constrained by economics. Long-term (2027+), the industry faces secular headwinds: per-capita wheat consumption is flat, China remains a tariff wildcard, and climate volatility is the new normal.
themes: Climate risk and drought-driven production collapse
Export dependence and geopolitical tariff exposure
Subsidy-reliant family farming under consolidation pressure
Technology adoption (precision ag) at odds with capital constraints
Trade war collateral damage (China retaliatory tariffs on sorghum)
sources: USDA Economic Research Service — Wheat Outlook June 2026
USDA Economic Research Service — Farm Sector Income Forecast February 2026
USDA World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) June 2026
Oklahoma Farm Report — Sorghum Exports China July 2025
NPR — China Tariffs on US Farm Exports March 2025
Brownfield Ag News — USDA Winter Wheat Production Forecast June 2026
Farm Progress — Plains Drought and Winter Wheat June 2026
one_sentence: Wheat, barley, and sorghum farming—a mature, export-driven, family-farm-dominated commodity sector—is reeling from a perfect storm of severe Plains drought (production down 29%), China's retaliatory sorghum tariffs, and six-year-low prices, pushing net farm income into structural decline despite federal support.

title: Waste-to-Energy Plant Operation
one_liner: A lean, consolidated utility that converts municipal solid waste into electricity and heat, facing growth headwinds from renewable natural gas, landfill innovation, and electricity price volatility—but gaining momentum from data center power demand and landfill methane regulations.
overview: The US waste-to-energy plant operation industry consists of only 64 establishments operating across 21 states, generating $1.4 billion in revenue annually (2025). The sector has declined 1.3% annually from 2020-2025 due to stagnant electricity prices and construction slowdowns, but faces a turning point driven by rising data center energy demand, methane reduction mandates taking effect in 2027, and the industry leader Covanta's 2024 rebrand to Reworld as part of a broader pivot toward diversified waste solutions. Employment stands at 1,870 workers (2025), down 5.1% over five years, reflecting capital-intensive operations and facility consolidation.

key_stats.profit_margin: 18-25% EBITDA (2025), compared to 8.7% net profit margin (2021 baseline)
key_stats.concentration: High—9 businesses, 64 establishments; Covanta/Reworld and Wheelabrator Technologies dominate; scattered across 21 states with concentration in Mid-Atlantic (30.7%) and New England (21.3%)

baseline_2022.growth: -4.3% CAGR (2016-2021) due to COVID-19 and low electricity prices

how_it_makes_money: Revenue flows from two streams: (1) tipping fees paid by municipalities for waste disposal and treatment (primary revenue, ~77% of contracts); (2) electricity and steam sales to manufacturers, utilities, and district heating systems (remaining ~23%). Operators also recover ferrous and nonferrous metals, which added about 500-600 kWh per ton of waste processed in 2022. Long-term municipal contracts typically index to retail electricity prices.
cost_structure: Highly capital intensive—plants cost $200-400 million to build and require continuous investment in pollution control equipment to meet Industrial Emissions Directive limits (nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, heavy metals, dioxins). Operating costs include staff wages (2,423 workers across 64 plants = high per-facility ratios), air pollution control systems, equipment maintenance, and electricity/fuel for internal plant operations (~25% of gross generation). Rising steel prices inflate equipment costs; lower electricity prices compress margins directly since 77% of output is sold electricity.
major_players: Reworld (formerly Covanta Holding Corp, rebranded April 2024) — 37 thermomechanical treatment facilities, processed 20.8 million tons waste in 2024, 5,000+ employees; five service lines (ReDirect360, ReKiln Fuels, ReDrop, ReMove, ReCredit); owned by EQT Infrastructure since 2021
Wheelabrator Technologies Inc. — multi-facility operator; South Broward facility acquired by FCC Environmental Services (Q2 2025), signaling market entry by global player

FCC Environmental Services — acquired Wheelabrator South Broward (Q2 2025); operates 12 international WTE facilities processing 824,000 tons annually; marks first major cross-border M&A in US WTE sector (2025)
current_dynamics: The industry stands at an inflection point. On the demand side, data center electricity consumption surged 17% in 2025 and AI-focused data centers are tripling power use, creating new contract opportunities for reliable baseload power; the tech sector signed 40% of all corporate renewable energy PPAs in 2025. On the supply side, landfill gas capture is intensifying competition—598 landfill gas systems now produce 64% of US renewable natural gas (2025), with 20 new projects launched in 2025 adding 39.9 Bcf biogas capacity; an updated methane rule (effective 2027) will push 705 additional landfills toward capture. Reworld's 2024 rebrand signals industry consolidation and shift away from pure incineration toward materials recovery and alternative fuels; the company processes 20.8 million tons annually and targets 25% more recycling/reuse by 2025. However, electricity price volatility persists—EBITDA margins range 18-25% when indexed (vs. landfill margins of 25-30%), and rising interest rates have slowed construction waste flows. Regulatory winds are shifting in the industry's favor: nine US states are drafting policies mandating landfill methane capture, and 31 states incorporate WTE into renewable portfolio standards, but environmental concerns about incinerator emissions (dioxins, heavy metals) remain a political barrier in densely populated regions.
whats_growing: Demand from data centers for renewable, dispatchable power (17% electricity growth in 2025); regulatory mandates for landfill methane capture (updated rule 2027); alternative technologies—pyrolysis market at 42.7% share of waste-to-fuel conversions, with Enerkem's Ecoplanta (Spain, Jan 2025) converting waste to methanol; materials recovery and engineered fuels (Reworld's ReKiln Fuels line expanding); workforce expansion (Reworld workforce up 17% since 2020, female employees +43%); international expansion (FCC Environmental enters US market, 2025).
whats_shrinking: Construction waste streams (interest rate hikes slowed nonresidential construction); traditional mass-burn incineration market share (Reworld explicitly shifting away); employment in pure WTE operations (1,870 workers down 5.1% over five years, though Reworld added headcount); competitive tipping fee positions (renewable natural gas from landfill methane now competing directly on carbon offsets and renewable energy credits).
recent_developments: April 2024: Covanta rebrands to Reworld under EQT Infrastructure ownership; shifts to regionalized structure with five service lines emphasizing materials recovery and alternative fuels over pure incineration
June 2025: FCC Environmental Services acquires Wheelabrator South Broward facility; marks entry of global waste operator (12 international facilities) into US WTE market
January 2025: Enerkem's Ecoplanta project (Spain) receives approval for waste-to-methanol conversion; signals industry pivot toward advanced chemical recycling
August 2025: Updated EPA landfill methane rule takes effect; new capture standards, third-party satellite leak monitoring, 705 additional landfills now candidates for gas projects

2025 Full Year: 20 new landfill gas projects launched, adding 39.9 Bcf biogas capacity (75% of all US biogas growth); RNG market now 64% supplied by landfill gas (598 active facilities), intensifying competition
2025 Reworld Sustainability Report: Company processed 20.8 million tons, achieved 39 million metric tons CO2e avoided, targets 25% more recycling by 2025 baseline
outlook: Cautiously optimistic. The sector is forecast to grow 1.1% annually through 2026 (IBISWorld baseline) but diverges into two futures. Short term (2025-2026): data center demand for renewable baseload power creates contract opportunities; updated methane rules push landfills to compete via RNG, not WTE displacement (complementary for first 3-5 years). Medium term (2027-2030): advanced technologies (pyrolysis, gasification) reach scale if capital costs fall; 31 state RPS provisions continue to favor WTE. Risks: (1) landfill methane capture at 705 new sites will saturate RNG supply and push down carbon credits by 2028, shrinking WTE revenue upside; (2) construction activity remains sluggish unless rates drop; (3) electricity price volatility constrains 18-25% EBITDA margins; (4) political opposition to incinerator emissions in population-dense Mid-Atlantic region may limit new plant siting. Revenue likely plateaus near $1.4-1.5 billion through 2026 unless data center contracting accelerates or advanced pyrolysis achieves commercial scale in non-recyclable plastics (currently 5% of US feedstock).
themes: Renewable baseload power for data centers amid AI boom
Landfill methane capture competing with incineration
Advanced chemical recycling and pyrolysis emerging
Regulatory tailwind: methane mandates and RPS provisions
Capital intensity and EBITDA margin compression from electricity volatility
sources: IBISWorld US Waste-to-Energy Plant Operation Industry Analysis (2025)
American Biogas Council Landfill Gas and Renewable Natural Gas Report (2025)
Waste Dive: Covanta/Reworld Rebrand and FCC Wheelabrator Acquisition (2024-2025)
IEA Data Center Electricity Use Report (2025)
Market Data Forecast US Waste-to-Energy Market (2025-2026)
Grand View Research Waste-to-Energy Technology Industry (2025-2026)
EPA Landfill Methane Outreach Program and Updated Rule (2025-2027)
one_sentence: The US waste-to-energy plant operation industry—a $1.4 billion, nine-company sector operating 64 plants across 21 states—is at a turning point: data center demand for renewable baseload power and updated methane regulations (2027) create growth opportunities, but direct competition from landfill gas capture and advanced pyrolysis technologies, combined with electricity price volatility and construction slowdowns, constrain margins to 18-25% EBITDA and employment to 1,870 workers (down 5% over five years).

title: Wind Turbine Installation
one_liner: Installation and construction services for onshore and offshore wind farms face a boom-bust cycle driven by federal tax credits, interconnection backlogs, and shifting policy certainty.
overview: The US wind turbine installation industry is experiencing a surge in 2025-2026 after years of volatility. Market size reached $162 billion in 2025 and is growing at 4.18% annually through 2034. The industry installs utility-scale turbines, assemblies, transmission systems, and provides maintenance on existing wind farms. Growth is heavily driven by the Inflation Reduction Act's extended tax credits, though new federal policy threatens to accelerate the phase-out after July 2026.

key_stats.employees: 28,400 new technicians needed annually 2022-2026; 49.9% growth in technician roles 2024-2034
key_stats.profit_margin: 12-20% net profit on turbine manufacturing; installation margins volatile
key_stats.concentration: GE Vernova and Vestas control 93% of US market (2025)

how_it_makes_money: Installation services account for the bulk of revenue: project development (3.6%), turbine assembly (10.4%), transportation (4.5%), and electrical infrastructure (14.7%). Maintenance of existing turbines (66.8%) is now the fastest-growing segment as new capacity additions slow. Onshore work dominates but offshore projects generate 4x the installation revenue per kilowatt.
cost_structure: CAPEX ranges $1,150-1,800 per kilowatt. Installation labor is the second-largest cost after turbines themselves. Fixed costs include site surveying, foundations, roads, and electrical interconnection. Operating costs average $190,000/month per farm in Year 1. Supply-chain pressures and transportation costs for massive turbine components drive margins. Domestic content mandates (45-50% for 2025-2026) increase labor costs.
major_players: GE Vernova (5.8 GW installed 2025; US market co-leader)
Vestas (12.9 GW installed 2025; global leader; dominant in US)
Siemens Gamesa (5.4 GW installed 2025)
Nordex Group (7.7 GW installed 2025)
Envision (4.2 GW installed 2025)
Chinese manufacturers (Goldwind, Windey, Mingyang, SANY; dominates globally)
current_dynamics: The industry is caught between opportunity and policy whiplash. Installations surged to 7.7 GW expected for 2025 (36% above 2024's 4 GW) as developers rushed to claim tax credits before December 31 expiration deadlines. However, the Trump administration's December 2025 stop-work orders on five offshore projects (5.8 GW combined) and August federal pause have cost Ørsted $1.5 million per day and triggered 2,000-job cuts. Interconnection queue times now stretch 4-9 years, with 220 GW of wind capacity in queues facing median 5-year waits. Onshore wind remains viable economically (LCOE $26-54/MWh in 2026), but offshore expansion is stalled. Regional shifts are dramatic: the West dominates 2026 installations (64% of new capacity), while the Midwest leads 2027 (40%+). Domestic content rules and prevailing wage requirements for IRA credits add 15-25% cost premiums. Supply chains stabilized post-COVID but face new tariff and labor pressures.
whats_growing: Maintenance and operations (66.8% of revenue, expanding): as aging turbine parks require gearbox replacements (10% of turbine cost each), rewiring, and blade repairs. Onshore projects remain strong through 2027, with 10.7 GW (2026) and 12.7 GW (2027) forecasted. Technician wages growing: median $64,120 (2025), up from $57,860 (2023); offshore roles pay 20-30% premiums. Workforce demand: 628,000 technicians needed by 2030. Regional expansion in Midwest and West. Domestic turbine manufacturing reviving under IRA (domestic content mandates).
whats_shrinking: Offshore wind projects in federal pause (5 projects halted Dec 2025; $679M in funding cancelled). Interconnection availability is de facto shrinking: 76 GW of wind with draft agreements can't reach operations. New business formation slowing due to policy uncertainty and consolidation (top 3 firms control 93% US market). Profit margins squeezed by supply-chain costs, tariffs, and labor inflation. Small-firm participation declining: entry barriers (permit complexity, interconnection waits, capital requirements) pushing consolidation. 2024 was lowest installation year since 2013 (4 GW); projects are withdrawing from queues at ~80% rate under current timelines.
recent_developments: December 2025: Federal pause on five offshore wind projects (Vineyard Wind 1, Sunrise Wind, Revolution Wind, Empire Wind 1, Coastal Virginia; 5.8 GW total). Ørsted stops construction; $1.5M/day costs. Affects 2,000+ jobs.
September 2025: Judge lifts Trump pause on Revolution Wind; project resumes partial operations after August stop-work order.
August 2025: Ørsted receives stop-work order for Revolution Wind. Announces 2,000-job cuts (~25% of workforce) citing US market uncertainty.

July 2026 deadline: IRA production tax credit (PTC) and investment tax credit (ITC) accelerate phase-out. Projects must begin construction by July 5, 2026 and be placed in service by Dec 31, 2027 to claim credit. Domestic content rises to 50% (wind) / 35% (offshore).
Q3 2025: Clean Energy Production Tax Credit replaces traditional PTC; wind rate $0.0275/kWh (2023 value) with prevailing wage requirements for projects over 1 MW.
2025 installations: 7.7 GW forecasted (51% in Q4 rush); 2026 projected 10.7 GW; 2027 projected 12.7 GW.
outlook: 2026-2027 will be the peak years under current IRA rules before the July 2026 construction deadline creates a cliff. Onshore installations expected to hit 10.7 GW (2026) and 12.7 GW (2027), then decline as credits phase out. Offshore wind remains highly uncertain: 5.9 GW projected by 2029 IF federal policy stabilizes, but current moratorium and military radar concerns could extend delays. Interconnection queues will remain the binding constraint: even strong permitting won't help if grid access takes 4-9 years. Maintenance revenue will stabilize the industry post-2027 as new capacity slows and aging fleets require work. Regional diversity will increase (West 2026, Midwest 2027, Texas 2028). Labor will remain tight and expensive (technician wages up 10-15% annually through 2030). Consolidation continues: only GE Vernova and Vestas have capital and scale to weather policy swings. Profitability margins under pressure from tariffs, domestic content mandates, and wage inflation. Long-term (2030+): industry growth resumes only if transmission infrastructure expands dramatically and offshore costs fall 30-40% from current levels.
themes: Policy volatility and tax-credit cliffs drive boom-bust cycles
Interconnection bottlenecks starve grid access despite strong capacity
Offshore expansion halted by federal pause and radar concerns
Domestic content mandates and prevailing wage rules raise costs 15-25%
Technician labor shortage driving wages up and regional redistribution
Consolidation: top 2 firms control 93% of US market
