title: Dollar & Variety Stores in the US
one_liner: The dollar store industry is a mature, consolidating retail sector anchored by value-seeking consumers across all income levels, now under pressure from tariffs, organized theft, and intensifying competition from supercenters.
overview: The US dollar and variety stores industry reached $123.5 billion in 2026, up 1.4% annually from 2021-2026—a sharp slowdown from the pandemic-era growth. Dollar General and Dollar Tree dominate a market with roughly 9,400 businesses operating over 39,000 locations. The industry has shifted from a low-income refuge to a destination for middle- and higher-income shoppers seeking value, driven by persistent inflation and economic uncertainty. However, tariffs, organized retail crime, and encroachment from Walmart (which operates within five miles of 87% of Dollar Tree stores) have created structural headwinds.

key_stats.concentration: High—Dollar General and Dollar Tree control majority share; Dollar Tree holds 16,500+ stores

how_it_makes_money: The industry retails general merchandise (apparel, hardware, home goods) and consumables (groceries, toiletries, beauty products, drugs) at steep discounts. Groceries now represent ~21% of revenue (2026), up from 17% in 2022. The model depends on high volume, thin margins (4-5%), and fast inventory turnover. Proprietary store brands alongside national brands widen appeal to higher-income shoppers. Multi-price-point formats (e.g., Dollar Tree's $1.25/$3/$5 tiers) allow retailers to capture both budget-conscious and middle-class households. E-commerce and omnichannel partnerships (DoorDash, local delivery) are emerging but still minor revenue sources. Retail media and advertising networks are nascent growth channels.
cost_structure: Labor is the largest cost pressure. Entry-level store associates earn $10-$15/hour at Dollar General (2025), with assistant managers at $15-$18/hour. Dollar General employs ~8 people per store and faces chronic understaffing, high turnover, and wage pressure from state minimum-wage increases (New York $16/hour, 2025). Tariffs have sharply raised cost-of-goods sold since 2024; most merchandise is imported from Asia (textiles, small appliances, toys). Supply-chain expenses remain elevated. Real estate leases are relatively low-cost due to small footprints. Technology investment (POS, inventory control, AI loss prevention) has accelerated to combat organized retail crime and inventory shrinkage, which cost U.S. retailers $90 billion in 2025.
major_players: Dollar General Corporation (largest market share; $42.7 billion sales FY2025)
Dollar Tree Stores, Inc. (16,500+ stores including Family Dollar; $9,000+ stores in multi-price format)
Five Below (higher-end discount; 5.2% traffic growth 2024-2025)
Five & Below (growing fast-casual version)
current_dynamics: The industry is locked between two opposing forces. On the demand side, persistent inflation and wage stagnation have made dollar stores the default destination for low-income households and an attractive "trade-down" venue for middle-income shoppers—a behavioral shift that proved structural in 2024-2025. On the supply side, tariffs (especially on Asian imports), organized retail crime (ORC), and labor-cost inflation are eating margins. Simultaneously, Walmart and Target have weaponized their size to undercut dollar stores on price while offering fresher produce and prepared foods, pulling away both price-sensitive and aspirational shoppers. Dollar stores are responding by remodeling stores, expanding fresh produce (DG Fresh now in ~7,000 locations, 2025), and ramping up omnichannel (e-commerce partnerships, retail media). Yet consumer sentiment collapsed to 48.2 in May 2026 (a record low), signaling that shoppers' financial strain is worsening rather than improving. The industry is stable but no longer growing—it's optimizing for a stagnant or slowly declining consumer base.
whats_growing: Grocery assortment (especially fresh produce, frozen foods, and packaged salads) and higher-priced categories that capture middle-income shoppers. Dollar Tree's 3.0 format (multi-price-point, 5,300+ locations converted) and Dollar General's remodeling/expansion strategy (450 new stores, 4,250 remodels planned for 2026) are growing. Omnichannel capabilities (e-commerce, delivery partnerships, retail media networks) are nascent but growing. Store count is still expanding—39,000+ locations in 2025, up ~5,000 since 2021—but growth is slowing. Profit margins edged up in early 2025 (gross margin +61 basis points in Q1 2025) due to operational efficiency gains and labor investments in store presentation.
whats_shrinking: Foot traffic is declining despite higher per-visit spending. The "essential" customer base is stabilizing rather than expanding. Fresh-produce rollout has slowed dramatically: DG added produce to 1,800+ stores in 2022-2023, but only ~300 in 2025. Consolidation of smaller chains continues; Family Dollar (Dollar Tree's subsidiary) was sold off to a private entity in July 2025 at a loss, signaling that even large players cannot profitably operate every banner under current conditions. Market growth has decelerated from 3.5% (2017-2022) to 1.4% (2021-2026)—a clear signal of industry maturation and market saturation.
recent_developments: May 2026: Consumer sentiment index hit record low of 48.2; Dollar General CEO reports customers say their financial situation has worsened.
May 2026: 87% of Dollar Tree stores are within five miles of a Walmart; tariffs and inflation eroding value perception.
Q1 2025: Dollar General reports 5.2% sales growth and +61 basis point gross margin expansion from $150 million labor and store remodeling investment.
2025-2026: DG Fresh produce rollout continues to ~7,000 stores total (slow pace relative to 2023 momentum); 450 new DG stores and 4,250 remodels planned for 2026.
July 2025: Dollar Tree sells Family Dollar subsidiary to private entity at a loss, signaling exit from less-profitable banner.
2025-2026: Organized retail crime remains elevated; retailers report 57% rise in ORC from 2022-2023, though shoplifting incidents declined 12.4% in 2025 due to AI loss-prevention tech.
outlook: The industry will remain stable but slow-growing through 2027. Consumer deleveraging, tariff pass-through, and wage pressures will keep margins under stress. Consolidation will accelerate; smaller chains and single-unit operators will exit. The two dominant players (Dollar General, Dollar Tree) will consolidate market share and invest heavily in store experience, fresh food, and omnichannel to defend against Walmart's gravity. Middle-income "trade-down" behavior will persist if inflation stays elevated and wage growth lags; if consumer confidence recovers sharply, dollar stores may see a reversal. Store count will grow modestly (1-2% annually) through new openings and acquisitions of struggling regional chains, but per-store productivity will decline as foot traffic remains soft. E-commerce and retail media will become meaningful but non-dominant revenue sources by 2028. Profit margins are unlikely to expand materially unless tariffs ease or labor cost inflation moderates.
themes: Tariff shock—import cost inflation eroding the value prop
Consumer deleveraging—middle-class trade-down structural, low-income strain deepening
Consolidation—large players defend turf, small chains exit
Omnichannel imperative—stores must offer delivery, pickup, and e-commerce or lose traffic
Organized retail crime—theft and shrinkage forcing tech investment and security spending
Margin compression—labor, tariffs, and loss prevention eating into thin 4-5% operating margins
data_year: 2026 (latest market size and earnings reports; 2025 partial year data for growth trends and consumer behavior)

title: Ethnic Supermarkets
one_liner: A consolidating $59B US retail niche squeezed by mainstream supermarket competition and tariff costs.
one_sentence: The US ethnic supermarkets industry is stalling at near-zero growth (0.1% in 2025) as mainstream grocers capture demand with private-label ethnic foods and online delivery scales.
overview: The US ethnic supermarkets industry reached $58.9 billion in 2025 and is projected to remain flat at $58.9 billion in 2026, marking nearly stalled growth after post-pandemic peaks. About 16,042 ethnic supermarket businesses operate in the US as of 2025, down 1.3% from 2024, reflecting consolidation as small independents struggle. Large regional chains like Vallarta Supermarkets, H Mart, and 99 Ranch are expanding into new markets and opening flagship locations, but growth is offset by business-count declines. The industry faces simultaneous pressure from tariff-driven cost inflation, competition from mainstream grocers adding ethnic sections, and the rise of online grocery delivery that large ethnic players cannot match with local logistics.

key_stats.profit_margin: ~3.3% (2022 baseline; 2025 data not yet published)
key_stats.concentration: Low to medium; consolidating toward larger regional chains (Vallarta, H Mart, 99 Ranch); business count declining 11.3% annually

how_it_makes_money: Ethnic supermarkets generate revenue by selling culturally tailored grocery assortments—specialty meats, fresh produce, international staple ingredients (flour, spices, oils), frozen foods, beverages, and non-food items—at higher price points than mainstream grocers due to sourcing complexity and community loyalty. Product mix (2022): Other Food Items (25.4%), Meats (23.4%), Produce (22%), Nonfood Items (17.2%), Dairy (4.3%), Frozen Foods (3.8%), Beverages (3.9%). Large chains (Vallarta, H Mart, 99 Ranch) add food halls and restaurants to increase per-store revenue and build destination appeal. Community sponsorship and cultural events generate repeat customer loyalty, particularly in Hispanic and Asian immigrant communities.
cost_structure: High labor costs (grocery is labor-intensive at ~15-18% of revenue); significant food waste in fresh categories; rent/occupancy for prime urban/metro locations; wholesale sourcing from specialized distributors (higher per-unit costs than mainstream chains); tariff exposure on imported ingredients (Asian noodles, Mexican spices, Vietnamese fish sauce); energy and refrigeration; transportation/logistics constraints compared to large national chains. 2025-2026 tariff environment significantly elevated costs: 647% increase in tariff collections on food/ag products in first four months of 2025 vs. 2024, passed partially to consumers but also absorbed. Small operators lack scale to negotiate supplier terms, widening margin gap vs. large chains.
major_players: Vallarta Supermarkets (63 CA + 1 AZ store as of 2026; family-owned Hispanic chain expanding nationally)
H Mart (expanding East Coast and South; building 100,000 sq ft flagship in Bay Area)
99 Ranch Market (entering major markets: NYC Flushing, Queens July 2025; Las Vegas expansion planned)
Northgate (still growing despite immigration headwinds)
Patel Brothers (Indian grocery; expanding to Austin and other US markets)
T&T Supermarket (Canada-based Asian grocer; planning US expansion starting 2026, Irvine CA)
Mitsuwa Marketplace (Japanese; smaller footprint, long-standing presence)

Mainstream competitors taking share: Kroger (Hispanic + global ethnic private labels since late 2023, expanded 2026), Albertsons (private label), Walmart (local demographic stocking), Amazon/Whole Foods (delivery + specialty)
current_dynamics: Growth has collapsed to 0.1% in 2025 from 1.9% in 2024, despite favorable demographics. Tariff shock—647% increase in collections on food/ag in early 2025 vs. 2024—is squeezing margins from already-thin 3% levels; ethnic supermarkets source more specialty imports (Asian noodles, spices, fish sauce) than mainstream competitors, making them vulnerable. Business count is falling 11.3% annually, a hidden crisis: small independents cannot compete with large chains on price or with Amazon/Walmart on delivery. Mainstream supermarkets (Kroger, Albertsons) have successfully captured ethnic demand through private-label expansion, narrowing the unique value ethnic specialists once held. Immigration enforcement crackdowns in early 2025-2026 dented foot traffic in LA and other immigrant-heavy cities, adding labor scarcity to cost pressures. Large regional chains (Vallarta, H Mart, 99 Ranch) are expanding with flagships and food halls, pursuing scale and destination appeal, but they cannot build delivery networks at Amazon/Walmart pace.
whats_growing: Large ethnic supermarket chains are expanding geographically: Vallarta planned up to 15 stores over the next decade after opening first Arizona store January 2026; H Mart opened Florida's first in Orlando September 2025 and is building flagship 100k sq ft location in Bay Area (late 2026 construction); 99 Ranch entered NYC (Flushing, July 2025, 37k sq ft with 23-vendor food hall) and planned Las Vegas. Demand from younger, non-traditional ethnic customers remains strong (Mintel data: 9 of 10 adults aged 25-34 cook ethnic food at home monthly). Online ethnic food sales (broader category, not just supermarkets) growing 9.12% annually. PepsiCo's $1.2B acquisition of Siete Foods (October 2024) reflects Big Food confidence in ethnic/Mexican-American CPG. Regional chains betting on experience (food halls, restaurants, community events) rather than price to differentiate.
whats_shrinking: Small, independent ethnic supermarkets are disappearing: business count fell 11.3% annually over five years to 2025. Specialty demand migration to mainstream channels eroding ethnic supermarket competitive moat; Kroger's ethnic private labels (late 2023 Hispanic line, 2026 global expansion with Korean/Chinese options) take margin-rich specialty sales and make them commodity. Store-level growth now negative even as ethnic populations grow, indicating market share loss to mainstream and online. Niche sourcing advantage diminishing as Amazon/Whole Foods enter specialty foods and as suppliers build direct-to-consumer e-commerce. Immigration enforcement headwinds reduced foot traffic in Hispanic-dominant areas in early 2025-2026. Old-format independent groceries with no food hall, restaurant, or e-commerce presence losing customers to both large ethnic chains (which invest in experience) and mainstream alternatives (which now stock ethnic SKUs).
recent_developments: October 2024: PepsiCo acquires Siete Foods (Mexican-American CPG) for $1.2 billion, Big Food's bet on ethnic foods
Late 2023 onwards: Kroger launches Hispanic-inspired private label line; expands 2026 with Korean bulgogi, Chinese mandarin chicken, global meals
January 2026: Vallarta Supermarkets opens first Arizona store (Glendale, 49k sq ft); plans up to 15 stores over next decade
July 2025: 99 Ranch Market opens flagship in Flushing, Queens (37k sq ft, 23-vendor food hall); plans Las Vegas expansion
September 2025: H Mart opens first Florida location (Orlando); planning Bay Area flagship (100k sq ft, late 2026)
2025-2026: Immigration enforcement crackdowns reduce foot traffic in LA and other immigrant-heavy cities; labor scarcity adds pressure
2025-2026: Amazon invests $4 billion to triple same-day delivery network by 2026, now offering perishables; Whole Foods pivot accelerates (closed all Fresh/Go stores January 2026)
July 2026: Kroger announces $1.7 billion acquisition of Giant Eagle, industry consolidation play
outlook: The industry will grow modestly (1-2% annually through 2027) but will not expand in business count; consolidation toward fewer, larger chains will continue. Tariff uncertainty is expected to persist into 2026 and beyond, keeping cost pressure elevated; ethnic supermarkets with higher import exposure will see tighter margins than mainstream competitors. Large, capitalized chains (Vallarta, H Mart, 99 Ranch) with food halls and restaurants will thrive by creating destination experiences and capturing scale economies; small independents will continue to exit. Mainstream supermarkets (Kroger, Albertsons, Walmart) will keep expanding ethnic private labels and local demographic stocking, taking share in volume but at commodity margins. Online delivery will claim 15%+ of ethnic grocery sales by 2027, mostly through Amazon/Whole Foods and Walmart, making physical-store-only ethnic chains increasingly vulnerable. Demographic growth (Hispanic and Asian population expansion) will continue to support absolute demand, but consolidated, experience-focused chains and mainstream competitors will capture it. The distinct ethnic supermarket category will persist but will be smaller, more concentrated, and less profitable than 2022 levels.
themes: Consolidation - business count falling, market concentrating in larger chains
Tariff pressure - import-heavy sourcing vulnerable to tariff shock, margins compressed
Mainstream cannibalization - Kroger, Albertsons, Walmart capturing ethnic demand via private labels
Online erosion - Amazon/Whole Foods and Walmart delivery undercutting physical ethnic supermarkets
Scale plays - large chains (Vallarta, H Mart, 99 Ranch) build food halls and restaurants to differentiate
Immigration headwinds - enforcement crackdowns reduce foot traffic and labor availability

title: Health Stores in the US
one_liner: Specialty health and supplement retail faces margin compression from online channels and mass-market competitors while tariffs on imported raw ingredients threaten to push prices higher and squeeze already-thin profits.
one_sentence: The brick-and-mortar health stores sector is stalled—market growth is slowing, major chains are in bankruptcy or being sold to private equity, and tariffs on vitamins and supplements are forcing difficult cost-pass-through decisions in 2025-2026.
overview: The US health stores industry—specialized retailers of vitamins, supplements, sports nutrition, and prosthetic equipment—is a mature market stuck in low-growth mode. In 2025, the market was valued at roughly $60.7 billion (a 3.8% increase from 2024), but that headline masks stagnation at the store level. Two of the three largest chains, The Vitamin Shoppe and GNC, went through bankruptcy or restructuring in 2024-2026, signaling that the model of high-margin specialty retail is broken. Online channels (Amazon, direct-to-consumer brands) now capture 23% of supplement sales and growing at 11.4% annually. Tariffs enacted in 2025—ranging from 10% to 34% depending on origin—are threatening to raise prices on an industry that already competes on price against Walmart, Target, and Costco. Meanwhile, consumers are shifting toward personalized nutrition and gummy formats, which skew smaller, harder to stock, and more expensive to fulfill.

key_stats.businesses: 98,303 establishments in 2022; highly fragmented with most regional/independent operators; major branded chains: The Vitamin Shoppe (acquired by private equity 2025), GNC (post-bankruptcy restructuring 2024-2026)
key_stats.employees: 178,276 in 2022; minimal employment growth forecast through 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: 5.5% (2022 baseline); likely compressing in 2025-2026 due to tariffs and online competition
key_stats.concentration: Low; highly fragmented. Top chains: The Vitamin Shoppe, GNC Holdings, regional independents. Amazon and online retailers dominating supplement sales but excluded from 'health stores' industry definition

how_it_makes_money: Health stores earn revenue by selling nutritional supplements (28.3% of revenue in 2022), convalescent care products (22.7%), orthopedic equipment (9.9%), sports nutrition (29.9%), and other wellness items. Margins typically range 40-50% on retail markup, but are compressed by high occupancy costs (brick-and-mortar overhead), employee wages, and competition from online retailers with lower cost structures. Private label products from mass merchandisers like Target and Walmart (which bundle supplements with groceries) are undercutting specialty stores on price.
cost_structure: Cost of goods sold comprises 50-60% of revenue. Largest variable costs: inventory (raw materials sourced 75-80% from China, now subject to 10-34% tariffs as of 2025), labor (retail staff), and fulfillment. Fixed costs: rent (declining store estate in urban/suburban markets), utilities, and shrinkage. Tariff exposure is massive: 94% of vitamin B6, 91% of vitamin C, and 78% of all vitamins sourced from China face 34% tariffs, raising raw material costs 20-30%. Companies face a choice: absorb margin loss or pass costs to consumers at risk of losing price-sensitive shoppers to Amazon/Walmart.
major_players: The Vitamin Shoppe (acquired by Kingswood Capital Management and Performance Investment Partners, April 2025, for $193.5 million after parent Franchise Group bankruptcy)
GNC Holdings (bankruptcy reorganization 2024-2026; under new management; seeking Harbin Pharmaceutical as acquirer)
Vitamin World
iHerb (online, major competitor)
Amazon (online, ~10% market share in vitamins/supplements)
Walmart (health section in general merchandise)
Target (with private label vitamin lines)
Costco
Regional independent health stores (majority of count but fragmented)
current_dynamics: The industry is caught between irreconcilable forces. Online supplements are growing 11.4% annually while brick-and-mortar stagnates; consumers buy vitamins from Amazon at lower prices, often not differentiating between generic and specialty brands. The two largest regional chains (The Vitamin Shoppe, GNC) filed for bankruptcy, meaning their store closures and asset sales to private equity will reduce physical footprint by 15-25% through 2026. Tariffs impose a 20-30% cost wedge on imported ingredients (China dependency is acute), forcing retailers to choose between raising shelf prices and accepting margin compression. At the same time, upstream market consolidation among supplement manufacturers is creating new private-label entrants that bypass specialty retail entirely (e.g., Target's exclusive personalized vitamin line in 2021-2022). Consumers are migrating toward personalized and convenience formats (gummies, subscription boxes) which specialty stores struggle to stock efficiently; personalized nutrition alone is growing at 15% annually. Regulatory scrutiny (FDA labeling, recall authority) continues to pressure operators' compliance costs. The middle is hollowed out: discount mass retailers and online upstarts are winning; small regional stores are surviving on local loyalty; only the very largest or most nimble will thrive.
whats_growing: Sports nutrition (8.4% year-over-year growth in 2025), personalized nutrition (15% annually, fastest-growing segment despite tiny base), gummy and non-pill formats (exceeding traditional tablets), proteins and amino acids (12.51% growth in 2025), plant-based supplements, and female-focused health solutions (pregnancy, menopause-specific). Direct-to-consumer (D2C) supplement brands via social media are growing rapidly, bypassing brick-and-mortar retail. Subscription box models are capturing younger, convenience-focused cohorts. Offline retail still dominates (77.1% of sales in 2025) but growth is concentrated online (11.4% CAGR). Aging population remains a structural tailwind—adults 50+ represent the largest customer segment and are growing 1% annually, but they are also the customer base most comfortable with Amazon.
whats_shrinking: Traditional vitamin and mineral supplements (which comprised 28.3% of revenue in 2022) are flattening as consumers shift to targeted, performance-focused products. Brick-and-mortar health stores are shrinking: store counts held roughly flat 2017-2022 and are forecast to decline 0.8-1.5% annually through 2026 as bankruptcies liquidate and underperforming locations close. Regional specialty chains (those without online capabilities) are losing share to Walmart, Target, and Amazon. Private-label vitamin sales from mass retailers (Walmart, Target, Costco) are encroaching on specialty store turf and growing faster than specialty retail itself. Premium-priced specialty supplements are losing price-sensitive consumers to generic/store-brand alternatives in a high-inflation environment. Regulatory cost as a percentage of revenue is rising, eating into thin margins.
recent_developments: April 2025: The Vitamin Shoppe acquired by Kingswood Capital Management and Performance Investment Partners for $193.5 million following Franchise Group bankruptcy filing in November 2024.
2024-2026: GNC Holdings bankruptcy proceedings; company reorganized under new management; seeking acquisition by Harbin Pharmaceutical (China-backed) amid legal/political resistance.

2025: US tariffs on supplements and raw ingredients imposed at 10-34% depending on country of origin (China 34%, Taiwan 32%, India 27%, South Korea 26%); applies to ascorbic acid, magnesium, amino acids, plant extracts affecting 75-80% of imported raw materials.
2025: Supplement industry grew $72.9 billion (+5.5% year-over-year); but growth concentrated in online channels and D2C brands, not brick-and-mortar.
2025: Personalized nutrition segment reached $15.97 billion globally (+15% annually); AI-driven customization platforms commanding 2-3x price premiums but available almost exclusively online.

2024-2026: CVS announced closure of 271 stores in 2025; Walgreens closing 500+ stores over three years; retail landscape consolidating around higher-productivity locations, depressing foot traffic in secondary markets where many health stores operate.
outlook: The health stores sector will remain flat to slightly negative through 2026. Growth will be driven by aggregate supplement demand (aging population, sports nutrition, personalized products) but captured almost entirely by online, mass merchants, and D2C brands—not by traditional specialty retail. Store closures will accelerate as remaining chains rationalize footprints post-bankruptcy. Tariffs will force price increases in late 2025 and 2026, which will further depress foot traffic among price-sensitive consumers (precisely the ones who have already switched to Amazon). However, consumers aged 65+ and those without strong online habits will continue to rely on local health stores, creating survivorship for small, high-margin regional operators that double down on personalization, local sourcing, or expert service (e.g., nutritionist consultations). Private equity consolidation of The Vitamin Shoppe, GNC and others will yield 1-2 larger operators with better data, supply chain efficiency, and omnichannel (online + store) capabilities. Overall industry revenue will grow 1-2% annually through 2026, well below supplement market growth, a sign that market share is permanently shifting away from the category.
data_year: 2025-2026 current data; 2022 baseline from IBISWorld; 2024 used for interim comparisons

title: Auto Parts Stores in the US
one_liner: Mature retail sector selling replacement parts and accessories to DIY consumers and repair shops, struggling against e-commerce cannibalization and rising EV complexity while consolidation favors giants.
one_sentence: The $77 billion US auto parts stores industry (2026) faces slowing growth (1.6% in 2026) as electric vehicles require fewer traditional repairs, e-commerce takes online sales, and tariffs on imported parts raise costs.
overview: The US auto parts stores industry is a mature, consolidating retail market selling roughly $77.1 billion in new and used parts annually as of 2026. Traditional physical retailers face structural headwinds: vehicles are aging (12.8 years average in 2025) which should boost parts demand, but EV adoption is now reducing need for engine oil, spark plugs, and traditional drivetrain repairs. E-commerce players and Amazon (now a $13.7 billion auto parts market) are siphoning away DIY buyers, while vehicle complexity is pushing amateur repairs toward professional shops. The Big Four chains (AutoZone, O'Reilly, Advance Auto Parts, and Genuine Parts) control roughly 30-35% of the market and are financially strong, but smaller independents and second-tier chains face acute pressure.

key_stats.concentration: Big Four hold 30-35% of DIY/DIFM market; top 7 companies contribute 16% (2024)

how_it_makes_money: Retail auto parts stores earn revenue from selling new and used automotive parts, accessories (seat covers, phone chargers, infotainment systems), and increasingly from installation and repair services. O'Reilly saw sales grow 6% year-over-year in 2025 to $17.78 billion, with comparable store sales up 4.7%, demonstrating the customer loyalty of major chains. The Big Four leverage scale to buy in bulk from manufacturers at lower cost and mark up inventory. Smaller operators depend on convenience (nearby location, quick inventory lookup) to compete. Installation services represent a growing margin opportunity as stores respond to customer demand, though they compete against dealerships and independent repair shops for this work.
cost_structure: Input costs—parts themselves, labor, rent, shipping—represent the bulk of expenses. Parts are sourced from manufacturers at wholesale; labor includes store staff and warehouse personnel. The industry is labor-intensive despite automation of inventory systems. Tariffs are a new and volatile cost pressure: 25% tariffs on most Chinese auto parts imports (April 2025 onward, with a 90-day truce negotiated in May dropping rates to 30%) added $2,500 in duties to a typical $10,000 parts shipment. Shipping, rent, and utilities scale with store footprint. Profit margin stands at 8.8% (2022 baseline), lower than many retail sectors, and has declined over the long term as competition and e-commerce discounting erode pricing power.
major_players: AutoZone (largest, ~$19.6 billion TTM revenue, 12.4% net margin, 2026)
O'Reilly Automotive ($17.78 billion revenue 2025, growing 8.1% comp sales Q1 2026)
Advance Auto Parts (struggling with store rationalization 2025)
Genuine Parts Company (NAPA brand)
LKQ Corporation
Amazon (now $13.7 billion auto parts, growing ~10% YoY 2026)
Regional independent retailers and used-parts specialists
current_dynamics: The industry is being remade by three colliding forces. First, electric vehicles are structurally shrinking the parts basket per vehicle: EVs need no oil changes, fewer spark plugs, simpler drivetrains, and less frequent brake service due to regenerative braking. Second, e-commerce—led by Amazon ($13.7 billion 2026) but also RockAuto, eBay Motors, and Walmart—has captured the price-sensitive DIY buyer; U.S. online auto parts sales (excluding marketplaces) reached ~$23 billion in 2025 and are forecast at 4.6% annual growth, while including Amazon/eBay/Walmart the total channel grows 6.7% annually. Third, tariff volatility (25% on Chinese parts from April 2025, fluctuating with trade negotiations) has raised wholesale costs for retailers and made inventory planning unpredictable. Meanwhile, the average vehicle age climbed to 12.8 years in 2025 (a record), which theoretically should drive parts demand for aging fleets, but this benefit is offset by EV adoption and fewer DIY repairs as modern cars become too complex for amateur mechanics. The Big Four are weathering this through scale and store productivity (O'Reilly posted 8.1% comp sales growth in Q1 2026), but Advance Auto Parts is undergoing restructuring, and smaller chains face margin compression.
whats_growing: The strongest growth segment is e-commerce and online marketplaces (6.7% CAGR 2020-2030 including marketplaces), with Amazon's auto parts division growing ~10% year-over-year in 2026. Among traditional retailers, the Big Four—especially O'Reilly and AutoZone—are expanding store counts and gaining market share through acquisition of weaker competitors and conversion of locations to higher-productivity formats. Installation services and do-it-for-me (DIFM) repair work at auto parts stores is growing as consumers shift away from DIY repairs; major chains are investing in this to compete against dealerships. EV-specific parts (high-voltage batteries, charging accessories, specialized tires rated for EV weight) represent a small but emerging category.
whats_shrinking: Traditional DIY demand is declining as vehicle complexity makes amateur repairs risky or impossible; consumers increasingly outsource to professionals. Engine oil replacement is shrinking with EV adoption. Brick-and-mortar store traffic has flattened or declined in many markets. Advance Auto Parts has been contracting store count as of 2025. Small, independent auto parts retailers continue to lose share to national chains and online sellers. The average independent shop's revenue from parts sales is under pressure from both big-box retailers and e-commerce competitors.
recent_developments: Q1 2026: O'Reilly Automotive reported record revenue and an 8.1% comparable store sales increase, with diluted earnings per share up 16% year-over-year, showing strong DIY/DIFM momentum among the market leader
May 2025: U.S. and China negotiate 90-day tariff truce; auto parts tariffs drop from 145% to 30% after April 2025's controversial 25% tariff announcement
April 2025: U.S. imposes 25% tariff on imported automobiles and auto parts under Section 232 (national security), driving immediate wholesale cost increases

2025: First Brands, a major auto parts supplier, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy; Japanese parts group Marelli also filed; industry analysts warn of a wave of bankruptcies in 2026 among smaller suppliers and marginal retailers due to tariff costs and soft demand
2025: O'Reilly Automotive full-year 2025 sales reached $17.78 billion (+6% YoY), with 33 consecutive years of comparable store sales growth
2025: S&P Global Mobility reports U.S. vehicle fleet age reaches record 12.8 years (average), with passenger cars at 14.5 years, due to high new-car prices and improved vehicle durability
outlook: The US auto parts stores industry will face persistent low-single-digit growth (1-2% annually) through 2027-2028 under current conditions. The tailwinds of an aging fleet are offset by secular headwinds from EV adoption and e-commerce. Market consolidation will accelerate: the Big Four will gain share through store expansion and acquisition, while second-tier chains and independents will shrink or disappear. Tariff policy remains the wild card; if 25-30% tariffs on Chinese parts persist, wholesale costs will remain elevated, squeezing smaller retailers who cannot absorb or pass on price increases. E-commerce will capture 20-25% of the addressable DIY market by 2030 (from roughly 10-15% today), while DIFM repair services at parts stores will grow modestly as consumers avoid complex amateur repairs. Profitability will bifurcate: large, efficient chains like AutoZone and O'Reilly will maintain or grow margins through operational leverage and pricing power, while regional and independent operators will face continued compression, with several forced exits or mergers. The industry will remain mature and cash-generative but not a growth story.
themes: Shift from DIY to DIFM services

title: Home Improvement Stores in the US
one_liner: A mature, hyper-consolidated retail sector dominated by Home Depot and Lowe's, facing headwinds from a frozen housing market and tariff-driven cost pressures while watching Amazon gain traction in online home improvement sales.
overview: The US home improvement stores industry remains deeply mature and dominated by two giants—Home Depot and Lowe's control roughly 80% of the market—but growth has stalled as the housing market froze due to high mortgage rates and low existing-home turnover. Consumers are deferring DIY projects and shifting toward professional services (DIFM), while labor costs and tariffs on imported materials are squeezing margins industry-wide. E-commerce has become a real threat: Amazon captured 12% of online DIY sales and is growing 25% annually in tools, pressuring traditional big-box retailers to compete on convenience and technology. Meanwhile, smaller independent hardware chains continue filing for bankruptcy, accelerating the industry's consolidation trend.

key_stats.concentration: Home Depot 51% + Lowe's 28.8% = ~80% combined market share (2025)
key_stats.profit_margin: 14.2% (2022 baseline)

current_dynamics: The industry faces a structural housing crisis: the "lock-in effect" from low existing mortgage rates has pushed housing turnover to multi-decade lows, making consumers reluctant to sell or relocate and triggering sharp deferred-spending behavior. Consumers who do engage are shifting from DIY to DIFM (do-it-for-me), with Lowe's reporting a 15% revenue surge in professional services in 2024. Tariffs have become a major pain point—material costs are up 4–6% on average, with kitchen cabinets and bathroom vanities facing 15–20% increases and even a proposed 50% import tax on cabinets. Labor costs are rising 6–8% annually due to workforce scarcity. E-commerce is reshaping competitive dynamics: Amazon now claims 12% of online DIY sales and grew 25% year-over-year in home improvement tools ($6.1 billion in 2024). Home Depot holds flat to slightly negative foot traffic (−0.08% in Q1 2026), while Lowe's alone shows momentum (+2.5% YoY early 2026), suggesting differentiation by execution. Meanwhile, smaller chains—Wren Kitchens, At Home, Miller's Hardware—are filing for bankruptcy or liquidating, unable to match the two giants' scale and pricing power.
one_sentence: Home Depot and Lowe's are hanging on in a frozen housing market by serving professional customers and investing in e-commerce, but Amazon is creeping in, tariffs are raising costs, and smaller competitors are vanishing.
major_players: The Home Depot (51% market share, 2025)
Lowe's Companies (28.8% market share, 2025)
Amazon (12% of online DIY sales, 2025)
Floor & Décor
At Home
whats_growing: Professional services (DIFM): up 15% for Lowe's in 2024. Smart home devices and energy-efficient appliances. E-commerce and online channels. Outdoor project materials. Services like installation and do-it-for-me offerings.
whats_shrinking: DIY foot traffic: consumers deferring projects due to housing market freeze and economic uncertainty. Traditional small-to-mid independent hardware chains and specialty retailers filing for bankruptcy. In-store DIY demand as younger consumers shift online (46% of Gen Z/Millennials try new online suppliers each year).
recent_developments: Home Depot announced ~800 corporate layoffs and distribution-facility closures in Mexico, Missouri, and Tennessee to streamline operations and shift to AI-based supply chain (2025–2026)
Lowe's reported 15% revenue growth in professional services segment in 2024, outpacing DIY growth
Amazon's home improvement tool and equipment sales reached $6.1 billion, up 25% YoY (2024)
Wren Kitchens, a major kitchen specialty retailer, filed for bankruptcy liquidation and closed all 15 US locations (2025)
At Home emerged from 2025 bankruptcy with reduced footprint of 229 stores
Miller's Hardware (80-year family operation in Florida) announced liquidation by end of May 2026 as it cannot compete with big-box retailers (2026)
Home Depot recorded $164.7 billion revenue in fiscal 2025, up modestly; issued guidance of flat-to-2% comparable sales growth for 2026
Lowe's outpaced Home Depot in comparable sales for second consecutive quarter; reported flat-to-slightly-positive comps guidance for 2026
how_it_makes_money: Home improvement stores generate revenue from four main channels: (1) Lumber and building materials (~32% of sales in 2022); (2) Household appliances, kitchen goods, and smart home devices (~31%); (3) Hardware, tools, plumbing, and electrical supplies (~24%); (4) Lawn, garden, and outdoor equipment (~13%). They buy from wholesalers and manufacturers, mark up products, and increasingly add services like installation, design consultation (DIFM), and contractor support for professional customers. Professional customers are now the largest revenue source and growing fastest. Loyalty programs, online channels, and markup on high-tech items (smart home, energy-efficient appliances) drive additional margin.
cost_structure: Cost of goods sold dominates (reflecting thin retail margins typical in home improvement). Labor is the second-largest cost, rising 6–8% annually. Tariffs and import duties on materials (particularly cabinets, fixtures) are adding 4–6% (or 15–20% on tariff-affected items). Supply chain and distribution costs remain significant; major retailers are automating and consolidating warehouses to offset inflation. Marketing and loyalty programs are moderate costs. Rent/occupancy is stable as the industry has few new store openings.
outlook: The industry will remain flat to modestly positive through 2026, constrained by the frozen housing market and consumer caution. Home Depot expects flat-to-2% comps in 2026; Lowe's slightly better at flat-to-positive. The professional/DIFM segment will continue outpacing DIY—this is structural, not cyclical, as aging homeowners prefer outsourcing and younger consumers prefer online convenience. Tariffs will remain a headwind unless policy shifts, keeping material costs elevated through 2026. E-commerce will accelerate, with Amazon and specialty retailers taking share from traditional big-box foot traffic; smaller chains will continue consolidating out. The two giants will maintain dominance through scale, brand, and technology (AI supply-chain tools, mobile apps, in-store pickup). Expect modest single-digit revenue growth (1–3% annually) until housing turnover recovers or mortgage rates drop meaningfully. Profit margins will stabilize near 14–15% as labor cost inflation is partially offset by price increases and operational efficiencies.
data_year: 2025–2026 (most recent; 2022 used for baseline comparison only)

title: Computer Stores in the US
one_liner: A declining brick-and-mortar retail sector worth $39.6 billion in 2026, hollowed out by e-commerce and shedding stores as consumers shift online.
overview: The US computer stores industry remains in structural decline through 2025-2026. The sector comprises roughly 5,258 retail locations in 2025—down 6.6% annually since 2020—selling desktops, laptops, peripherals, and software. Market revenue holds at $39.6 billion in 2026, growing only 0.4% annually from 2020-2025, despite underlying demand for computing equipment. Prices for key components like RAM and GPUs are rising sharply in 2026 due to tariffs and supply constraints, making consumer purchases harder to close. What growth exists is captured almost entirely by online retailers, big-box chains (Walmart, Costco, Target), and direct-from-manufacturer channels.

key_stats.businesses: 5,258 retail locations in 2025 (down 6.6% per year since 2020; -4.3% from 2024 to 2025)
key_stats.employees: Computer-store specific employment not separately reported; consumer electronics stores employ 417,560 in 2025 and 419,275 in 2026, down 2.3% annually since 2021
key_stats.profit_margin: Not publicly disclosed in 2025-2026 reports; 2021 baseline was 4.9%
key_stats.concentration: Highly consolidated: Apple Inc. and Best Buy Co. Inc. hold majority market share; remainder fragmented among independents and regional chains

current_dynamics: Tariffs on Chinese electronics climbed to 35% effective (25% Section 301 + 10% Section 122 surcharge) by early 2026, with some components facing rates as high as 145%, dramatically raising wholesale and retail prices. US computer imports from China collapsed 70% to $10.8 billion in 2025 as a result, forcing retailers into narrower margins and price-sensitive consumers toward older, discounted inventory or outright postponement. Meanwhile, PC shipments fell 7% in 2024 and are forecast to drop 11.3% in 2026 according to IDC, driven by memory shortages (no relief until end of 2027), rising average prices (+18.3% in 2026), and consumer pullback on budget systems (projected to drop 28%). Apple is shifting from mall locations to upscale outdoor shopping areas—closing 3 US stores in mid-2026 while opening others in higher-growth metros like Detroit and Miami. Best Buy reduced store count by 24-40 locations annually in 2024-2025. E-commerce continues to grow and capture the majority of available demand, while independent retailers shrink as a share of the total.
one_sentence: Computer retail is a slowly shrinking $39.6 billion market in 2026 losing customers to online sellers and squeezed by tariffs and component shortages.

baseline_2022.growth: -2.6% CAGR 2016-2021 (before COVID bounce of +2.6% in 2021 alone); projected -0.3% CAGR 2021-2026

how_it_makes_money: Desktop and laptop sales account for roughly 61% of revenue; peripherals, software, and accessories make up the remainder. Repair services contribute minimally (~2%). Unlike consumer electronics stores that blend computers with TVs and appliances (31% of that industry), computer retailers focus narrowly on computing products. Gross margins are thin (5-6% profit-to-revenue) because prices have fallen for two decades while unit volumes matter most, favoring large retailers that can move volume efficiently. Independent stores compete on specialized knowledge and customization; most cannot match online pricing.
whats_growing: E-commerce computer sales continue their long-term climb; online channels are estimated to account for 94.5% of services conducted online by 2021-2026 (up from 81% in 2016). Private business investment in computers and software is forecast to grow 8.3% over 2021-2026, benefiting manufacturers more than traditional retailers. Direct-to-consumer sales by Apple, Dell, HP, and Lenovo bypass retail entirely. Repair and value-added services (virus removal, custom builds, IT consulting) remain bright spots for stores that can position themselves as local experts.
whats_shrinking: Brick-and-mortar store locations are in free fall: 6.6% annual decline since 2020, with -4.3% from 2024 to 2025 alone. Unit sales of PCs are contracting hard in 2025-2026 due to component shortages and price hikes. Budget-segment laptops and desktops (sub-$500) are forecast to drop 28% in 2026. Software revenue as a share of retail is minimal now (5.6% in 2021) because most users download or stream rather than buy boxed copies. Store traffic is declining as consumers complete research online before (rarely) visiting a showroom, then order online anyway.
recent_developments: US tariffs on Chinese electronics reached 35% effective (25% Section 301 + 10% Section 122) by early 2026, with some categories hitting 145%; China's effective tariff rate jumped from 2.3% (Jan 2025) to 33.9% (Jan 2026). Section 122 surcharge set to expire ~July 2026, creating near-term pricing uncertainty (2026).

US computer imports from China dropped 70% to $10.8 billion in 2025, forcing retailers to source from Mexico and Taiwan; supply chain diversification underway but still adds friction to availability and pricing (2025).

IDC forecasts PC shipments down 11.3% in 2026 with Q4 potentially seeing 20% year-over-year declines; memory shortage with no relief until end of 2027 is the primary driver. Budget PCs hit especially hard (-28% expected) (2026).
PC average selling prices forecast to rise 18.3% in 2026 and remain elevated through 2027, pressuring consumer purchasing power and deferring upgrades (2026).

Apple announced permanent closure of 3 US stores in mid-2026 (Trumbull CT, Escondido CA, Towson MD) citing mall decline, offset by 11 new stores opened globally since early 2025, including in Miami and Detroit; strategic shift from malls to upscale outdoor locations (2026).
Best Buy closed 24 stores in fiscal 2024, closed 10-15 in fiscal 2025, and continues 1-2% annual closures; retrenchment reflects e-commerce pressure and operational inefficiencies (2024-2025).
outlook: The computer stores industry will continue to shrink through 2026-2027. Market revenue is flat to slightly positive (0.4% growth through 2025, outlook 0.7% in 2025 alone), but this masks ongoing store closures and consolidation around a few large players (Apple, Best Buy, and big-box generalists like Walmart). Tariff-driven price hikes will temporarily depress demand in early 2026, with PC shipments falling sharply; by 2027-2028, rising prices should stabilize but won't reverse structural e-commerce gains. Independent computer stores will continue to exit or transform into repair and IT-service shops. Mall-based locations will close fastest. The surviving traditional retail footprint will be smaller, more specialized, and concentrated in high-traffic outdoor/urban centers. Online and direct-to-consumer will account for nearly all growth in computing sales, leaving legacy computer stores as a slow-motion minority channel.

title: Consumer Electronics Stores in the US
one_liner: A shrinking brick-and-mortar sector pinched by online dominance, tariffs, and shifting consumer spending, where survival means blending in-store expertise with digital reach.
overview: The US consumer electronics retail store industry is in managed decline. Physical stores held 56.7% of the market in 2025, down from past dominance as e-commerce soars (growing at 9.3% annually through 2031). Tariff shocks in 2025 pushed effective rates to 27% before moderating to 13.7% by early 2026, dampening discretionary spending and pricing in hardware. Best Buy, the sector's dominant player with $41.7 billion in revenue (2026), has stopped closing stores and is expanding selectively while fixing its omnichannel game—and this small pivot signals the real fight: who can afford to keep the lights on while offering expertise that e-commerce can't match. Smaller independents have largely exited.

key_stats.growth: 0.2% projected for 2026; long-term decline of 0.6% annually through 2027 (2022 projection)
key_stats.concentration: Best Buy + GameStop account for roughly 30% of industry revenue; top 5 global retailers control under 40% of worldwide sales
key_stats.profit_margin: 3.7% (2022); modest for discretionary retail

current_dynamics: The industry is fractured. Amazon owns 60.5% of e-commerce electronics and appliances (2025), while Walmart holds 9.2% of overall online retail. Physical stores are bleeding: Best Buy closed 24 stores in 2024 and plans 15 more in 2025, but just announced its first store expansion in a decade—a rare bet that small-format, high-touch shops can survive in tech-forward cities. Tariff volatility hit hard: 2025 saw phones drop 37% in demand, gaming consoles down 58%, laptops down 68% as prices spiked and household budgets tightened. By early 2026, retailers adjusted pricing strategies and tariffs eased to 13.7%, but damage was done—higher-income shoppers kept buying, while lower and middle-income customers retreated. Best Buy itself is betting on omnichannel (one-third of revenue from e-commerce) and AI-powered shopping tools to survive. GameStop remains trapped in structural decline as gaming goes digital, with hundreds of closures and a failed attempt to buy eBay. Appliances have outperformed consumer electronics because they're purchased in-store more often (big-ticket, consultation-heavy), but even appliances are moving online. The remaining industry is essentially Best Buy, a handful of regional chains, and a long tail of independents; consolidation has already happened.
one_sentence: Consumer electronics retail in the US is a mature, consolidating industry where brick-and-mortar stores are losing share to e-commerce and manufacturers' direct sales, leaving only the largest, most agile players (mainly Best Buy) with sustainable paths forward.
whats_growing: Appliances segment (better for in-store purchases than consumer electronics). Omnichannel fulfillment (e.g., Buy Online Pickup In Store). Premium devices and services (repair, tech support, warranties). Direct-to-consumer sales by manufacturers. High-end 4K/OLED TVs and gaming consoles (among affluent consumers). AI-powered tools in retail apps. Online channels (growing 9.3% CAGR through 2031).
whats_shrinking: Physical store footprint (15,000+ closures projected by end 2025). CDs, DVDs, legacy media players. Smartphones and tablets (saturated market). Small-format specialty stores. Smaller regional electronics chains. Older product categories (MP3 players, digital cameras). Lower-income consumer electronics spending (tariff-driven). GameStop and video game retail specifically.
recent_developments: Best Buy reported full-year 2026 revenue of $41.7 billion, with first positive comp sales (+0.5%) since fiscal 2022 (Jan 2026).
US tariff rates spiked to 27% (April 2025) then moderated to 13.7% (Feb 2026); consumer tech purchases fell 37–68% across devices during peak tariff period.
US retailers shuttered 7,325 stores in 2024 (highest since 2020), with analysts tracking 5,800+ closures by mid-2025 and projecting 15,000+ for the full year.
Amazon captured 40.5% of overall US online retail (2025) and 60.5% of e-commerce electronics/appliances; Walmart second at 9.2% overall.
Best Buy announced first store expansion in a decade, backed by new CEO Jason Bonfig, betting on omnichannel and AI-enhanced shopping.
GameStop submitted failed $55.5 billion unsolicited offer to acquire eBay (2026), signaling desperation amid structural decline in video game retail.
outlook: The industry will continue to consolidate around 2–3 national players (Best Buy dominant) and a scatter of regional specialists. Physical store count will keep falling through 2027, but the closure rate is likely to moderate—the industry has shed most unprofitable units. Revenue growth for 2026 is projected at just 0.2%, reflecting tariff-driven consumer caution and ongoing channel shift online. Best Buy's new store expansion is a credible signal that high-touch, knowledgeable retail has a niche in premium/complex products (appliances, gaming, TVs), especially in dense markets. Appliances will stabilize growth better than consumer electronics because bigger-ticket items favor in-store consultation and in-person delivery logistics. Profit margins will remain tight (3–4%) as online competition forces price discipline. Tariff policy remains a wild card: if rates stay elevated through 2026, consumer demand for discretionary electronics will lag. Most likely outcome: a bifurcated market where Best Buy thrives (omnichannel + services + scale) and independents survive in niche categories (gaming, audiovisual, premium appliances), while mass-market consumer electronics migrate almost entirely online.
major_players: Best Buy Co., Inc. ($41.7B revenue, 2026; 1,000+ stores)
GameStop Corp. (hundreds of closures, video-game focused, struggling)
Amazon (60.5% e-commerce share in electronics/appliances, 2025)
Walmart (9.2% online retail share, growing faster than Amazon in eCommerce)
Regional chains (Best Buy remains dominant; most others have exited or narrowed)

title: Furniture Stores in the US
one_liner: A mature, fragmented retail sector under pressure from e-commerce, tariffs, and recessive housing trends, though online channels and luxury niches are growing.
overview: The US furniture retail industry entered 2025–2026 weakened by a multiyear housing slump, tariff burdens, and inventory buildup. Major retailers including American Signature and Value City Furniture filed for bankruptcy in late 2025 as cash-conscious consumers delayed big-ticket purchases. Simultaneously, the online channel is capturing market share—now roughly 28% of sales—while direct-to-consumer brands and design-forward retailers like Wayfair are winning younger customers. The broader furniture market (including manufacturing and wholesale) sits at USD 195.7 billion in 2025, though traditional brick-and-mortar showroom operators face margin compression from both tariffs (25% on upholstered goods and cabinets since October 2024) and intense price competition from Amazon, Wayfair, and big-box retailers.

key_stats.concentration: Highly fragmented; no single player controls >10%
key_stats.profit_margin: 3% (2022); compressed by tariffs and price competition

current_dynamics: The furniture sector is caught between opposing forces. Housing demand—the core engine—weakened in early 2026 after a brief 2025 rebound; new home sales dropped 17.6% month-over-month in January 2026 and 11.3% year-on-year, directly suppressing furniture demand. Tariffs have become a structural drag: 25% duties on upholstered furniture, cabinets, and vanities (effective October 2024) forced retailers to either absorb costs, eroding already-thin 3% margins, or pass increases to consumers. Online channels now claim 28% of sales and grow 5–10% annually, while Wayfair alone holds ~14% of the 2025 US furniture market share, signaling a permanent shift to e-commerce and DTC models. Inflation-weary consumers are trading down to lower-priced goods, accelerating failures among independent and mid-market retailers. At the same time, sustainable and modular furniture is emerging as a premium niche (76% of consumers willing to pay 9.7% more for eco-friendly goods), and ergonomic/gaming-focused seating is gaining traction among remote workers.
one_sentence: The US furniture retail market is contracting in physical showroom footprint as online channels (28% of sales, growing 5–10% annually) and tariff pressures squeeze traditional operators, while housing-market weakness and consumer retrenchment trigger waves of bankruptcies and strategic repositioning toward DTC, sustainability, and omnichannel logistics.
whats_growing: Online and direct-to-consumer channels (DTC projected to grow 10% CAGR through 2031, reaching $51 billion by 2026); sustainable/eco-friendly furniture (8.6% CAGR through 2035, reaching $133 billion); specialized niches (ergonomic gaming and remote-work furniture, luxury premium brands). Omnichannel players with micro-fulfillment centers (e.g., Rooms to Go, Wayfair) expanding; AI-driven personalization and AR shopping experiences becoming table stakes.
whats_shrinking: Traditional showroom-based retailers and independent furniture stores (many filing Chapter 11 in 2024–2025, including American Signature, Sohomod, Walker Edison, Metro Mattress, American Freight). Brick-and-mortar traffic and same-store sales declining as consumers shift online. Mid-market price-point retailers under pressure from both low-end big-box (Walmart, Costco) and high-end online (Wayfair, DTC luxury). Profit margins compressed industry-wide by tariffs and price competition.
major_players: Ashley Furniture (vertically integrated, world's largest manufacturer-retailer)
Wayfair (dominant e-commerce player, ~14% 2025 market share)
Rooms to Go (room-package model, automated logistics pivot)
IKEA (mass-market, low-price leadership)
Ethan Allen (high-end, interior design services)
American Signature / Value City Furniture (Chapter 11 bankruptcy, Nov 2025)
Amazon (indirect competition via marketplace and private label)
Overstock, Furniture.com, and DTC brands (pure-play online)
recent_developments: American Signature Inc. filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy November 2025, closing Value City Furniture stores

Furniture tariffs delayed: 25% rate on upholstered goods and cabinets held for one year (through late 2026) instead of jumping to 30–50%; however, new Section 301 tariffs (10–12.5%) on Vietnam and 60+ countries took effect July 24, 2026
Walker Edison Furniture and affiliates filed Chapter 11 August 2025, sold to Twin-Star International for $20 million
Online furniture channels reached 28% of total market share in 2025; DTC brands projected to hit $51 billion US revenue by 2026
Housing starts declined 17.6% month-over-month in early 2026, triggering inventory buildup and downward price pressure across retail
Wayfair and Rooms to Go scaled micro-fulfillment hubs and smaller urban showrooms as 'inspiration centers' rather than full showrooms
outlook: The furniture industry will likely remain under pressure through 2027–2028 unless housing demand rebounds sharply. Most forecasts project 3–6.8% annual growth (2026–2035) for the broader market, but traditional brick-and-mortar retail will continue losing share to e-commerce and DTC. Tariff uncertainty—particularly from new Section 301 investigations covering Vietnam and other key sourcing nations—creates pricing risk and margin volatility. Cost-cutting will dominate retail strategy: store closures, logistics consolidation, and culling of SKUs. Premium and sustainable segments will outperform, while mainstream price-point retailers face continued consolidation via Chapter 11 filings, asset sales, and M&A. Omnichannel players investing in micro-fulfillment and AI-driven personalization will gain market share; pure online and DTC brands will grow 10%+ annually while traditional showrooms shrink.
cost_structure:
- Raw materials (wood, upholstered fabrics, hardware): exposed to tariffs (+25% for upholstered goods, cabinets since Oct 2024); lumber and shipping costs remain elevated
- Labor: ~238K employees (2022); wage pressures and unionization activity in logistics sector
- Showroom/retail real estate: high fixed costs; traditional retailers shedding square footage
- Fulfillment and logistics: capex-intensive shift to micro-fulfillment centers, last-mile delivery
- Marketing and digital: rising spend on e-commerce, AR/AI, and brand differentiation
how_it_makes_money:
- Retail margin on furniture sales (living room 37.8%, bedroom 32.8%, dining 18%, other 11.4% of revenue, 2022 mix; margins typically 25–40% gross, but net margin down to 3% after operating costs)
- Consumer financing (BNPL, lease, store credit lines): growing revenue stream as credit-constrained buyers prefer payments
- Interior design services and consultations (premium tier)
- E-commerce and DTC: higher margins if manufacturer-direct, lower fulfillment costs if drop-shipped
- Extended warranty and delivery/assembly services

title: Jewelry Stores in the US
one_liner: A mature, contracting brick-and-mortar sector facing structural decline as online channels and alternative retailers erode market share, offset only by strong consumer interest in lab-grown diamonds and self-gifting trends.
one_sentence: The US brick-and-mortar jewelry stores industry contracted sharply in 2025-2026 (12.1% and 2.2% respectively) as tariffs, high gold prices, and e-commerce competition accelerated store closures, even as lab-grown diamonds and wealthy consumers sustained pockets of resilience.
overview: The US jewelry stores industry (traditional brick-and-mortar shops) is in managed decline as 2026 unfolds. The sector generated $61.7 billion in 2025 but shrank 12.1% that year and fell another 2.2% in 2026, reflecting a permanent migration of sales to online channels (which now account for approximately 25% of total jewelry purchases versus 72% offline in 2025). Brick-and-mortar stores are squeezed between mass retailers and online-only competitors offering lower prices, while tariff costs (18-22% increases) and surging gold prices (60% annual rise in 2025) compress margins. Affluent households remain active buyers, lab-grown diamonds command 56.8% of the US engagement ring market (2025), and younger consumers drive fashion jewelry and customization. Store closures accelerated sharply in 2025 (167 stores in Q1 alone, up 21% year-over-year).

key_stats.businesses: Approximately 17,100 retail jewelry businesses remain, down 3.2% in 2024 with continued contraction through 2025-2026
key_stats.employees: 137,866 (2022 baseline); declining through 2026 due to store closures and shift to e-commerce
key_stats.concentration: Low concentration; Signet Jewelers (Kay, Zales, Jared) is the largest chain; many independent and regional players; online retailers operate outside the brick-and-mortar category
key_stats.profit_margin: Approximately 3.0-3.4% (2025-2026), pressured by tariffs, gold prices, and channel shift

current_dynamics: The industry faces a perfect storm of structural and cyclical pressures in 2025-2026. Gold prices surged approximately 60% annually in 2025, peaking near $4,400 per ounce in October, pushing entry-level jewelry prices from around $99 to the $200-$500 range and cutting off the mass market. Tariffs on Chinese imports reached 145% by late 2025, increasing wholesale costs 18-22%, with most new stock expected to reflect inflated prices by summer 2025 and beyond. Simultaneously, a bifurcated consumer market has emerged: affluent households remain confident spenders, while lower and middle-income households struggle with inflation and job market weakness. Online channels (now $85.7 billion globally in 2026, growing 13% annually) have permanently captured an estimated 25% of jewelry purchases globally, with mobile commerce accounting for over 60% of online transactions. Lab-grown diamonds have captured 56.8% of the US engagement ring market as of late 2025 (up from 1.31 carats average in 2019 to 2.45 carats in 2025), fundamentally reshaping product mix and pricing. Store closures are accelerating: 167 closures in Q1 2025 alone (up 21% from Q1 2024), with 747 discontinuances in 2024. Major bankruptcies include Claire's (August 2025, its second in seven years) and Lugano Diamonds (November 2025). Brick-and-mortar retailers are investing heavily in omnichannel capabilities, personalization, and sustainability messaging to compete, particularly targeting affluent Gen Z and millennials who value self-gifting, customization, and ethical sourcing.
major_players: Signet Jewelers (Kay, Zales, Jared) - largest US chain; FY2026 sales ~$6.8 billion, same-store sales +1.2-1.3%
Independent and regional jewelry retailers (majority of establishments)
Amazon and specialty online retailers (not counted in brick-and-mortar category)
Walmart and Costco (selling jewelry via mass channels, not classified as jewelry stores)
LVMH luxury jewelry (Tiffany & Co., acquired 2021)
whats_growing: Lab-grown diamonds (capturing 56.8% of engagement ring market, 2025), self-gifting and self-purchasing (80% of adults 18+ now buy fine jewelry for themselves), fashion jewelry and lower-priced items, luxury and high-end segments (targeting affluent households), customization and personalized pieces (Gen Z preference), omnichannel and digital capabilities, sustainability-focused sourcing and transparency messaging.
whats_shrinking: Brick-and-mortar foot traffic and store count (167 closures Q1 2025, 21% increase year-over-year; 747 total discontinuances in 2024), traditional engagement ring sales tied to marriage rate decline, entry-level mass-market jewelry (squeezed by tariffs and gold prices), smaller independent retailers (consolidation accelerating), traditional watches (competition from smartwatches).
recent_developments: Gold prices surged approximately 60% annually in 2025, peaking near $4,400 per ounce in October 2025, fundamentally reshaping entry-level pricing and consumer purchasing patterns.

Tariffs on Chinese imports reached 145% by late 2025; wholesale costs increased 18-22% as of spring 2025; retailers estimated $25-30 million additional cost impact if applied to full fiscal year (2025).
Claire's filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August 2025 (second bankruptcy in seven years); Lugano Diamonds & Jewelry filed in November 2025.
Store closures accelerated: 167 US jewelry stores closed in Q1 2025 (21% increase from Q1 2024); 747 total discontinuances recorded in 2024.
Lab-grown diamond market reached USD 27.7 billion globally (2025), with US market share at 38%; penetration in engagement rings reached 56.8% by late 2025.

Signet Jewelers (largest US chain) reported FY2026 sales approximately $6.8 billion with same-store sales growth of 1.2-1.3%, AUR up 6-7%, responding with lab-grown diamond expansion and lighter gold designs (2025-2026).
Online jewelry sales reached approximately $85.7 billion globally (2026), growing at 13% CAGR, with mobile commerce accounting for over 60% of online transactions.
outlook: The brick-and-mortar jewelry stores industry faces continued structural contraction through 2026-2027. Market research projects the sector will shrink further as online channels and mass retailers capture share, though pockets of resilience will persist in luxury and affluent-focused segments. Smaller retailers will continue consolidating or exiting; Signet and other large players will accelerate omnichannel integration and brand differentiation. Lab-grown diamonds will continue displacing mined diamonds in engagement rings and mid-priced categories, enabling affordable fashion jewelry to offset tariff and gold price pressures. Tariff dynamics remain highly uncertain; if elevated tariffs persist, retail prices will rise further, potentially softening consumer demand for non-essential jewelry. The marriage rate's continued decline (projected -3.2% CAGR through 2027, per 2022 baseline) will continue to weigh on bridal segment revenue. Winning retailers will be those offering seamless omnichannel experiences, personalization and customization, transparent and ethical sourcing narratives, and targeted marketing to affluent households and younger self-gifting consumers. Pure-play brick-and-mortar establishments with limited digital capabilities or weak brand positioning face elevated exit risk.

title: Family Clothing Stores in the US
one_liner: Mature brick-and-mortar apparel retail facing tariff shocks, deepening e-commerce squeeze, and consumer pullback on discretionary clothing spending.
overview: The family clothing stores industry is in a difficult position heading into late 2026. Market revenue sits at $226.5 billion (2026), up just 0.4% year-over-year after 2.3% growth in 2025, showing clear deceleration. Tariff rates on apparel imports have surged to 35.1% (December 2025), up from 14.7% before Trump's second term, raising costs and forcing supply chain restructuring away from China. E-commerce now captures 24% of fashion retail (2026), growing at 4.9% annually, while brick-and-mortar trails badly. Consumer spending on apparel has collapsed, with monthly clothing spending down 21.7% from Q4 2024 to Q1 2025, as inflation and tariffs push retail prices up 5.1% year-over-year.

key_stats.businesses: Approximately 53,000 establishments (2022); declining through 2025-2026 via bankruptcies and closures
key_stats.employees: 820,384 (2022 baseline); ongoing contraction from store closures
key_stats.profit_margin: 4.0% (2022 baseline); pressured lower by tariffs, inventory write-downs
key_stats.concentration: Fragmented; TJX Companies, Ross Stores, Gap Inc., Kohl's are largest; many small/regional chains closing

current_dynamics: Tariff shocks have become the defining force. The December 2025 tariff rate of 35.1% on apparel imports is nearly 2.4 times the January 2025 rate of 14.7%, creating immediate cost pressure across inventory and pricing. Retailers are racing to nearshore production to USMCA-qualifying countries and exit China by H2 2026, but supply chain lag means Q1-Q2 2026 shipments will absorb the full tariff hit. Meanwhile, consumers are cutting apparel spending sharply—monthly spending fell 21.7% in early 2025 versus late 2024—with price-sensitive lower-income households pulling back furthest as apparel CPI jumped 5.1% year-over-year. E-commerce continues its relentless march, capturing 24% of fashion retail in 2026 (up from ~21% in 2024) and growing 4.9% annually, while traditional brick-and-mortar sales growth lags e-commerce by 62%. High-profile bankruptcies accelerated the contraction: Forever 21 liquidated all 364 stores (May 2025), Francesca's announced closure of 400 locations (2026), Torrid plans 180 store closures, and Liberated Brands liquidated 122 stores. Industry veterans like Kohl's are shrinking aggressively, with 2026 earnings guidance suggesting operating margins of only 2.8%-3.4%.
one_sentence: The US family clothing stores industry faces converging crises: tariffs doubling import costs in months, e-commerce capturing a quarter of fashion sales, and consumers slashing discretionary apparel spending amid inflation.
how_it_makes_money: Family clothing retailers operate on low-margin, high-volume economics. They purchase apparel (men's 26.5%, women's 39.8%, children's 11.5%, footwear 14%, accessories 8.2% of revenue) from wholesalers and manufacturers, then mark up 35-50% for retail sale. Revenue comes from direct store sales, with some chains adding e-commerce. Profit comes from inventory turns, seasonal demand spikes (holiday season), and careful cost control. Tariffs and supply disruptions have squeezed margins severely. Labor is typically minimum wage, limiting wage-cost flexibility. Chains succeed by holding inventory tight to trends while discounting slower-turning stock—a balancing act that tariffs and volatility have made harder.
whats_growing: E-commerce apparel sales (4.9% annually, 24% of fashion retail by 2026), luxury and specialty segments (higher-end branded stores gaining share), and value/discount chains like TJX and Ross (which deliver 35.1% tariff protection via USMCA nearshoring). Virtual fitting rooms and AR try-on tech (Zeekit, True Fit, DressX) are emerging but still niche. Casual and athletic wear continue to outpace formal wear—the remote-work shift from 2020-2021 has persisted.
whats_shrinking: Traditional department-store-anchored family clothing chains (Kohl's, Gap flagship stores), mid-market mall retailers closing en masse (8,100+ store closures across US retail in 2025, up 12% from 2024), children's discretionary clothing (as birth rates remain flat and families prioritize essential items), and formal/office wear (even as offices recall workers, casual dress codes remain the norm). Regional and small-chain retailers cannot absorb tariff costs and are exiting. Consumer spending on apparel specifically fell 21.7% in Q1 2025 vs Q4 2024.
recent_developments: December 2025: Tariff rates on apparel imports surge to 35.1%, up from 14.7% in January 2025, as Trump administration imposes sweeping reciprocal tariffs across non-USMCA countries; retail industry warns of higher prices and job losses

May 2025: Forever 21 liquidates all 364 stores after filing Chapter 11 on March 16, 2025; Liberated Brands (Volcom, Billabong, Quiksilver portfolio) liquidates 122 stores after February 2025 bankruptcy
Q1 2025: Consumer spending on apparel collapses 21.7% month-over-month (Q4 2024 to Q1 2025); apparel CPI reaches 135.8 (March 2026), up 14% over 5 years and 5.1% year-over-year driven by tariffs
Q3 FY2026 (Summer 2026): TJX Companies reports 5% comp sales growth and raises FY2026 guidance; Ross Stores projects 6-7% comp growth for FY2026, benefiting from value positioning
August 2025: Claire's files for bankruptcy a second time, sold to Ames Watson private equity, ~950 stores continue operating; Torrid announces closure of up to 180 underperforming stores
2026: Francesca's announces closure of all ~400 locations; apparel brands begin massive nearshoring push out of China toward Mexico, Central America, and Vietnam to escape tariffs by H2 2026
major_players: TJX Companies (Marshalls, TJ Maxx, HomeGoods; FY2026 sales $60.4B, up 7%)
Ross Stores (Ross Dress for Less; FY2025 sales $22.8B, up 8%; FY2026 projecting 6-7% comp growth)
Gap Inc. (Gap, Old Navy, Banana Republic; FY2025 EPS $2.13)
Kohl's (department-store hybrid; FY2025 EPS $2.38 adjusted; 2026 outlook weak at $1.00-$1.60 EPS)
Macy's (department store; heavy liquidation through 2024-2026)
Nordstrom (department store; shrinking footprint)
Target (general merchandise with significant apparel; holding up better than pure-play clothing chains)
outlook: 2026-2027 outlook is dark. Tariff absorption will suppress margins through at least Q2 2026; supply chain adjustment to nearshoring will take 6-12 months. Consumer apparel spending is unlikely to rebound until tariff-driven CPI moderates, which forecasters do not expect before late 2026 or 2027. E-commerce penetration will continue climbing, squeezing traditional retail harder. The industry is consolidating by attrition—weaker regional and mid-market chains will continue closing (200-400+ store announcements expected through 2026). TJX, Ross, and other value/discount chains will outperform full-price retailers due to tariff-hedging via nearshoring and lower-income consumer preference for deals. Luxury boutiques and high-end branded stores will hold share. The "family clothing store" category as defined by IBISWorld (general apparel for all genders/ages without specialization) is fragmenting into winner-take-most dynamics for value chains and survival-mode pricing for mid-market generalists. Revenue growth will remain near-flat or negative in 2026, with recovery only if tariffs ease or consumer confidence rebounds in 2027+.
