title: Automobile Engine & Parts Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature manufacturing sector whipsawed by tariffs, EV slowdown, and supplier insolvencies, now pivoting to hybrids and flexible-platform engines as gasoline demand holds steady.
overview: The US automobile engine and parts manufacturing sector is fighting for equilibrium in 2025–2026. The market has stabilized at around $43.8 billion (2026, up 2.5% year-on-year), but growth is anemic and uneven. Major automakers—GM, Ford, and Stellantis—are hedging their bets: they're investing in new gasoline engine designs (48-volt systems, higher compression), scaling hybrid output aggressively, and keeping EV tooling flexible rather than irreversible. Meanwhile, suppliers face a perfect storm: tariffs (25–50% on auto parts from China and non-FTA countries), bankruptcies (First Brands in September 2025, Accuride in October 2024), and shrinking order books from OEMs pulling back on electrification timelines. The industry is neither collapsing nor booming—it is recalibrating.

key_stats.concentration: Medium concentration; led by integrated OEM suppliers and independent Tier 1s (Denso, Bosch, Continental, AAM, Lear)

current_dynamics: The sector faces a paradox: electric vehicles are growing (hybrids up 10+ percent year-on-year), yet gasoline engine demand has *not* collapsed. Instead, OEMs are stretching ICE platform life by investing in turbocharging, variable compression, and 48-volt mild-hybrid architecture. Tariff regimes—US 25% on auto parts effective April 2025, Mexico 25–50% tariffs on non-FTA parts starting January 2026—are crimping margins at suppliers and forcing nearshoring decisions. CAFE standards have been reset in June 2025 to exclude EV credits from compliance calculations, giving OEMs more breathing room to sell gasoline vehicles without penalty. Bankruptcies and restructurings among smaller suppliers (First Brands, Accuride, Tayco) signal consolidation pressure. Denso, Bosch, and Continental are doubling down on EV electronics and thermal systems, while traditional engine makers are repositioning as powertrain integrators—producing not just gasoline blocks but hybrid modules and control systems.
one_sentence: Gasoline engine manufacturing is no longer dying; it is evolving into a three-fuel ecosystem (gasoline, hybrid-electric, mild-hybrid 48V) while tariffs and supplier bankruptcies force consolidation and nearshoring.
whats_growing: Hybrid engine production and aftermarket support; 48-volt mild-hybrid systems and variable compression platforms; turbo and downsizing technologies; software-defined powertrain controls and thermal management systems. Investment by OEMs: Stellantis $13 billion over four years (2025–2029) including engine plant expansion in Kokomo; GM $150+ million in Saginaw casting plant (2026). Aftermarket parts and repair services, driven by aging vehicle fleet.
whats_shrinking: Pure gasoline ICE models (stable count but facing displacement by hybrids); export volume (tariffs and trade friction); import value from non-USMCA sources (Mexico's new tariffs effective January 2026). Smaller, independent engine suppliers (bankruptcies, consolidation). Consumer demand for standalone gasoline vehicles in new-car sales (hybrids now ~30% of market, 2025).

Ford Motor Company

Denso (Japan-based, growing US footprint in EV electronics)
Robert Bosch GmbH (Germany-based, global reach)
Continental AG (Germany-based, ADAS and power electronics)
American Axle & Manufacturing (AAM)
Lear Corporation
Magna International
ZF Friedrichshafen
themes: CAFE standards reset favors flexible platforms
EV electronics as new competitive frontier
recent_developments: First Brands (FBG) files Chapter 11 bankruptcy (September 2025); portfolio included Raybestos, Centric, Cardone, Autolite, FRAM engines and parts
US imposes 25% tariffs on autos and auto parts, effective April 2025
Mexico introduces 25–50% tariffs on auto parts from non-FTA countries, effective January 2026
Stellantis announces $13 billion US investment plan (October 2025); Kokomo engine plant to produce new four-cylinder GMET4 EVO starting 2026 with 100+ new jobs
NHTSA issues June 2025 interpretive rule excluding EVs from CAFE compliance credits, resetting regulatory pressure on ICE manufacturers
Hybrid vehicle model availability rises 10% year-on-year to 200+ models in 2025; ICE model count remains flat
Denso invests $4.8 billion in Silicon Carbide technology (early 2025) to shift from parts supplier to power-electronics leader
outlook: The sector will likely muddle through 2026–2027 without major upheaval. Gasoline engines will remain ~60–70% of new vehicle powertrains through 2030, supported by hybrid growth and regulatory flexibility. Tariffs will persist as a cost headwind, pressuring margins at suppliers but creating incentives to build or expand US capacity (nearshoring). Three to five more mid-sized supplier bankruptcies are possible if order visibility remains weak. OEMs will continue to invest in flexible assembly lines capable of producing hybrids, mild-hybrids, and select ICE models from the same platform. The real inflection point is 2028–2030, when BEV penetration could rise sharply if battery costs fall and charging infrastructure matures. By then, the industry will likely have two tiers: Tier 1 suppliers deep in power electronics and software (Denso, Bosch, Continental) and Tier 2 specialists in mechanical components and aftermarket services. Traditional engine-block casting and machining will consolidate further, with fewer but larger foundries serving the market.

title: Hybrid & Electric Vehicle Manufacturing
one_liner: The US EV and hybrid manufacturing industry has hit a growth wall: surging from $26.6B in 2022 to $108.2B in 2026, but now facing demand collapse as tax credits expired, tariffs spiked, and automakers took $65B in writedowns.
overview: The hybrid and electric vehicle manufacturing industry expanded rapidly through 2024-2025 on the back of the Inflation Reduction Act, improved battery technology, and accelerating consumer interest. However, the industry has entered a sharp downturn in 2026 after Congress ended consumer EV tax credits on September 30, 2025, and trade policies shifted dramatically with 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs and 25% tariffs on batteries. Domestic automakers—GM, Ford, and Toyota—all announced major production cuts and billions in EV-related losses. Sales growth stalled in 2025 at just 1.28 million units (down 2% year-over-year), the first decline after a decade of expansion, with profitability collapsing to 4.8% margins in 2026.

key_stats.businesses: 258 establishments, 210 enterprises (2022); Tesla 46.2%, GM 13%, Ford 7%, Toyota and others (2025)
key_stats.concentration: Very high; Tesla's dominance eroding but still largest player

current_dynamics: The end of federal tax credits (September 30, 2025) eliminated the primary demand driver for mainstream consumers, crushing sales momentum. Tariff policy has become the second major headwind: 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs and 25% on lithium-ion batteries are expected to raise vehicle prices and squeeze margins, pushing battery costs up despite earlier cost reductions. The Big Three automakers (GM, Ford, Toyota) collectively took over $65 billion in EV-related losses and writedowns through early 2026, forcing production delays, hybrid strategy pivots, and workforce reductions. Battery manufacturing costs fell 8% in 2025 to $108/kWh on average, but LFP batteries saw 15%+ price reductions while tariff-constrained NCM811 cells rose. China dominates battery supply (80%+ of global production) while US-EU capacity expanded 50%, creating dependency dynamics. Consumer demand shifted sharply: affordability is now the number one barrier, replacing range anxiety, with 17% expecting to buy an EV next (up from 11% in 2023 but off prior highs). Charging infrastructure expanded 20% in 2025 but lags demand, with 30 EVs per charger (up from 19 in 2024).
one_sentence: A boom-and-bust cycle: the industry rode regulatory tailwinds and falling battery costs to $108B in 2026, but policy reversals and tariffs triggered the first sales decline in a decade and $65B in industry writedowns.
whats_growing: Battery manufacturing capacity in the US and EU (both expanded 50% in 2025). Hybrid vehicle sales and production—GM, Ford, and Toyota all reinvested in plug-in and conventional hybrids as a hedge. GM's EV production grew 48% in 2025, driven by affordable models like the Chevy Equinox EV ($34,995), which became the best-selling non-Tesla EV. Public fast-charging infrastructure (30% growth in ultra-fast chargers to 70,000 in US in 2025). Consumer intent for EV purchase (17% of consumers in 2026). International EV exports from China ($59B in 2025, despite US tariffs).
whats_shrinking: Consumer EV purchase credits (terminated September 30, 2025). EV sales growth (1.28M units in 2025, down 2% YoY from 1.3M in 2024; first decline on record). Ford EV production (84,113 in 2025, down 14% from 98,000 in 2024). Tesla's market share (46.2% in 2025, down from 49% in 2024). EV-related capital investment (over $20B in previously announced projects canceled in 2025). Toyota's 2026 BEV production targets (cut by one-third). Profit margins on EV models despite lower battery costs, due to pricing pressure and tariff burden.
recent_developments: June 2024: Fisker filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy after producing only 10,000 vehicles; assets ($500M-$1B) exceeded liabilities ($100M), highlighting startup capital burn and market competition failures.

September 30, 2025: Federal consumer EV tax credits (Section 30D for new vehicles, Section 25E for used) ended as Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, immediately eliminating the primary purchase incentive.
Q4 2025: General Motors took $6B in EV-related charges; Ford took $19.5B charge; both delayed EV models and pivoted to hybrid expansion; Toyota cut 2026 BEV production by one-third.
Late 2025: EV sales fell 4% nationally as tariffs and incentive expiration cascaded; first annual decline after ten years of growth; demand shifted to used vehicles and hybrids.
H1 2026: Over $65B in cumulative EV and battery investment losses and writedowns absorbed across the industry; IBISWorld reported 'EV sales plummeting through first half of 2026.'
2026: US fast-charging rollout accelerated with 550 NEVI-funded chargers operational and 1,000 more in pipeline; battery costs diverged sharply (LFP -15%, NCM811 +tariff pressure).

baseline_2022.growth: 19.1% CAGR 2017-2022; projected 16.67% CAGR 2022-2028 in the 2022 forecast

outlook: The 2026-2027 outlook is bifurcated. In the near term (2026), the industry faces continued headwinds: federal tax credits will not return under current policy, 100% tariffs on Chinese EV imports remain in force, and consumer demand is price-sensitive with affordability as the top barrier. Automakers will continue hybrid-focused strategies while selectively launching affordable EV models (Chevy Equinox EV, Ford's sub-$40k pickup planned for 2027). Battery costs will stabilize or modestly decline, but tariff-driven price increases on components may limit margins. By 2027-2028, modest recovery is possible if: (1) state-level incentives fill the federal gap in high-EV markets (California, New York); (2) manufacturing costs fall enough to hit $30k-$35k price points without subsidies; (3) charging infrastructure reaches critical mass (target of 500,000 chargers by 2030 via NEVI); or (4) used EV market matures and attracts price-sensitive buyers. Long-term (2030+), structural growth should resume as battery costs approach parity with ICE vehicles, but without federal support and amid tariff-driven reshoring, the path is steeper and slower than 2022 forecasts predicted. Industry concentration will likely increase: Tesla, GM, Ford, and Toyota will dominate, while EV startups without funding face extinction.
major_players: Tesla (46.2% market share, 2025; down from 49% in 2024)
General Motors (13% market share, 2025; 169,887 EV units sold, +48% YoY)
Ford (7% market share, 2025; 84,113 EV units sold, -14% YoY)
Toyota (significant hybrid share; cut 2026 BEV targets by one-third)
Chevrolet Equinox EV (best-selling non-Tesla EV in 2025, 27,000+ units H1)
Rivian and Lucid (struggling startups; Lucid near bankruptcy as of mid-2026)
Chinese EV makers (BYD, NIO, XPeng) blocked by 100% US tariffs but exporting internationally
themes: Battery cost floors and supply concentration (China 80%)
Charging anxiety vs. range anxiety (new consumer barrier)

title: Automobile Steering & Suspension Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A shrinking domestic sector under pressure from tariffs, shifting to electronics and steer-by-wire, while global suppliers consolidate and smaller US players face insolvency.
overview: The US steering and suspension manufacturing sector is caught in a pincer: foreign tariffs at 17.0% effective rate by April 2025 are straining supply chains and costs, while the shift to electric power steering and steer-by-wire systems demands R&D investment that only the biggest players can afford. Domestic revenue dropped 3.8% in 2025 to an estimated $17.7 billion. The industry is tier-one suppliers like Bosch, ZF, and Nexteer thriving through scale and technology, but smaller US shops are under water. Consolidation accelerated in 2024-2025 through deals like Tenneco's sale of Ohlins Racing to Brembo and Rane's full acquisition of its JV, while bankruptcy filings among smaller suppliers hit decade highs.

key_stats.employees: 35,493 (2022 baseline); likely lower in 2025 due to revenue contraction
key_stats.concentration: High: Robert Bosch, Magna International, Hyundai Mobis dominate tier-one; three players control majority of volume
key_stats.profit_margin: 2.6% (2022); under pressure from tariffs and OEM price demands

current_dynamics: Tariffs are the acute shock. The average effective US tariff rate spiked from 2.2% at end-2024 to 17.0% by April 2025, with China specifically targeting US steering racks and control arms in retaliatory duties. This forces manufacturers into a crunch: absorb the cost and destroy thin margins, or nearshore to Mexico and Europe to avoid duties, which collapses domestic US volume. Supply chain disruption ranks as the top concern across respondents (45% cite it), with inventory planning now unreliable under changing duty regimes. Simultaneously, the industry is undergoing forced obsolescence. Electric power steering is now standard across most compact and mid-size vehicles in North America and Europe by 2025, replacing hydraulic systems. Steer-by-wire (fully electronic steering with zero mechanical backup) reached production milestones in 2026 with Mercedes-Benz (ZF supply) and a Chinese EV (Nexteer supply), signaling the beginning of the end for mechanical steering columns. Only firms with deep pockets and global reach can afford the software, sensors, and electronics R&D. Smaller suppliers cannot compete.
one_sentence: Tariff shock, electrification, and steer-by-wire are hollowing out the domestic US steering and suspension manufacturing base, leaving only global tier-ones with scale to survive.
major_players: Robert Bosch GmbH
ZF Friedrichshafen AG
Nexteer Automotive Group Limited
JTEKT Corporation
Hyundai Mobis Co Ltd.
Magna International Inc.
NSK Steering Systems
Mando Corporation
Skyjacker Suspensions
Tenneco Inc.
whats_growing: Electric power steering (EPS) market growing at 6.7% annually from $30.3 billion (2025) to $32.4 billion (2026) globally. Steer-by-wire and by-wire chassis systems expanding rapidly, reaching $4.8 billion market in 2026 headed toward $22.3 billion by 2035 at 18.6% CAGR. Nexteer achieved record $4.6 billion revenue in 2025 (up 7.2% YoY) with 320 basis points of market outperformance; secured $4.9 billion in new bookings, 50% supporting fully electric or hybrid platforms. ZF's adjusted EBIT margin rose to 4.5% in 2025 from 3.5% in 2024. Electronically controlled adaptive damping and rear-wheel steering seeing new award wins.
whats_shrinking: Domestic US steering and suspension manufacturing revenue fell 3.8% in 2025 to $17.7 billion. Exports facing headwinds from stronger dollar and tariffs. Hydraulic power steering is being phased out in favor of electric systems, reducing value of mechanical components. Smaller tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers under severe stress. Job losses mounting in domestic plants as production nearshores to Mexico. Traditional internal-combustion suspension components declining as EVs require different architectures.
recent_developments: Nexteer launched Motion-by-Wire innovations in September 2025, including first Steer-by-Wire systems in series production with ASIL D certification on Chinese new-energy vehicles (Nexteer released 2025 year-end results showing record $4.6 billion revenue)
Tenneco sold Ohlins Racing suspension brand to Brembo for $405 million in January 2025 to focus on core electric steering capabilities

ZF Friedrichshafen secured Mercedes-Benz supply agreement for Steer-by-Wire technology beginning 2026, representing industry's first major OEM steer-by-wire deployment; ZF posted 2025 sales of €38.8 billion with 4.5% adjusted EBIT margin

US tariff rate jumped to 17.0% effective rate by April 2025 (from 2.2% at end-2024), forcing OEMs like Volkswagen to prioritize nearshoring of parts supply chains to Mexico and other NA locales in 2025
Automotive parts supplier bankruptcies reached decade highs by 2025; FBG (First Brands Group) filed Chapter 11 in September 2025 with ~$6 billion in debt; Accuride and Hypertech also filed 2024-2025

China approved new industry standard for steer-by-wire systems officially coming into force July 1, 2026; vertical Z-axis suspension evolving from passive to electronically controlled dampers and fully active suspension
themes: Nearshoring to Mexico under duty pressure
outlook: Expect continued pain through 2026-2027. The domestic US industry will shrink further as tariffs persist and push production southward. Nexteer, ZF, and Bosch will emerge stronger by capturing EV platforms and by-wire system awards globally. Many smaller US suppliers will file for Chapter 11 or be acquired at distressed prices. The industry is bifurcating: tier-ones with global scale, software chops, and EV platforms thriving; everyone else in survival mode. Revenue stabilization is unlikely before 2027-2028 once tariff uncertainty drops and EV platform ramps accelerate overseas. The steer-by-wire transition, though technologically driven, will happen slowly (2026-2032 window) because OEMs are conservative and mechanical steering is proven. But once it begins, mechanical steering column plants will shutter quickly, eliminating thousands of US manufacturing jobs in suspension and column assembly. Nearshoring to Mexico will accelerate as the competitive play: lower costs, USMCA access, and escape from Chinese tariff retaliation targeting US plants.

title: Automobile Transmission Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: The US transmission manufacturing industry is shrinking as electrification eliminates the need for traditional transmissions, supply costs rise, and consumer demand for light vehicles wavers.
overview: The US automobile transmission manufacturing industry reached $44.6 billion in 2026, down 1.7% annually since 2021. The sector faces structural headwinds from the shift to electric vehicles, which require simpler or no transmissions at all. Vehicle sales have grown more volatile after hitting a four-year high in March 2025 before falling sharply, and hybrid adoption is climbing (up 20.5% through July 2026) while battery electric vehicles lose market share. Rising costs from tariffs, steel prices, and supply chain disruptions have crushed profit margins and driven consolidation across the industry.

key_stats.employees: Approximately 93,000 workers (2022); manufacturing sector lost 68,000 jobs during 2025
key_stats.concentration: Moderate—top three players (Dana Inc., Allison Transmission, ZF TRW) dominate; low customer concentration across Big Three automakers plus aftermarket
key_stats.profit_margin: Compressed; specific 2026 margin not disclosed but deteriorating from cost pressures

current_dynamics: The industry is caught between two opposing forces. On one side, hybrid vehicles are booming—hybrid sales surged 20.5% through mid-2026—and hybrids need efficient multi-speed transmissions, creating a temporary lifeline for traditional transmission makers. On the other side, battery electric vehicles do not need conventional transmissions at all; BEVs dropped to 5.9% of market share by July 2026 after federal tax credits expired in September 2025, but long-term EV adoption remains a systemic threat. Light vehicle sales are skittish, hitting 16.3 million units annualized in July 2026, down 1.4% year over year, and tariffs, geopolitical tensions, and volatile input prices (steel, crude oil) have squeezed margins and triggered manufacturing job losses. Consolidation is accelerating: Allison Transmission acquired Dana's off-highway business for $2.7 billion in early 2026, and the closure of TransAxle (a Pennsylvania-based drivetrain remanufacturer) in 2025 signaled weakness among smaller suppliers. USMCA labor-cost compliance and CAFE fuel-economy rules continue to drive technology investment in eight-speed and higher-gear transmissions, but that innovation pipeline is no longer enough to offset the existential EV transition.
one_sentence: Transmission manufacturers are shrinking as EVs eliminate transmission demand, hybrid sales offer only temporary relief, vehicle demand falters, and rising tariffs and input costs compress profitability.
major_players: Dana Inc. (market leader; off-highway division acquired by Allison in 2026)
Allison Transmission Holdings Inc. (acquired Dana off-highway for $2.7B in early 2026)
ZF TRW Automotive Holdings Corp.
Stellantis (electrified dual-clutch transmissions for hybrids)
Ford, GM (OEM customers; Stellantis investing $100M+ in new engine + transmission production at Kokomo through 2026)
whats_growing: Hybrid vehicle production and multi-speed transmission development for efficiency; electrified dual-clutch transmissions (eDCT) leading hybrid sales in Europe and gaining traction in the US (53% EU hybrid sales growth for Stellantis hybrids); AI-driven transmission control systems adopted by 48% of OEMs in 2025 to optimize torque and extend EV range. CAFE fuel-economy standards pushing 71% of automakers to deploy eight-speed and advanced transmissions.
whats_shrinking: Traditional automatic transmissions for internal combustion engines; conventional transmission manufacturing capacity and employment (manufacturing sector shed 68,000 jobs in 2025, with transportation equipment losing 14,000); BEV sales (market share fell from 7.8% to 5.9% after EV tax credits expired in September 2025); company count (down 1.5% CAGR); small and mid-size suppliers (TransAxle closed 13 locations in August 2025, laying off 209 workers). Exports declining (down 1% CAGR through 2022, no recent reversal).
recent_developments: June 2026: Allison Transmission completed acquisition of Dana's off-highway drive and motion systems business for $2.7 billion, consolidating powertrain capabilities and generating ~$120 million in annual synergies
August 2025: TransAxle, a New Jersey-based drivetrain remanufacturer, shut down all 13 locations and laid off 209 workers; permanent closure (no bankruptcy filing)

2025: USMCA compliance in auto manufacturing surged from 44% (2024) to 67% (2025), requiring $16/hour minimum wages in Mexican plants; early 2026 compliance exceeded 80%, forcing US reshoring of some transmission component production
September 2025: Federal EV tax credits expired, triggering a 1.9-percentage-point drop in BEV market share through July 2026

2026 Q1-Q2: Stellantis doubled down on hybrid eDCT production, launching 30 hybrid models with six more planned by 2026; invested $100+ million in Kokomo facilities for new GMET4 EVO four-cylinder engine production beginning 2026
May 2025: Light vehicle sales crashed to 15.65 million units annualized (SAAR), the steepest monthly decline in nearly five years, signaling demand weakness post-tariff volatility
outlook: The transmission manufacturing industry faces a declining 2030s unless it pivots aggressively to EVs and hybrid drivetrains. Near-term (2026-2027): Hybrid production will sustain the industry at moderate levels as 20% annual hybrid growth continues, and CAFE standards will keep demand for efficiency-focused transmissions alive. However, this masks a deeper erosion. Medium-term (2027-2030): EV penetration is expected to accelerate beyond current 5-6% share; every 10-percentage-point gain in EV sales eliminates roughly $3-4 billion in traditional transmission demand. Long-term (2030+): Transmission manufacturing reverts to a niche for hybrids, performance EVs (which may use multi-speed gearboxes), and off-highway/commercial vehicles (where heavy-duty transmissions remain essential). Cost pressures from tariffs and supply chain fragmentation will continue squeezing margins and forcing smaller suppliers out. M&A will intensify as Tier 1 suppliers consolidate to survive the transition. Investment is already flowing into EV drivetrain components and electric motor-gearbox integration; legacy transmission makers that fail to invest heavily in this pivot risk obsolescence by 2035.
themes: Hybrid momentum and multi-speed transmission innovation
tariff and trade volatility crushing margins

title: Aircraft, Engine & Parts Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Defense spending and commercial aircraft backlogs are driving double-digit growth, but engine shortages and skilled labor constraints threaten to choke the recovery.
overview: Aircraft engine and parts manufacturing is in the strongest growth phase in nearly a decade, powered by record commercial aircraft backlogs and a 42% increase in U.S. defense spending for 2026. The industry hit $287.9 billion in revenue in 2026, up 7% that year. Yet the boom is constrained by a bottleneck crisis: Pratt & Whitney's defective Geared Turbofan engines have grounded roughly 350 commercial aircraft and forced Airbus to cut production targets, while shortages in critical materials (titanium up 90% since 2022), skilled manufacturing labor, and qualified engineers are slowing both Boeing and Airbus. These structural frictions—not cyclical downturns—are now the main limit to how fast the industry can grow.

key_stats.employees: 2.23 million workers (A&D sector, including indirect); 409,895 in this industry as of 2022
key_stats.profit_margin: 7.1% (2026 forecast)
key_stats.concentration: Boeing holds largest share; Raytheon Technologies and GE Aviation also major players

current_dynamics: The US aircraft and defense industry is firing on all cylinders: pent-up airline demand after the pandemic is meeting a record backlog of over 10,000 aircraft orders, and geopolitical tensions (Ukraine, Asia, Middle East) have triggered defense budgets not seen since the Cold War—the Pentagon is spending 4.5% of GDP on national security in 2026. Yet the industry cannot scale fast enough. Pratt & Whitney's contaminated powdered-metal components in Geared Turbofan (GTF) engines grounded 1,200 engines and ~350 aircraft through 2026; Airbus has had to throttle back A320 family production from 75 units/month (2027 target) because P&W won't commit to promised engine deliveries. Boeing is also stuck: its 787 production slipped below 8/month in Q1 2026 due to GEnx engine delays, and the 777-9 first delivery was pushed to 2027. Beyond engines, the supply chain is crimped by titanium and copper shortages (titanium costs +90% since 2022), and the workforce crisis is acute—29% of the A&D workforce is over 55, the industry needs 3,800 new aerospace engineers per year through 2031, and there is a net shortage of 5,200 skilled machinists and fabricators expected in Washington state alone by end-2026. These are not short-term blips: they are structural capacity ceilings that manufacturers must solve to unlock growth.
one_sentence: The industry is booming on defense budgets and commercial demand, but production bottlenecks in engines, materials, and skilled labor are the new constraint.
whats_growing: Commercial aircraft orders and deliveries. Airbus targets 870 deliveries in 2026 and is shifting toward high-margin A321neo. Boeing is ramping 737 MAX production (planned 38/month by mid-2025) and has record 787 backlog. Defense spending on F-35 stealth fighters (156/year sustained production by Lockheed Martin), KC-46 tankers, B-21 stealth bombers, missiles, and unmanned systems. International defense exports, especially to allies wanting F-35s and to Middle East and Asia amid geopolitical tension. Reshoring of aerospace manufacturing and supply chain investments to reduce China dependency.
whats_shrinking: Margin growth is being compressed: profit margins are improving to 7.1% in 2026 (up from pandemic lows) but are still below pre-2020 levels. Aircraft engine lease rates have surged (GTF engines ~$200,000/month), making older aircraft less competitive. Wide-body aircraft demand remains softer than narrow-body as airlines optimize fleets. Supplier consolidation continues, squeezing smaller operators. Some uncertainty around sustained F-35 buys: the Air Force is now buying only 24 F-35s in fiscal 2026 (half the prior plan), though Lockheed Martin is holding production at 156/year betting on strong international demand.

baseline_2022.growth: -3.6% CAGR (2017–2022); rebound to +2.36% CAGR projected 2022–2028 per 2022 report

recent_developments: 2026 Q1: Boeing 787 production slipped below 8/month due to GEnx engine delays; 777-9 first delivery pushed to 2027. Airbus A320 family monthly rates capped at ~65-70 due to Pratt & Whitney engine delivery shortfalls.

2026 Q2: Pentagon proposes $913.9 billion defense budget (Senate Armed Services Committee authorizes $32.1B above request for F-35, shipbuilding, munitions). Lockheed Martin sustains 156 F-35/year production; Air Force requests 24 F-35A (half prior amount) but Navy/Marine orders remain steady.

2026 ongoing: Pratt & Whitney confirms GTF engine deliveries up >50% vs. 2019 but contaminated metal defects in 1,200 engines ground ~350 commercial aircraft; company claims it will largely resolve by end-2026 but airlines and Airbus remain skeptical.

2025–2026: Titanium costs +90% since 2022; tariffs on aerospace materials add complexity; reshoring initiatives launched to build domestic supply chain redundancy. Skilled labor shortage crisis: 29% of A&D workforce >55 years old; shortage of 5,200 machinists/fabricators in Washington state projected by end-2026.

2026: Airbus targets 870 commercial aircraft deliveries (vs. 900 prior guidance); shifts portfolio to A321neo which is now ~67% of A320-family backlog. Boeing aims to deliver highest commercial aircraft in 7 years but supply chain caps production.

2024–2026: GE Aviation, CFM, and Rolls-Royce engines also experiencing supply and reliability issues beyond Pratt & Whitney; wider engine industry capacity constraints evident across all three major OEMs.
outlook: Through 2027 and beyond, the industry will remain supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained. Commercial aircraft orders are firm (airlines want to replace aging fleets and meet green mandates), and defense budgets will stay elevated due to geopolitical risk. However, the main limit to growth is operational capacity: Pratt & Whitney, GE Aviation, and CFM will take years to fully resolve engine production and quality issues; titanium and specialized materials will remain expensive and intermittently scarce; and the aerospace workforce will struggle to hire and retain qualified engineers, machinists, and composite fabricators. Manufacturers are responding by investing heavily in vertical integration, adding capacity, training programs, and digital supply chain visibility—but these measures take 18–24 months to yield results. The industry will likely grow 5–8% annually through 2028, but growth will be erratic month-to-month and aircraft delivery schedules will remain hostage to engine supplier performance. By 2027, if Pratt & Whitney and GE solve their reliability and capacity problems, growth could accelerate to low double-digits; if not, the industry may struggle to exceed 6% growth even with record order backlogs.

Raytheon Technologies Corporation (defense platforms, F-35 production support)

GE Aviation (commercial and military engines, supply constraints)

Pratt & Whitney / RTX (Geared Turbofan engines, major bottleneck in 2026)

title: Iron & Steel Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature, consolidating industry gaining tariff-driven price relief but trapped by global oversupply and weakening demand from construction and automotive.
overview: The US steel industry recovered ground in 2025-2026 after years of decline. Tariffs imposed in early 2025 boosted prices 20-30%, lifted domestic production to world third-largest, and narrowed imports by 30%. Profit margins improved to 12.3% EBITDA in 2026. But this is tactical relief, not structural recovery. Global oversupply is worsening (745 million tonnes excess capacity projected by 2028), demand from construction and autos is flat or declining, and the shift to electric vehicles and lightweight materials will suppress steel consumption for years. The industry is shrinking toward a smaller, more efficient footprint dominated by EAF mills and a handful of integrated producers.

key_stats.profit_margin: 12.3% EBITDA (Q2 2026 TTM); sub-5% net margins
key_stats.concentration: Highly concentrated; top 3 control majority of capacity

current_dynamics: Tariffs imposed in February-June 2025 created a 50% import wall (with later refinements), triggering a price spike and domestic production surge—the US became third-largest steel producer in 2025. However, this windfall is eroding. Raw material costs (iron ore +9%, coking coal +17%, scrap +2% for 2025) are rising, and the margin between input and selling prices has tightened since spring 2025. Demand from construction (flat volume despite 2.6% spending growth) and automotive (10.2M units, steady but shrinking per-vehicle steel content as EVs grow to 42% of output by 2031) is not rallying. Global oversupply is the immovable problem: China exported a record 131 million tonnes of steel in 2025 (up 153% since 2020), and the OECD warns global excess capacity will grow from 640 to 745 million tonnes by 2028 as producers add 139 million tonnes of capacity while demand grows only 34 million tonnes. The industry is consolidating rapidly—Cleveland-Cliffs acquired ArcelorMittal and Stelco, and Nippon Steel completed its $14.2 billion buyout of US Steel in June 2025 under government oversight. Employment remains depressed (net decline since 2021), and labor shortage is now the number-one constraint on growth.
one_sentence: US steel bounced from tariffs in 2025-2026 but faces structural headwinds: global oversupply, flat demand, and the permanent shift to lighter vehicles—making recovery unlikely despite short-term margin gains.
whats_growing: Electric arc furnace (EAF) capacity and specialty/value-added steel grades (high-strength alloys for EVs and advanced structures). EAF represented 93% of newly announced steelmaking capacity in 2024. Profit margins improved sharply in 2025-2026 on tariff-driven prices (EBITDA rose from low single digits to 12.3%). Domestic production surged nearly 5 million tons in 2025 under tariff protection, pushing US to third-largest global producer.
whats_shrinking: Traditional integrated blast furnace mills and commodity carbon steel grades face permanent margin pressure and market share loss. Global demand has declined four straight years and is down over 2% in 2025. Automotive steel demand is falling as EVs use less steel and more aluminum; IC vehicle steel consumption falls from 64% of production (2025) to one-third by 2031. Employment in the US industry has declined 2.3% annually since 2021. Number of steelmaking businesses fell from 332 (2022) to 196 (2026). Construction volume is flat despite nominal spending growth (growth doesn't offset inflation and labor cost growth).
major_players: Nucor Corporation (largest independent EAF producer)
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. (now largest US integrated producer after ArcelorMittal/Stelco acquisitions, forming alliance with POSCO)
Nippon Steel Corporation (owns US Steel as of June 2025, with US government oversight)
Steel Dynamics (major EAF operator)
Commercial Metals Company (North America steel group, improving margins)
recent_developments: June 2025: Nippon Steel completed $14.2 billion acquisition of US Steel under US government 'Golden Share' veto provision
June 2025: US became third-largest steel producer globally in 2025, surpassing rivals due to tariff-driven capacity boost
April 2026: Trump administration refined Section 232 tariffs—derivative articles at 25%, industrial equipment at 15%
February 2025: Trump imposed initial 25-50% steel tariffs; June 2025 doubled to 50% for most countries, expanded June 2025 to appliance products
Early 2026: Steel imports down 30% year-to-date; raw material costs rising (iron ore +9%, coking coal +17% for 2025)
September 2025: Algoma Steel completed transition to EAF with first heat in new Danieli facility
themes: Tariff-driven price floor (temporary relief masking structural oversupply)
EAF dominance (93% of new capacity; traditional mills in retreat)
Global overcapacity crisis (745M tonnes excess by 2028)
Automotive electrification (EVs rise to 42% by 2031; less steel per vehicle)
Labor shortage and wage pressure (number-one constraint on growth)
Consolidation and foreign ownership (Nippon-USS, Cleveland-Cliffs scale-up, POSCO investment)
outlook: Tariff protection will keep US domestic prices elevated relative to global commodity prices through 2026-2027, supporting EBITDA margins near 12%. However, global oversupply and falling demand will eventually overwhelm tariff effects. Revenue is likely flat to declining through 2028 (2026 OECD and recent forecasts vs. 2022's optimistic 0.1% growth). The industry will likely shrink to a leaner footprint: EAF mills and specialty producers thrive, integrated mills rationalize or exit, and employment continues to decline despite automation offsetting some job losses. Profit margins will oscillate with steel prices but remain compressed by input cost pressure (raw materials and labor). The structural shift to EVs (42% by 2031) is permanent and will suppress total steel consumption. Tariffs may redirect trade flows and slow Chinese exports to the US, but cannot reverse global oversupply or EV-driven demand decline. Consolidation accelerates—more M&A and closures expected. The best-case scenario is a stable but shrinking industry with decent returns for EAF operators and specialty mills; worst-case is a price war as global overcapacity forces competitors to cut margins to gain share.

title: Aluminum Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: The US aluminum industry is booming on surging prices, tariffs, and EV demand, but facing a severe energy crunch that keeps smelters shut despite record global prices.
overview: The US aluminum manufacturing industry has swung from slow decline into robust growth since 2023. Tariffs jumped from 25% to 50% in 2025-2026, driving prices up 25% year-over-year by mid-2026 to $3,273/ton. Domestic automakers are piling into aluminum to lighten EVs, offsetting decades of outsourcing. Yet the industry faces a crippling bottleneck: electricity costs have risen 10-20% globally, and tech companies are outbidding smelters for power, leaving half of US primary smelting capacity idle despite record aluminum scarcity.

key_stats.employees: 165,000 direct jobs (2025-2026); secondary/recycling jobs up 20%+ since 2024
key_stats.profit_margin: Data not available for 2025-2026
key_stats.businesses: Four primary smelters (Alcoa and Century Aluminum); Novelis and 100+ secondary processors; 364 enterprises (2022 baseline)
key_stats.concentration: Alcoa and Century control US primary smelting; Novelis dominates rolled products (secondary)

current_dynamics: Aluminum prices surged 25% year-over-year by August 2026 to $3,273/ton, driven by China's production ceiling (45.5M tons by end-2026) capping global supply, Russia's export collapse, and the 50% US tariff rate enacted June 2025. Automotive demand accelerated as EV makers demand aluminum for battery enclosures and body panels to offset battery weight. However, the primary smelting sector remains half-idled: four US smelters produce only 683,500 tonnes/year with just two at full capacity because electricity now costs $115+/MWh—tech companies outbidding aluminum makers for renewable power. Secondary (recycled) aluminum boomed as energy-efficient alternative: 85% of US-made aluminum is now recycled, up from 20-30% in the 1980s. Novelis, the largest rolled-products maker, lost production due to fires at Oswego, NY (Sept-Nov 2025) but is opening Bay Minette, Alabama (600 kt capacity) in H2 2026. Century Aluminum restarted Mt. Holly capacity in June 2026 after $50M investment.
one_sentence: US aluminum manufacturing is supply-constrained and price-booming in 2025-2026, with tariff protection and EV demand driving growth—but kept from expanding by an electricity crisis that makes smelting uncompetitive against AI data centers.
whats_growing: Electric vehicle demand (EV body/battery enclosures accounted for surge in automotive aluminum), secondary/recycled aluminum production (now 85% of US output, up from 30% in 1980s, with jobs up 20%+ since 2024), aluminum exports (tariff protection making US smelting competitive again), downstream sheet/plate manufacturing, and wage growth (full-time average $73,675/year).
whats_shrinking: Primary aluminum smelting capacity utilization (only 2 of 4 smelters at full capacity despite record prices), import volume ($18B in 2025 vs. $19B in 2024), and China's global export share (expected to drop 9% in 2025 due to tax rebate removal).
recent_developments: June 2025: US tariffs on aluminum imports doubled from 25% to 50%; aluminum prices climbed from $2,400-2,700/ton range.
July 2026: Trump administration announced 50%→25% tariff reduction for companies committing to domestic investment, extending beyond North American suppliers.
June 2026: US aluminum industry jobs hit 165,000 with secondary/recycling employment up 20%+ since 2024; direct economic output reached $115 billion (highest since 2013).
Sept 2025–Nov 2025: Novelis suffered two major fires at Oswego, NY facility, disrupting rolled-product shipments 5% in fiscal 2026.
June 2026: Century Aluminum completed Mt. Holly smelter restart (+50k tonnes/year), bringing it to full capacity after $50M investment.
Aug 2026: LME aluminum price reached $3,273/ton, up 25.13% year-over-year; forecast to test $3,000/ton in H1 2026 then moderate to $2,700-2,800/ton.
major_players: Alcoa Corporation (two primary smelters, full production; 2025 revenue $12.8B, net income $1.2B; 2026 forecast 2.4-2.6M metric tons)
Century Aluminum (two primary smelters, half-idled until Mt. Holly restart June 2026; 2025 revenue $2.5B, adjusted EBITDA $425.1M)
Novelis Inc. (secondary/rolled products, largest in North America; FY2026 revenue $18.4B; Bay Minette plant (600 kt) opening H2 2026)
Rio Tinto, Constellium (international competitors with US operations)
outlook: The 2026-2027 outlook is bifurcated. Prices remain elevated at $2,700-3,000/ton through 2026 due to China's production ceiling and tariff protection, supporting Alcoa and Century earnings. Automotive aluminum demand stays strong as EV penetration deepens (automotive aluminum market projected $117.76B in 2026, up to $283.67B by 2035 at 9.7% CAGR). Secondary aluminum and downstream processors (sheet, foil, extrusions) will capture most of this demand growth because primary smelting stays constrained. The central risk is electricity: unless US policy prioritizes smelter power allocation or renewable capacity doubles, primary capacity will remain half-idle even with $3,000+ ton prices. China's capacity ceiling will support prices through 2026-2027, but if new non-Chinese smelting (Indonesia, Kazakhstan) comes online and US tariff relief continues, prices could ease to $2,200-2,400/ton by 2027, pressuring margins. Employment will remain stable at 165k+ due to secondary/recycling growth offsetting primary smelting declines.
themes: Secondary aluminum dominance (85% of US production)

title: Chemical Product Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Mid-sized intermediate chemical manufacturers face tariff shocks and commodity volatility, swinging between margin pressure and selective M&A-driven consolidation as downstream demand weakens short-term but recovers through 2027.
overview: The US chemical product manufacturing industry is a mature, capital-intensive sector worth $53.1 billion in 2026, growing at 1.9% CAGR since 2021. Roughly 1,616 businesses compete in custom resin compounding, toners, and specialty chemicals, with tariffs imposed in early 2025 raising raw material and feedstock costs by 8-15%. Domestic demand from automotive and construction weakened through mid-2026 as manufacturers delayed projects in response to tariff uncertainty, but the industry is posting strong short-term growth (6.8% in 2025) as prior inventory drawdowns reverse and crude oil volatility stabilizes. Regulatory pressure on emissions (PFAS, greenhouse gases) and accelerating automation adoption are reshaping production economics.

key_stats.profit_margin: 6.5% (2022); current compressed by tariff pass-through; firms struggling to pass all costs downstream
key_stats.concentration: Moderate; Lubrizol Corp. is largest player but no monopoly; specialty chemicals fragmented

current_dynamics: Tariffs imposed in early 2025 at 10% universal rates plus 20-50% levies on selected countries immediately raised feedstock costs 8-15%, forcing many makers to absorb losses rather than fully pass costs to buyers still reeling from prior price spikes. Crude oil swung from $64/bbl baseline (2022) to $84.81/bbl in June 2026, creating ongoing feedstock volatility; chemical makers cannot easily forecast production costs. Downstream demand collapsed in automotive and construction through mid-2026 as those sectors delayed projects under tariff and rate uncertainty, but Q1-Q2 2026 showed early recovery as inventory-drawdown demand rebounded and trade policy stabilized slightly. Manufacturers are now investing heavily in automation, digital twins, and predictive maintenance (which can cut maintenance costs 25%) to preserve thin margins. M&A activity rebounded sharply in 2025 (global deal value +18% YoY), with large players like Borouge acquiring NOVA for $13.4B and Covestro ($14.7B) as they consolidate into specialty/high-margin segments and exit commodities.
one_sentence: Tariffs and volatile crude oil are squeezing margins on intermediate chemical production, forcing selective consolidation and automation investment while downstream demand swings from weakness to tentative recovery.
whats_growing: Specialty chemicals (coatings, composites, high-durability polymers), custom resin compounding for automotive electrification and lighter materials, digital transformation and AI-powered R&D, green chemistry and sustainable manufacturing (green chemicals market projected $156B in 2026), and medical/health/nutrition polymers as strategic buyers shift there.
whats_shrinking: Photographic chemicals and materials (declining for over a decade as digital replaces film), general commodities facing tariff-driven margin compression, small regional competitors unable to absorb tariff losses, and traditional bulk chemical production in favor of specialty/performance segments.
recent_developments: Early 2025: U.S. imposed 10% universal tariff + 20-50% targeted levies; China reciprocal tariffs set at 125%; chemical feedstock costs rose 8-15%
2025: Global M&A volume surged 18% YoY; Borouge/NOVA ($13.4B), ADNOC/Covestro ($14.7B), Carlyle/BASF coatings ($7.7B stake)
Mid-2025: U.S. chemical production rebounded 3.3% after 2024 recovery, but growth forecast slows to 0.6% in 2025 and turns negative (-0.8%) in 2026 before recovery
2025-2026: EPA shifted to deregulation focus but TSCA fee authority expires Sept 30, 2026; PFAS reporting and ELGs remain active; Congress weighing TSCA modifications

Q1-Q2 2026: Inventory-driven demand recovery; crude oil volatile ($84.81/bbl June 2026); automotive/construction demand remains soft but expectations turn positive for late 2026 on expansionary fiscal policy
2026: Digital transformation in chemicals valued at $20.45B; AI in chemicals at $2.18B; predictive maintenance adoption accelerating (up to 70% reduction in breakdowns)
outlook: Over 2026-2027, the industry faces a two-phase outlook. Near-term (rest of 2026) remains pressured: tariff uncertainty, automotive and construction weakness, and crude oil volatility will keep profit margins thin (well below the 6.5% 2022 baseline). Production is forecast to contract 0.8% in 2026 before rebounding. However, 2027 onwards looks brighter: U.S. chemicals production is forecast to rebound 4.2% in 2027 and sustain 3%+ annual growth in 2028-2029 as fiscal stimulus lifts consumer and business spending, housing recovers, and automotive electrification continues driving specialty chemical demand. Tariff policy uncertainty remains the single biggest wild card. Industry consolidation will continue as commodity players retreat and specialty-focused firms expand via M&A. Automation and AI adoption will become table stakes for margin preservation. Regulatory costs will rise on emissions and PFAS compliance, but deregulation push may soften some pressures. The green chemicals market ($156B in 2026) is a bright spot attracting capital. Small independents will struggle; scaled, strategic players focused on performance additives, medical polymers, and sustainability will thrive.
themes: automation and digital transformation for margin defense
crude oil and feedstock price pass-through friction

title: Cement Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: The US cement industry (84 million tons in 2025) is caught between strong infrastructure demand, tariff headwinds, green cement acceleration, and stubborn capacity constraints.
overview: The US cement market was valued at USD 16.94 billion in 2025 and is estimated to reach USD 17.49 billion in 2026, with growth running 3–4% annually through the decade. The industry remains dominated by five players—LafargeHolcim, Martin Marietta Materials, CEMEX, HeidelbergCement, and Buzzi Unicem—who control pricing and capacity. Production is running around 82–84 million metric tons per year, flat to declining from 2023 levels, constrained by idle plants and underutilization. The core tension: federal infrastructure spending (IIJA) is still flowing (only 40% deployed by September 2025), yet domestic production capacity cannot keep pace, so imports fill 21% of demand. Tariffs on cement hit 25% starting April 2025, shifting competitive dynamics sharply.
one_sentence: The US cement industry navigates a paradox: federal infrastructure projects are boosting demand, but domestic capacity is maxed out, tariffs deter imports, and a shift to lower-carbon cement is reshaping production economics.

key_stats.growth: 3–4% CAGR through 2034; consumption declined 1.6% in 2025, recovery expected 2026–2027
key_stats.businesses: 5 major firms (LafargeHolcim, Martin Marietta, CEMEX, HeidelbergCement, Buzzi Unicem); 187 establishments (2022, declining at 1% annually)
key_stats.concentration: Top 5 control 60–65% of market; medium-to-high concentration after decades of M&A
key_stats.profit_margin: 4–5% EBIT margin (tight); CEMEX achieved USD 939M net income in 2024 but on flat/declining volumes

current_dynamics: Domestic production capacity is frozen around 102–105 million metric tons annually, yet consumption sits 105–108 million tons, forcing reliance on 25–26 million tons of imports (21% of apparent consumption in 2025). The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) deployed only USD 500 billion of USD 1.2 trillion committed to roads, bridges, and utilities—only 40% spent by September 2025—but created a durable multi-year pipeline of highway and bridge projects (207,000+ miles of roadway, 11,400+ bridge projects underway). This props up demand even as residential construction saturates and nonresidential office slackens. The 25% cement tariff (effective April 2025) has begun to shrink import competition: Canadian and Mexican imports, which used to account for 27% of the market, are now price-uncompetitive, while Turkish cement (lowest tariff rate) and Vietnamese suppliers face punitive duties (46% on Vietnam). Portland-limestone cement (PLC, Type IL) now dominates: 97% of blended cement shipments are PLC; all 50 states approved it by April 2024, and PLC's 10% lower CO2 footprint versus traditional Portland makes it the industry standard going forward.
whats_growing: Green and low-carbon cement (PLC, Vertua-branded products): CEMEX's Vertua line hit 63% of cement sales and 55% of concrete sales in 2024, exceeding 2025 targets. Global green cement market running 9–10% CAGR; North America holds 37% of global green cement share. Nonresidential construction (commercial, industrial, data centers): 2025 saw steady 6% price increases for civil work and 6–8% for ready-mix concrete. Data center construction is emerging as a new cement end-market as semiconductor and AI infrastructure expands. Infrastructure projects tied to IIJA: highway and bridge work will sustain cement demand through 2027.
whats_shrinking: Portland cement consumption (pure OPC phasing out in favor of PLC/blended). Domestic production volume: 82–84 million tons in 2025 vs. 84 million in 2024 and 86 million in 2023. Residential cement demand: saturated markets and rising mortgage rates suppress single-family housing starts. Masonry cement: down 2.7% in 2025 to 2.1 million tons.
how_it_makes_money: Cement manufacturers sell to ready-mix concrete plants (70% of revenue), precast concrete makers, concrete pipe and block producers, and wholesalers who serve construction end-users. Revenue is volume times price. Margins compress due to high energy costs (coal for kilns, electricity for grinding), raw material costs (limestone, clay, clinker), and labor. Price-based competition is fierce; differentiation is minimal. Vertical integration into aggregates and ready-mix (as Martin Marietta does) and into finished concrete products (CEMEX's strategy) captures downstream margin. Switching to alternative fuels (waste-derived fuels, biomass) and lower-carbon clinker recipes reduces energy cost and improves carbon positioning for regulatory compliance and premium pricing on green cement.
cost_structure: Energy (coal, electricity, alternative fuels): 30–40% of cost. Raw materials (limestone, clay, silica, gypsum, clinker): 20–30%. Labor: 10–15%. Kiln and grinding operations are capital-intensive but relatively automated. Transportation (cement is heavy, 50–150 mile distribution radius typical) drives costs sharply after leaving the plant.
recent_developments: April 2025: 25% tariff on cement imports takes effect; import volumes already declining (8% year-on-year in 2024, 25.4 million tons in 2025)
July 2025: CRH announced acquisition of Eco Material Technologies to scale near-zero-carbon cementitious materials
Q3 2025: CEMEX reported 19% EBITDA growth to USD 2.27 billion, first consolidated net sales increase since Q1 2024, signaling demand recovery
Q1 2026 (expected): Martin Marietta's exchange of Midlothian cement plant to QuikCrete for Virginia, Missouri, Kansas aggregates assets (announced 2025, closes Q1 2026)
November 2024: HeidelbergCement acquired Giant Cement Holding to expand East Coast footprint and capacity
Ongoing: All 50 US states adopted Portland-limestone cement (PLC) by April 2024; OPC supply phasing out; green cement (Vertua, Type IL) now over 97% of blended shipments
major_players: LafargeHolcim Ltd (formed 2015 merger of Lafarge SA and Holcim Ltd) – number-two player, multinational
Martin Marietta Materials Inc (acquired Texas Industries Inc in 2014) – number-three player, vertically integrated into aggregates and ready-mix
CEMEX SAB de CV – largest player, multinational Mexican company; Vertua low-carbon brand leader
HeidelbergCement – German multinational; acquired Giant Cement in November 2024 for East Coast expansion
Buzzi Unicem – Italian-based player, global footprint
themes: Capacity constraint and import dependency (21% of consumption via imports, 25% tariff risk)
Tariff regime reshaping trade (25% on cement, Turkey favored over Vietnam)
Green cement transition (PLC/Type IL now over 97% of blends; 10% CO2 reduction)
Consolidation and vertical integration (5 majors dominating, asset swaps ongoing)
Margin pressure and energy costs (4–5% EBIT, alternative fuels adoption race)
outlook: 2026–2027 will see modest recovery (1–2% growth) as IIJA infrastructure projects ramp and nonresidential construction rebounds. Residential construction remains soft but stable. Tariffs will remain a structural headwind, protecting domestic producers from Turkish and Asian imports but raising input costs and consumer prices 2–3%. Green cement adoption will accelerate; PLC will become 70% or more of shipments by 2027. Capacity utilization will improve only if new plants open or existing idled capacity reactivates—unlikely without major capex commitment. Import reliance will stay at 18–22% despite tariffs. Consolidation will continue; smaller players will either sell assets or merge. Long-term (2028–2030): Infrastructure spending will moderate post-IIJA, flattening demand back to low single-digit growth. Carbon pricing or stricter NOx regulations (EPA 2026 NOx rule beginning) may accelerate alternative fuel adoption and carbon capture investment.

title: Computer Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US computer manufacturing is accelerating due to AI server demand and government reshoring policy, but consumer PC shipments face a 13% collapse in 2026 from supply constraints and price spikes.
overview: The US computer manufacturing industry is experiencing sharp bifurcation in 2025-2026. Consumer PC demand has weakened dramatically—shipments are forecast to drop 13% in 2026 as memory and storage costs spike 60–70% and the Windows 11 refresh cycle ends. Meanwhile, AI-driven server demand is booming: AI server shipments grew 42% year-over-year in 2025, and hyperscalers plan $400 billion in data center capex in 2026. Tariffs on Chinese computer imports (ranging 10–40% since 2025) are reshaping supply chains, though computers were briefly exempted in April 2025. Government CHIPS Act investment has spurred 18 new semiconductor fabs under construction, with production expected 2026–2027, signaling a real domestic foundry resurgence led by Intel's Arizona operation now producing 18A chips.

key_stats.concentration: Six major PC makers dominate: Lenovo 25.4%, HP, Dell, Apple, ASUS, Acer; server segment led by Dell, Super Micro, HPE

current_dynamics: The market is cleaved between consumer and enterprise. Consumer PC shipments hit 18.2 million units in Q4 2025 (3% growth), but Q1 2026 dropped 7% to 15.8 million units as DRAM and SSD costs surged 40–70% year-to-date, with further 60% increases expected in Q1 2026. Predictions now show 13% annual decline for 2026 and no recovery to 2025 levels until 2029. Conversely, AI servers are the bright spot: Dell shipped record $113.5 billion revenue in FY2026 (ending Jan 30) with 40% growth in infrastructure solutions and a $43 billion order backlog. HP's PC revenue grew 11% in Q1 FY2026 despite the broader market weakness. Tariff policy is volatile—computers were exempted from reciprocal tariffs in April 2025 but the Administration plans separate computer tariffs within months; Chinese laptop exports to the US fell 47.6% YoY in April 2025. Semiconductor reshoring is accelerating: Intel's Fab 52 in Arizona now produces 18A chips, TSMC is expanding Arizona operations, and Samsung/SK Hynix are building US fabs, all supported by $52.7 billion in CHIPS Act funding spread across 18 planned factories.
one_sentence: US computer manufacturing rebounds via server buildout but consumer PC demand collapses 13% in 2026 from component shortages and tariff uncertainty.
whats_growing: AI server demand (42% YoY shipment growth in 2025, hyperscalers committing $400B in 2026 capex), domestic semiconductor fabs (18 new plants under construction via CHIPS Act), enterprise infrastructure buys (Dell infrastructure revenue +40% FY2026), and higher-end workstations for AI/ML workloads.
whats_shrinking: Consumer PC shipments (forecast -13% in 2026), mainstream laptop demand (especially sub-$500 segment hit by DRAM/SSD cost spike of 60–70%), and import volume from China (laptop exports to US -47.6% YoY April 2025); also memory chip production capacity outside US data centers is constrained.
how_it_makes_money: Computer manufacturers assemble PCs, laptops, and servers by sourcing standardized components (motherboards, CPUs, memory, storage, GPUs) from semiconductor and component suppliers, then sell through direct/retail channels and OEM channels to consumers, businesses, and cloud operators. High-margin segments: enterprise servers (sold to data centers and corporates), AI-optimized platforms (3–5x ASP premium vs general-purpose servers), and software/services bundles. Low-margin segments: consumer laptops and desktops (commoditized, price-competitive, vulnerable to imports). Revenue from services (IT consulting, support, cloud platform integration) growing as a diversification strategy among top players (Dell, HP).
major_players: Dell (infrastructure group $60.8B FY2026 revenue, 40% growth, $43B order backlog)
HP (PC revenue +11% Q1 FY2026, $14.4B quarterly revenue)
Lenovo (25.4% laptop market share, 70.9M units shipped in 2025)
Apple (high-end/design segment, domestic Mac Pro assembly in Texas announced 2019)
ASUS (top 5 PC maker, gaming/prosumer focus)
Acer (top 6 PC maker)
Intel (Fab 52 Arizona producing 18A chips domestically)
Super Micro Computer (enterprise servers, AI infrastructure specialist)
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE, data center and server focus)
recent_developments: January 15, 2026: US and Taiwan sign $250B direct-investment semiconductor agreement to strengthen US chip reshoring (Taiwanese firms commit to US fabs)
CES 2026 (January): Intel launches first 18A chip production at Arizona Fab 52; Panther Lake (Core Ultra 300) claims 50% CPU/GPU perf gain; CEO notes AI demand exceeds capacity
April 2025: Trump administration exempts computers (and smartphones, parts) from reciprocal tariffs but signals plans for separate computer tariffs within 1–2 months
Q1 2026 (March): US PC shipments drop 7% to 15.8M units; Omdia forecasts 13% annual decline for 2026 due to memory/storage cost spike of 40–70% YoY
Q4 2025 (December): US PC market returns to 3% growth (18.2M units) driven by Windows 11 refresh and vendor inventory build ahead of supply crunch

2025 (ongoing): 18 new semiconductor factories planned to start construction with 2026–2027 production dates; CHIPS Act $52.7B funding supports reshoring across US and allied nations (Taiwan, South Korea investments)
outlook: The next 18 months will be defined by bifurcation and reshoring momentum colliding with near-term pain. Consumer PC shipments are forecast to remain depressed through 2027 (not recovering to 2025 levels until 2029) due to persistent memory/storage cost pressure and the cooling of the Windows upgrade cycle; sub-$500 laptops will take the worst hit. However, enterprise and AI server demand will remain robust—Dell's infrastructure backlog and NVIDIA/AMD's AI chip momentum suggest server shipments will grow 8–12% annually through 2027. Tariff policy will be key: if computer tariffs land at 15–25% (vs. the current 10–40% range on China electronics), it may accelerate reshoring of assembly but slow consumer demand further. CHIPS Act funding will begin delivering new US fabs (Intel 18A production now live, TSMC/Samsung Arizona operations ramping), reducing semiconductor import dependency and potentially lowering component costs by 2027–2028. Long-term (2027+): industry revenue could stabilize at $23–25B annually ($22.3B in 2026 + modest growth) as server-heavy revenue mix offsets consumer PC decline, and domestic chip supply reduces BOM costs and import penetration. Employment will edge up 2–3% annually as fab operations ramp (skilled manufacturing jobs) and AI/ML support roles grow.
themes: Consumer PC collapse and recovery delay
Component cost inflation and memory shortage

title: Engine & Turbine Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Diesel and turbine makers face a narrow growth window as tariffs spike costs, regulators tighten 2027 emissions rules, and supply chains buckle under surging demand for power and freight.
one_sentence: The US engine and turbine manufacturing industry generates $55 billion in 2026 with 1.6% annual growth, but tariff-driven input costs, stretched supplier capacity, and aggressive EPA emissions deadlines are reshaping competitive advantage toward domestic firms that can absorb higher costs and retool fast.
overview: The US engine and turbine manufacturing industry is a $55.0 billion market in 2026, growing 1.6% annually and driven by steady freight demand, infrastructure spend, and a global power shortage hunger for turbines. Cummins, Caterpillar, and GE dominate. The industry operates in a squeeze: tariffs on imported steel and components now cost producers $2–2.4 billion yearly, forcing pricing power tests and supply-chain reshoring; new EPA 2027 emissions rules cut nitrogen oxide limits 82–90%, pushing R&D spend and truck prices higher; and turbine makers face 5–8 year backlogs as data-center and AI-driven power demand outpaces manufacturing capacity. A small group of market leaders is consolidating via software and hybrid tech acquisitions (Caterpillar+RPMGlobal, Cummins+First Mode), while smaller competitors are getting squeezed on margin.

key_stats.employees: ~86,000–87,000 (estimated for 2026, based on 0.82% annual growth trend from 2022)
key_stats.profit_margin: 6.8% (2022 baseline); 2026 margin likely in 7–8% range based on tariff absorption and modest pricing power
key_stats.concentration: High: Cummins Inc. (largest), Caterpillar Inc., General Electric Company account for majority of revenue

baseline_2022.growth: -3.1% CAGR (2017–2022); +0.1% growth in 2022 itself as post-pandemic recovery peaked

current_dynamics: Tariffs are the defining headwind: 25% levies on imported steel, aluminum, and engine components inflated landed costs by an estimated $2–2.4 billion across 2026 for major producers like Caterpillar; some firms are reshoring components and locking in long-term US supplier contracts, raising operating leverage but spreading risk. Regulatory urgency is mounting: the EPA's 2027 heavy-duty engine rule cuts NOx limits 82–90%, forcing every truck and locomotive engine maker to redesign with tamper-proof emission controls and warranty extended 5–7 years; Detroit Diesel, Cummins, and John Deere are already shipping Gen-6 and 2027-compliant models, but the technology lift is steep and truck prices climb. Demand is uneven: freight trucking grew 70% in spot loads year-over-year (Q1 2026), and construction surged on rate cuts; but electrification is nibbling edges—China's new-energy HDTs now outsell diesel, and fleets are adopting hybrid short-haul—so the long-haul diesel franchise is secure but not booming. Supply-chain agony persists: turbine makers report 5–8 year lead times (up from 2–3 years), nickel superalloy and cobalt scarcity is acute, and skilled labor is tight; GE Vernova is scaling from 55 to 70–80 turbines per year by 2026 but has already sold out through 2029–2030, and competitors are lagging. Alternative fuels are real but not disruptive yet: Cummins and Volvo are in field trials on hydrogen engines, and natural-gas engines hold steady at ~15% of revenue, but diesel remains 60%+ and will until cost or regulation shifts faster.
whats_growing: Turbine manufacturing and power-generation equipment are booming: data-center power demand and AI-driven compute spending pushed GE Vernova's backlog to 80 GW extending into 2028–2029, with revenues forecast to rise ~25% in 2025 and ~20% in 2026. Heavy-duty diesel engines for trucks and construction are stable-to-growing as freight tonnage rises 3–5% annually and infrastructure spend continues; Detroit Diesel's order book jumped 125% year-over-year in 2026, pacing 36% ahead of last year. Natural-gas engines for power generation and industrial use are holding ground at 12–15% of revenue. Alternative-fuel platforms (hydrogen, hybrid, CNG) are ramping in R&D but volume is still under 5% of shipments.
whats_shrinking:
Legacy diesel exports are flat-to-down: US export share is capped by tariff friction and stronger dollar headwinds; exports likely hold near 46% of revenue. Commodity-sensitive demand (mining, oil-and-gas equipment) remains depressed post-2016 collapse and never fully recovered. Imports are under pressure: tariff barriers and reshoring are nudging the import penetration rate down from 47% of domestic demand (2022) toward 43–44% by 2026, as US makers invest in onshore capacity. Smaller regional engine makers continue to fade as consolidation favors large, diversified players like Cummins and Caterpillar that can absorb tariff shocks and fund emissions-compliance R&D.</shrinking>

Tariff wave, 2024–2026: 25% US tariffs on imported steel, aluminum, engine components; Caterpillar alone faces $2.2–2.4 billion annual tariff costs; reshoring initiatives launched by Cummins, Caterpillar

GE Vernova turbine expansion, 2025–2026: Capacity target raised from 55 to 70–80 heavy-duty turbines annually; 80-GW backlog sold out through 2028–2030; $300M capex for South Carolina, New York plants
Cummins hydrogen and multi-fuel platform launches, 2026: ConExpo rollout of 13L, 2600 Series multi-fuel engine; X15 available in diesel, biofuel, hydrogen at 400–700 hp
Caterpillar RPMGlobal acquisition, February 2026: Mining software company acquisition to boost predictive analytics and equipment efficiency; part of broader software-asset strategy
Cummins First Mode acquisition, February 2025: Hybrid retrofit kits for mining and industrial equipment; signals move into electrification retrofit market
Freight demand surge, Q1 2026: Spot load requests jumped 70% year-over-year; trucking freight tonnage forecast +3.1–4.8% for 2026 (construction materials +4.7%, consumer goods +5.2%)
outlook: Modest expansion through 2026–2027, then a juncture: the industry is on track for low-single-digit growth (1.5–2.5% annually through 2027) as long as freight holds and tariffs stabilize, but 2027 regulatory cliffs (EPA emissions, potential tariff escalation) will test pricing power. Turbine makers will stay supply-constrained; backlogs suggest prices will hold firm through 2028. Diesel engines remain core revenue (60%+), but the 2027 emissions crunch will accelerate natural-gas and hydrogen market-share capture; Cummins, Detroit Diesel, and Caterpillar are all shipping alternative-fuel platforms, so consolidation among smaller engine builders is likely. Tariffs favor large integrated producers that can absorb costs and relocate supply-chain chunks onshore; smaller regional players and pure imports face margin compression. Supply-chain normalization is 2–3 years away at best; nickel and cobalt scarcity will linger as EV demand competes. Outlook confidence is **moderate**: freight and power demand are strong, but tariff and regulatory uncertainty, stretched supplier capacity, and the slow pivot to zero-emission trucks create execution risk for the next 18–24 months.
themes: Alternative fuels (hydrogen, CNG, biofuel) entering volume
Consolidation via software and hybrid-tech acquisitions
how_it_makes_money: Diesel engines for trucks, locomotives, and marine vessels generate ~20% of revenue; natural-gas and alternative-fuel engines add ~12–15%; industrial turbines and generator sets for power generation add ~25%; mechanical power-transmission equipment (gears, drives) adds ~8%; remaining revenue from parts, accessories, and overhaul services. Exports (46% of revenue in 2022, likely holding near 45% in 2026) and domestic industrial/utility sector supply are roughly balanced. Margins compress during tariff spikes and inventory buildup but expand on volume and operational leverage once supply chains normalize.
cost_structure: Raw materials (steel, aluminum, nickel superalloys, castings) account for 50–60% of cost of goods sold; labor (skilled manufacturing, engineering) adds 15–20%; overhead (R&D, emissions compliance, quality, regulatory) adds 15–25%. Tariffs now inflate material costs by ~4–5 percentage points. Supply-chain complexity—turbine castings, rotor forgings, precision bearings, electronic controls—requires vertical integration or long-term contracts with tier-1 suppliers, limiting cost flexibility. Working capital is high due to long build cycles (6–18 months per engine or turbine) and customer advance deposits.
