title: Expert Networks
one_liner: A $1.8 billion US market of professional matchmakers connecting investors and corporate strategists with specialized experts through phone calls and consultations, rapidly expanding via AI-powered automation and consolidation around incumbents.
one_sentence: Expert networks are shifting from pay-per-call consulting to AI-driven transcript synthesis and agentic research workflows, with consolidation accelerating around players who control large, curated call libraries.
overview: The US expert networks industry stood at $1.8 billion in 2025, a 4.3% increase from the prior year. The global market—double that size at roughly $3–4 billion in 2025–26—is growing 12–16% annually, driven by large hedge funds and private equity firms seeking competitive edges on deal analysis. The industry has matured from its insider-trading scandal reputation of 2009–2012 into a compliance-focused research utility. In 2024–25, the big story was AlphaSense's $930 million acquisition of Tegus (June 2024), which merged the two largest expert-transcript libraries and signaled a shift away from expert sourcing toward AI-powered synthesis of existing call data. The competitive landscape is tightening: five players (AlphaSense-Tegus, GLG, Third Bridge, AlphaSights, Guidepoint) control roughly 60% of the market, while newer entrants are fragmenting the remainder. AI is no longer a future feature—it is the new battleground.

key_stats.growth: 12–16% CAGR globally; 4.3% in US in 2025; 7.0% CAGR past five years (US)
key_stats.businesses: ~65 independent companies in the US; five major players dominate 60% of market
key_stats.profit_margin: ~14% (down from 15.6% in 2016 due to higher labor and compliance costs)
key_stats.concentration: Moderate to increasing; top 5 control ~60%, but new entrants fragmenting the long tail

current_dynamics: The expert networks industry is at an inflection point where AI is rapidly redefining the business model itself. Historically, revenues came from scheduling one-off phone consultations between clients and experts at $1,200–$5,000 per call. Today, the profit engine is shifting toward platforms that ingest thousands of past call transcripts, apply large language models to synthesize insights on demand, and automate the sourcing and vetting of new experts. AlphaSense's acquisition of Tegus in mid-2024 was a watershed moment: by merging the two largest transcript libraries, the combined entity can now generate synthetic research from existing data at near-zero marginal cost, undercutting traditional pay-per-call models. This threatens the historical revenue stream but is offset by massive efficiency gains—a typical research project that took 2–5 days now takes 2 hours. Meanwhile, AI voice agents and automated channel checks (costing $100–$300 per data point instead of $2,000 per expert call) are emerging as a parallel threat from outside the industry. To compete, networks are racing to integrate agentic AI that can autonomously discover experts, schedule calls, transcribe sessions, and surface key themes without human intervention. The regulatory environment remains stable but vigilant: the SEC continues to scrutinize expert networks for material non-public information (MNPI) leakage, yet no new rules have been written since 2013, implying industry self-regulation is holding. Compliance costs are rising as firms adopt real-time monitoring, cooling-off periods for recent insiders, and documented audit trails. Client demand is broadening beyond hedge funds (the historical base) into private equity, corporate strategy, and market research teams—roughly half of spending now comes from consulting and market research, not just trading desks. The industry is also globalizing: Asian markets (particularly China) show high growth and laxer regulatory oversight, attracting aggressive expansion by GLG, AlphaSights, and others. Valuations remain strong despite AI disruption: venture funding continued to flow in 2024–25, with Arbolus raising $20 million in November 2024 and AlphaSense itself raising a new $650 million Series E in April 2026, valuing it at $4 billion.
recent_developments: AlphaSense completes $930 million acquisition of Tegus (June 2024), merging the two largest expert-transcript libraries under one roof and triggering analyst predictions of accelerating industry consolidation.
AlphaSense raises $650 million Series E funding, reaching a $4 billion valuation (April 2026), affirming investor confidence in AI-driven consolidation plays.

Slingshot Insights acquires Noble Insights (June 2025); Bridger acquires Deepbench (February 2024); and Levine Leichtman Capital Partners acquires The Expert Institute legal library (September 2024)—all signaling buy-vs-build dynamics in specialty transcript segments.

AI adoption accelerates: 61% of expert networks now use AI-driven expert matching, 56% schedule consultations within 24 hours, and agentic AI systems begin automating entire end-to-end research workflows in 2026—reducing sourcing time from 2–5 days to 2 hours.
Global user base expands to ~11,200 firms utilizing expert networks as of 2026, up 150% since 2022, with corporate and market-research adoption overtaking traditional hedge fund dominance.

Regulatory scrutiny persists without new rule changes: SEC enforcement actions against insider trading via expert networks continue; industry relies on self-imposed compliance (MNPI monitoring, cooling-off periods, audit trails) rather than statutory rules.
major_players: Gerson Lehrman Group (GLG) – largest by headcount with 1M+ experts, 19 global offices, $400M+ annual revenue (2025)
AlphaSense-Tegus (post-June 2024 merger) – dominant in transcript synthesis and AI; $4B valuation; 2026 Series E $650M
AlphaSights – 500K+ experts, 9 offices, $300M+ revenue; strong among consulting and PE clients
Third Bridge – $287M revenue in 2025 (15% YoY growth); focused on corporate strategy and innovation consulting
Guidepoint – top-5 player; competes on speed and C-suite access
how_it_makes_money: Expert networks charge clients (hedge funds, private equity, corporate strategy teams, law firms, market researchers) between $1,200 and $5,000 per expert consultation, typically 1–2 hour phone calls or in-person meetings. Clients also pay recurring retainers for on-demand expert access. The industry is transitioning from transaction-based revenue (per call) to platform revenue (transcript synthesis, API access, agentic AI workflows). Leading players like AlphaSense are monetizing backlogs of thousands of transcripts through natural-language search and AI-generated research syntheses, shifting from variable to fixed revenue streams and dramatically improving unit economics. Some firms offer specialized services—site visits, roundtables, advisory-board placements—at premium rates. Global expansion into Asia, where regulatory oversight is lighter and demand is high, is a growing revenue vector for players like GLG and Capvision.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant cost: expert networks pay consultants (academics, corporate executives, scientists, retired officials) a flat fee or hourly rate to participate in calls, plus commissions on scheduled time. Compliance costs have grown substantially—staff training, call monitoring, audit systems, and third-party monitoring partners (e.g., ACA Compliance Group) now consume 5–10% of revenue. Technology costs are rising with AI integration: building proprietary matching algorithms, LLM-based synthesis engines, and agentic automation requires significant R&D spend. Real estate and infrastructure costs are moderate: most networks maintain lean corporate headquarters and rely on experts working remotely. As the industry pivots toward transcript synthesis and away from live expert sourcing, marginal expert-acquisition costs should decline, but platform and AI engineering costs will rise.

baseline_2022.market_size: $903 million (2021 estimate from IBISWorld; report dated Jul 2021)

whats_growing: AI-powered expert matching and transcript synthesis (12–16% annual growth); demand from corporate strategy and market research teams (broader adoption beyond hedge funds); agentic AI research automation (emerging 2026 capability); global expansion in Asia-Pacific markets (lax regulation, high deal activity); platform-as-a-service models (retainer-based recurring revenue replacing transaction-based fees); specialized niches like legal transcripts (via Expert Institute acquisition) and Asia-focused sourcing (Capvision growing in APAC). Second-generation platforms (built post-2015) now claim 44% of market share vs. legacy incumbents' 37%.
whats_shrinking: Traditional pay-per-call business model (being cannibalized by transcript synthesis and agentic AI); exclusive reliance on expert sourcing as a competitive moat (AI matching is commoditizing); regulatory complexity and compliance costs as a business deterrent (reputational recovery since 2012 scandals has removed this drag, but MNPI risk remains). AI voice agents and automated channel checks ($100–$300 per data point) are encroaching on the $2,000+ per call premium, creating a new competitive threat from outside the industry.
outlook: The expert networks industry will likely grow 12–16% globally through 2030, but the nature of the business is being redefined by AI. Within 3–5 years, the majority of revenue will shift from live expert consultations to platform-based access to transcript libraries and AI-synthesized research. This favors consolidation around players with large, curated transcript backlogs (AlphaSense-Tegus) and strong brand reputations with compliance-conscious clients (GLG). Smaller, transaction-focused players will either be acquired, pivot to specialty niches (legal, medical, Asia-focused), or exit. The regulatory environment is unlikely to tighten further absent a major new insider-trading scandal, but compliance infrastructure will remain a table-stakes cost and a barrier to entry for new competitors. AI voice agents and automated channel checks will carve out a portion of the lower-end market (corporate suppliers, operational due diligence), but expert networks will retain pricing power for high-stakes strategic and investment decisions where human expertise and judgment still command premiums. International expansion, particularly in APAC, will be a key growth driver as deal activity and corporate investment rise in China, India, and Southeast Asia. The biggest long-term risk is LLM commoditization: if transcript synthesis becomes a free or nearly-free utility (via open-source models or AI platforms), the industry's high margins (14%) will compress significantly, forcing consolidation around network effects (largest transcript libraries) and brand loyalty. However, this is a 5–10 year concern; for the next 2–3 years, AI is a growth accelerant for well-capitalized incumbents.
themes: AI as industry redefinition, not replacement
Consolidation around transcript libraries and brand trust
Compliance as a moat and cost center
Platform transition from transactions to recurring revenue
New competitive threat from AI voice agents

title: Advertising Agencies in the US
one_liner: The US advertising agencies industry is shrinking as AI erodes margins and clients build in-house capabilities, despite $88.7 billion market size and 1.8% growth in 2026.
overview: The US advertising agencies industry in 2026 sits at $88.7 billion in revenue, but faces profound structural headwinds. Holding companies are shedding jobs—WPP cut 9,000 employees and Omnicom eliminated 4,000+ after acquiring Interpublic in late 2025—as clients shift spending away from traditional agencies. AI-powered tools now handle copywriting, design, and media buying that once required teams of specialists. The Omnicom-IPG merger, finalized November 2025, created a $25 billion behemoth, reshaping an industry that once had clear separation between creative and media buying. Across the sector, 60% of senior marketing leaders say they spend less on agencies in 2025 as a direct result of AI adoption, while WPP's stock collapsed 62% in 2025 alone due to client defections and margin compression.

key_stats.employees: Falling as automation advances; Forrester predicts 15% agency job losses in 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: 5.7% (2022 baseline); declining due to price pressure
key_stats.concentration: Consolidating; Omnicom-IPG merger creates largest player; Big Six narrowing to Big Five

current_dynamics: The industry faces simultaneous pressures from automation and client flight. Generative AI now produces ad copy, visuals, and campaign strategies that previously required human teams, compressing margins across the board. WPP lost Coca-Cola's US/Canada media account and Mars' $1.7 billion global media business to Publicis in 2025—two seismic shifts signaling clients now believe AI tools and smaller specialist shops can replace traditional full-service agencies. The Omnicom-IPG merger consolidates two of the Big Six into one $25 billion entity, yet this mega-deal itself reflects weakness: acquirers are betting that scale and AI investment can stem client losses, not that the holding company model remains valuable. Profitability is under siege; WPP's operating margin fell from 15% to 13% in 2025, and top 25 clients saw revenues drop 6.3% in H1 2026. Workforce layoffs are accelerating—WPP cutting 9,000 jobs, Omnicom 4,000+—as agencies de-staff to match shrinking engagements and bet remaining headcount on AI-powered delivery. Smaller agencies without AI capabilities and recurring revenue models face existential risk.
one_sentence: AI and client self-service are hollowing out traditional advertising agencies, forcing consolidation and mass layoffs despite a $88.7B market that grows at only 1.8% in 2026.
whats_growing: Digital advertising agencies ($56.9 billion in 2026, up 6.6%) and AI-native, recurring-revenue-focused boutiques. Agencies with proprietary AI tools, data analytics capabilities, and defensible tech moats command premium valuations. Retail media and connected TV specialization. Consulting firms (Accenture Song, Deloitte Digital, IBM Consulting) acquiring creative shops to build in-house capabilities.
whats_shrinking: Traditional full-service holding company models losing prestige and pricing power. Client spending on large, integrated campaigns. Headcount across the sector—Forrester predicts 15% job losses in 2026. Margins under compression from both client price negotiation and AI-driven commoditization of creative work. WPP, once a global blue-chip, shrinking in market cap from £24B (2017) to £3.1B (2025).

Publicis Groupe (claimed top spot in net revenue late 2024; aggressively winning WPP accounts)

how_it_makes_money: Commission-based pricing (flat % of media spend) is eroding. Agencies now bundle creative services, media planning/buying, and account management into tiered retainers or project fees. Digital-first shops generate recurring revenue from managed services (social, programmatic, influencer management). Traditional agencies extract value from creative expertise, media negotiation, and client relationships; holding companies add scale economics and cross-selling across subsidiaries. AI tools are shifting model toward efficiency plays—fewer humans, higher output—which commoditizes pricing.
cost_structure: Labor-intensive. Creatives, account managers, media buyers, analysts are the core cost; at traditional agencies, ~60% of revenue goes to salaries and benefits. Technology costs (AI platforms, analytics, martech) rising as % of budget. Freelance and subcontracting used to absorb fluctuations. Media buys are pass-through (little margin). Overhead (office space, infrastructure) high but being cut during 2026 restructurings.

2025: WPP loses Coca-Cola US/Canada media account and Mars' $1.7 billion global media business to Publicis; market cap drops from £24B to £3.1B; stock falls 62% in 2025
H1 2026: WPP reports top 25 clients revenue down 6.3% (Q1: -9.4%, Q2: -3.2%); operating margin compressed to 13% from 15%
2026: WPP plans to cut hundreds more jobs globally by end of year; Omnicom cuts 4,000+ jobs and shuts legacy agency brands post-IPG merger
2024-2025: M&A activity in advertising agencies down 37% (52 deals vs 82 in 2023), but strategic/capability-focused deals rising (retail media, connected TV, influencer marketing)

outlook: The industry faces a brutal 2026-2027. Consolidation will accelerate as small and mid-sized shops without AI IP get absorbed or fold. Margins will continue to compress until agencies stabilize workforce and repricing power improves—unlikely near-term given client self-service momentum. Holding companies like Omnicom (post-IPG) will ruthlessly cut legacy overhead and invest in AI/data, but face the structural reality that clients now believe in-house AI + boutiques can replace them. Publicis and others investing early in generative AI tools may gain share, but overall industry pricing and employment will remain under pressure through 2027. Agencies that survive will be either (a) specialist shops with proprietary data/tech/content IP, (b) embedded within consulting or tech firms (Accenture, Deloitte), or (c) rare full-service powerhouses with unbreakable client relationships and genuine AI advantage. The Big Six will likely become Big Four by 2028 as mid-tier holding companies get acquired or dissolve. Overall revenue growth will remain anemic at 1-2% CAGR through 2028; expect contraction in 2026-2027 before stabilization.

Digital and programmatic dominance over traditional media

title: Cable Networks in the US
one_liner: Cable networks face accelerating subscriber loss and advertising collapse as streaming overtakes linear TV, forcing major industry restructuring.
overview: In 2025-2026, the US cable networks industry is undergoing rapid reorganization rather than managed decline. The fundamental business model—licensing content to cable providers for per-subscriber fees plus advertising revenue—is broken. Streaming now accounts for 47.5% of all TV consumption as of December 2025, while cable's share has dropped to 20.2%. Pay-TV penetration fell from 88% of US households in 2010 to an expected 42% by 2026. Major players are fleeing the sector: Comcast is spinning off NBCUniversal's cable networks (USA, CNBC, MSNBC, E!, Golf Channel) into a separate company; Warner Bros. Discovery is separating its cable portfolio ahead of a planned merger with Netflix or Paramount; and the industry is bracing for ten cable network shutdowns in 2026. This is not a cyclical downturn but a structural unraveling.

key_stats.market_size: $127.5 billion (US broadcast and cable TV combined) - 2025
key_stats.businesses: Approximately 1,019 cable network establishments in the US; dominated by Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, Comcast, and Fox
key_stats.concentration: Highly concentrated; top 4 companies (Disney, WBD, Comcast/NBCU, Fox) control majority of premium cable networks
key_stats.employees: 54,338 in cable networks; total industry workforce declining
key_stats.profit_margin: Operating margin ~18.66%, EBITDA margin ~22.19% as of Q1 2026

current_dynamics: Cable subscriptions fell from 96.3 million to 68.7 million by 2024, with Comcast losing 1.15 million TV subscribers in 2025 alone (roughly 3,500 per day). Cable advertising revenue crashed from $22.5 billion in 2024 to $20.2 billion in 2025—a 10% drop in one year—with an additional 6% decline expected in 2026 and 8% in 2027. Live sports remains the last pillar keeping linear cable alive: ESPN launched ESPN Unlimited streaming in August 2025 ($30/month), and Fox rolled out Fox One DTC service ($20/month) bundling sports content. The profitability picture masks the underlying crisis: while EBITDA margins remain healthy at 22%, revenue is shrinking so fast that absolute profit dollars are collapsing. Streaming viewership overtook cable in 2025 (47.5% vs 20.2%), and only 52% of Americans watched cable or satellite TV in 2025, down from near-universal adoption a decade ago. The competitive landscape has shifted from cable vs. streaming to a multi-tier system where consumers buy Netflix, Disney+, ESPN Unlimited, and one or two niche streaming services separately—destroying the bundling economics that once made cable networks valuable.
one_sentence: Cord-cutting has pushed cable TV from serving 88% of US households in 2010 to just 42% by 2026, forcing industry giants to divest cable networks and concentrate on streaming while advertising revenue falls 6-8% annually.
whats_growing: Live sports streaming (ESPN Unlimited, Fox One launching 2025). Premium direct-to-consumer tiers bundled with existing services (Disney+, Max, Peacock). High-value event coverage (NFL, college football, Premier League, Olympics, WNBA). Regional sports networks serving niche audiences. International cable networks in growth markets.
whats_shrinking: Traditional cable TV subscriptions (projected 42% penetration by 2026 vs. 88% in 2010). Linear cable advertising revenue (down 10% in 2025, another 6% expected in 2026). Cable network licensing fees (per-subscriber rates compressed as subscriber bases shrink). Viewership of non-sports cable programming (down significantly as audiences age out and younger cohorts skip cable entirely). National cable advertising as a percentage of total ad spend (shifting to digital and streaming platforms).

June 2026: Comcast announced spinoff of NBCUniversal including Peacock, NBC broadcast, cable networks (USA, MSNBC, CNBC, E!, SYFY, Golf Channel), Sky International, and theme parks into a separate public company called Versant Media (Comcast Spins Off NBCUniversal: Three Takeaway Questions, 2026)

major_players: The Walt Disney Company (ESPN, ABC, Disney Channel, FX networks)
Warner Bros. Discovery (CNN, TNT, Adult Swim, Cartoon Network, Discovery Channel, HGTV, TCM)
Comcast/NBCUniversal (NBC, Peacock, CNBC, MSNBC, USA, E!, Golf Channel, Bravo — mostly spinning off to Versant)
Fox Corporation (Fox News, Fox Sports, FS1, FX, National Geographic)
Paramount Global/Skydance (CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon, BET, Comedy Central, Paramount Network)
Charter Communications (regional cable provider)
Smaller operators and independent networks facing consolidation or shutdown pressure
how_it_makes_money: Cable networks earn money three ways. First: content licensing fees paid by cable/satellite providers (typically per-subscriber fees, e.g., $0.50-$5 per home per month depending on network value). Second: advertising sold on linear cable (down sharply from $22.5B in 2024 to $20.2B in 2025). Third: subscription revenue from direct-to-consumer streaming tiers (ESPN Unlimited at $30/month, Fox One at $20/month, premium sports tiers on Max and Peacock). Licensing fees are collapsing because the subscriber base is shrinking, forcing networks to rely more on advertising and DTC revenue—neither of which can make up the lost licensing revenue fast enough. This is why consolidation is happening: combining networks lets surviving companies sell bundled tiers to cable operators (forcing them to carry less popular networks alongside hits) and creates DTC services with enough content depth to justify subscription prices.
cost_structure: High fixed costs. Cable networks must acquire or produce large volumes of content year-round to fill channel schedules, signing talent to multi-year deals regardless of rating fluctuations. Infrastructure (satellite uplinks, distribution systems, broadcast centers) is capital-intensive. Labor costs are significant (on-air talent, producers, newsroom staff). Variable costs track with content acquisition and production. Profit margins are highest among large consolidated players with bundling power; independent and regional networks face rising cost-per-subscriber as subscriber bases shrink. Cost-cutting is now the norm: layoffs at Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, and others; cancellations of low-rated shows; reduction in original series production. Networks are also cutting sports licensing budgets as subscriber losses make sports rights (historically the largest line item) harder to justify.
outlook: The cable networks industry will continue structural contraction through 2027. Revenue will fall 3-4% annually as subscribers decline further and advertising continues eroding. Consolidation will accelerate: by 2027, expect 8-12 cable networks to shut down and the top 3-4 media conglomerates to own 80%+ of remaining cable properties. Profitable networks will be those with irreplaceable live sports or news (ESPN, Fox News, CNN), owned by companies with DTC platforms to absorb stranded subscribers. Smaller networks without scale or unique content (specialized discovery or lifestyle channels) will disappear or fold into bundled services. The business will become split into two tiers: (1) a shrinking, high-margin linear segment serving legacy cable subscribers (50+ demographic), and (2) a growing but lower-margin DTC streaming tier selling à la carte access to premium content (sports, news, prestige drama). By 2028-2030, traditional cable networks as a revenue engine will likely represent less than 20% of revenue for major media companies; streaming, production, and ad-supported DTC will dominate. Regulatory pressure (FCC rate deregulation effective 2026) will ease cable pricing constraints but is irrelevant to the fundamental cord-cutting dynamic. Macroeconomic tariff threats (2025-2026) will increase content production costs if tariffs hit international TV production, raising pressure to cut production budgets. The outlook is decline with consolidation—not revival.

title: Movie Theaters in the US
one_liner: American movie theaters are clawing back from a pandemic collapse, but structural forces—streaming saturation, fragmented hits, and shortened windows—keep attendance 25% below 2019, forcing chains to lean on premium formats and shrinking margins.
overview: The US movie theater industry remains in recovery mode in 2025-2026, with box office reaching $8.6-8.8 billion in 2025, still well below the $11.4 billion pre-pandemic peak of 2019. Attendance fell 10% year-over-year in 2025 with 780 million admissions (down from 820 million in 2024), though Gen Z attendance surged 25% and average ticket prices climbed 5.7% to $13.29. The larger story is a permanent structural shift: casual moviegoing has collapsed, leaving only event-driven behavior for major franchises. Theater chains are responding by closing unprofitable locations, consolidating market share, expanding premium formats (IMAX, Dolby, 4DX), and raising prices—a squeeze that works so far only for strong theatrical releases.

key_stats.growth: −5% to −10% year-over-year 2024–2025; remains 23–27% below 2019 pre-pandemic peak
key_stats.employees: ~193,000 estimated (2022 baseline 193,789; likely flat to declining 2025-2026)
key_stats.businesses: ~2,200 enterprises (2022: 2,193); AMC, Cinemark, Regal dominate; iPic, LOOK, CMX filing bankruptcy 2024-2026
key_stats.profit_margin: ~7.3% industry average (2022); AMC Q2-2026 EBITDA margin 20% on rebounds, Cinemark 18.6% (2025)
key_stats.concentration: High—AMC 10%+ share, Cinemark and Regal (Cineworld) significant; top 3 chains control ~65% of US box office

current_dynamics: Attendance is stuck in two modes: event movies (Inside Out 2, Deadpool & Wolverine) draw crowds; everything else fails. The 2019–2025 drop of 34% in total ticket volume (1.225B down to 780M) masks this bifurcation. Streaming has become the structural competitor, with 1.1 billion SVOD subscribers now permanent (2x pre-pandemic), yet studios are reversing course: at CinemaCon 2026, every major studio committed to 45-day (or longer) theatrical windows. The data shows a 26-45 day window maximizes both box office and downstream streaming, forcing a détente. Ticket prices rose 5.7% in 2025 to offset attendance loss, but volume-price tradeoff is tightening. Consolidation accelerated: AMC shuttered 200+ theaters; iPic, LOOK, CMX filed Chapter 11; Cinemark and Regal are the survivors with lower debt and better fundamentals. Theater closures, market concentration, and premium format proliferation are now the defining moves.
one_sentence: US movie theaters recovered to $8.6B (2025) from pandemic lows but face permanent attendance loss—event-driven hits now carry the load while casual moviegoing has died, forcing chains to close unprofitable locations, raise prices on premium formats, and negotiate longer theatrical windows to compete with streaming.
major_players: AMC Entertainment Holdings (~10% share, 600+ US theaters)
Cineworld Group/Regal Cinemas (~850 US theaters)
Cinemark Holdings (~600 US theaters, strongest margins)
iPic Theaters (luxury dine-in, filing bankruptcy 2026)
LOOK Cinemas II (dine-in, Chapter 11 late 2024)
Metropolitan Theatres Corp. (16 theaters West/Southwest, distressed)
whats_growing: Premium large-format screens (IMAX, Dolby Cinema, 4DX, RPX) driving per-patron spend (+$5–10 format premiums). Gen Z theater attendance (+25% YoY 2024-2025, 87% within past 12 months). Average ticket prices (up 5.7% to $13.29 in 2025; national average now $16.08 for standard 2D). Loyalty/subscription programs and event programming (concerts, sports, sports events). Theater renovation and rebranding by surviving chains (Cinemark, AMC).
whats_shrinking: Total admissions (−34% from 2019 to 2025: 1.225B to 780M). Number of screens (5,700 shut down 2020-2025). Casual moviegoing behavior (habitual visits replaced by event-only trips). Second-run and discount theaters. Concession as a percentage of theater revenue (pressure from inflation). Theater chains: AMC closed 200+ theaters; iPic, LOOK, CMX in or exiting bankruptcy.
outlook: 2026 outlook is cautiously optimistic but conditional. Box office is projected to approach $9 billion in 2026 if blockbuster slate holds (Marvel, Avatar, Dune, etc.). The 45-day theatrical window consensus—backed by data showing optimal streaming conversion—should stabilize studio behavior and reduce piracy pressure. However, structural challenges remain: streaming is now the norm (1.1B+ subscribers), habitual moviegoing has not returned, and price resistance is rising. Theater chains will continue consolidation, premium format expansion, and targeted closures through 2027. Survival depends on blockbuster density and pricing power; casual audiences will not return. North American industry is in a "new normal" at 75-78% of 2019 volume, not recovering to it.

Pricing power: format premiums and inflation offsetting volume loss
Consolidation: weak chains exit; strong survivors concentrate market
Streaming détente: 45-day window consensus stabilizing theatrical economics
Premium formats: IMAX, Dolby, 4DX driving per-patron revenue
Generational divergence: Gen Z engagement up, older demographics declining

title: Music Publishing in the US
one_liner: Digital streaming now dominates US music publishing, where major consolidation, higher mechanical royalty rates, and AI copyright disputes are reshaping how publishers, platforms, and independent artists split an industry growing 5-7% annually toward $12+ billion.
one_sentence: Streaming accounts for 58% of music publishing revenue in 2025, mechanical royalty rates hit record highs in 2026, and the industry is consolidating into four major players while independent publishers gain direct-licensing alternatives.
overview: The US music publishing market reached $7 billion in 2024, marking a decade of double-digit annual growth fueled almost entirely by streaming platforms. Mechanical royalty rates climbed to 15.3% of US streaming revenue in 2026—the highest ever negotiated—with Spotify alone paying $10 billion to the music industry in 2024, the largest payout from any single retailer in history. The industry is consolidating: BMG and Concord merged in 2026 to create a fourth major competitor, Sony bought Recognition Music Group for $3.5+ billion, and Blackstone acquired Hipgnosis for $1.58 billion in 2024. At the same time, independent publishers are gaining footholds through direct-licensing: Spotify and NMPA opened an opt-in portal in 2025 for indie publishers to keep audiovisual rights and higher payouts.

key_stats.growth: 13.4% year-over-year in 2024; projected 5-7% CAGR through 2030; expected to reach $12.37 billion by 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: 12-12.5% estimated (stable)
key_stats.concentration: Highly concentrated: Big 3 majors (Universal, Sony, Warner) plus new fourth player (BMG-Concord, formed 2026)
key_stats.employees: 14,000+ workers; independent publisher segment growing faster than major-label affiliated firms
key_stats.businesses: Publishers acquire and license music copyrights; PROs (BMI, ASCAP, SESAC) collect performance royalties; streaming platforms distribute mechanical and performance payments; direct-licensing platforms connect independents to users

current_dynamics: Streaming audio now generates 58% of music publishing revenue (2025), having completely displaced physical album sales. The Copyright Royalty Board sets mechanical rates every five years; 2026 brought the highest songwriter payout rates in history at 15.35% of platform revenue—up from 15.2% in 2024. Spotify pays roughly $0.003-$0.005 per stream while Apple Music pays $0.01 per stream; Apple shifted to a per-subscriber model in 2025, paying only the artists that subscriber actually listened to, while Spotify remains pro-rata pool. Sync licensing (TV, film, gaming) grew to $600-650 million globally in 2025, creating a new revenue avenue for both indie and major publishers. However, the 1,000-stream threshold Spotify imposed in 2024 to qualify for royalties demonetized 86% of available tracks, sparking songwriter boycotts over royalty fairness. AI-generated music training remains legally unresolved but increasingly licensed: Warner and Suno struck a deal, UMG and Udio settled in late 2025, establishing that AI companies need licensing agreements. TikTok, with 58% of global music publishing deals, renewed its Universal licensing agreement in May 2026 with expanded AI protections.
whats_growing: Streaming mechanical and performance royalties grow fastest (6-7% annually); sync licensing for video platforms, gaming, and short-form video (TikTok, YouTube Shorts) expands rapidly; direct-licensing for independent publishers accelerated in 2025 with 150,000+ direct licenses granted, bypassing traditional intermediaries; artist-owned publishing catalogs and estate acquisitions (Queen for $1.27 billion in 2024) attract institutional investors (Blackstone, Singapore's GIC) seeking inflation-hedged cash flows.
whats_shrinking: Physical album sales and downloads continue their two-decade collapse; traditional performance royalties (concerts, radio) lag streaming growth, though live venues rebounded post-pandemic; independent publishers' share of catalog ownership shrinks as majors and financial sponsors acquire high-value catalogs and dedicate capital to estate representation.
recent_developments: May 2026: UMG and TikTok renewed global multi-year licensing deal with expanded AI-removal safeguards and creator attribution tools, covering 700+ million users
Early 2026: BMG and Concord merge to create the industry's fourth major player with mid-term $1.2 billion EBITDA target, ending decades of big-three dominance
2025: Spotify and NMPA launch opt-in direct-licensing portal for indie publishers to retain audiovisual sync rights and access higher rates than blanket agreements
Late 2025: Major labels (Warner, UMG) finalize AI licensing deals with Suno and Udio after 2024 lawsuits; copyright ownership and training data protocols remain unsettled for pure AI output
2024: Sony acquires Queen's entire catalog (recorded and publishing) for USD $1.27 billion, largest music deal ever; Blackstone buys Hipgnosis from public investors for $1.58 billion

2024: Copyright Royalty Board approves mechanical rate increases through 2027 (15.2%-15.35%), responding to publisher pressure; Spotify implements 1,000-stream minimum, sparking artist boycott over fairness
major_players: Universal Music Publishing Group (UMG) – largest publisher, ~24% market share; renewed TikTok deal May 2026
Sony Music Publishing (SMP) – second-largest; acquired Recognition Music Group ($3.5B+, 2025) and Queen catalog ($1.27B, 2024)
Warner Music Publishing (WMP) – third-largest; active in AI licensing and TikTok/YouTube deals
BMG and Concord (merged 2026) – new fourth major player, $1.2B EBITDA target
Reservoir Media (RSVR) – independent public publisher, fastest-growing independent firm, active in direct deals
Hipgnosis Songs Fund – $2.2B portfolio (owned by Blackstone as of 2024); high-profile catalog investor
Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music – platforms that now determine publisher economics via rate-setting and per-stream payouts
NMPA (National Music Publishers Association) – advocacy and direct-licensing portal operator for indie publishers
outlook: Music publishing is moving from maturity into growth phase, defying earlier 2022 forecasts of 2-3% annual expansion. Four forces will shape 2026-2027: (1) Streaming remains the growth engine—projected 5.4% CAGR through 2030, driven by subscriber additions in developing markets and TikTok/YouTube shorts monetization; (2) Royalty rate negotiations every five years will favor publishers as mechanical rates now hit all-time highs, though platform margin pressure may cap future increases; (3) Consolidation by majors and financial sponsors (Blackstone, Singapore's GIC, HPS Investment Partners) will concentrate high-value catalogs while independents grow via direct licensing and niche sync markets (gaming, podcasts, AI training); (4) AI copyright will evolve from litigation (largely settled with major labels by late 2025) to standardized licensing models, potentially opening new training-data revenue streams for publishers. The 2024-2026 surge from 13% growth to 5-7% "normalized" growth reflects streaming's maturing penetration, not contraction. Unresolved risks include regulatory rate-setting favoring platforms, artist pushback on low per-stream payouts (Spotify boycotts), and a potential recession reducing downstream demand for sync licensing and live performances.
themes: Streaming dominance – 58% of publishing revenue, replacing physical products entirely
Catalog consolidation – institutional investors (PE, sovereign wealth) treating catalogs as inflation-hedged assets
Rate setting battles – royalty rates now set every 5 years; mechanical rates hit record highs in 2026
AI copyright flux – licensing emerging as the solution, but pure-AI ownership and training-data compensation unresolved
Direct licensing – independent publishers and artists bypass traditional intermediaries via Spotify-NMPA portal and others
Short-form video monetization – TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram Reels now material revenue drivers alongside streaming apps

title: Book Publishing in the US
one_liner: US book publishing is stabilizing around $49 billion (2026) as digital audio booms, independent authors reshape the market, and brick-and-mortar stores unexpectedly thrive despite Amazon's dominance.
overview: The US book publishing industry is entering a new chapter in 2025-2026. After years of decline and digital disruption, the market is finding equilibrium around $49-50 billion annually. The Big Five publishers still control most trade revenue but are losing ground to self-published authors who now account for 77 percent of new ISBN titles. Audiobooks exploded to $2.43 billion in 2025 with 9 percent growth, while print books have stabilized around 762 million units sold. Indie bookstores, unexpectedly, are opening faster than closing, driven by TikTok trends and community appeal, yet rising rents remain a real threat.

key_stats.market_size: $49.1 billion in 2026 (primary US book publishing market; broader publishing sector $65.8 billion in 2026)
key_stats.growth: 0.4% growth in 2025; 4.5% CAGR 2026-2033 for books segment; audiobooks 9% growth in 2025
key_stats.businesses: Approximately 2,200 active publishers; Big Five control 80+ percent of trade market
key_stats.concentration: Penguin Random House 48.8% of Big Five revenue; Amazon 71% of reader purchases; self-published titles now 38.7% growth YoY
key_stats.profit_margin: 6.7-7.0% EBIT margin for major publishers (up from 5.4% in 2017)

current_dynamics: The US book market bifurcated sharply in 2025-2026. Print books stabilized at 762 million units sold, defying a decade of decline, driven by romance, romantasy, and graphic novels—categories that thrive on social media. Audiobooks became the growth engine, reaching $2.43 billion in 2025 as AI narration made production cheap and fast; now 45 percent of self-published authors use AI tools for production. Self-publishing exploded with 3.5 million ISBN-registered titles in 2025 (up 38.7 percent YoY) and grew at 16.7 percent CAGR toward $6.16 billion by 2033. Meanwhile, Amazon maintained dominance at 71 percent of reader purchases and 77 percent of all book sales revenue through PublishDrive, but indie bookstores staged a shocking comeback—422 new openings in 2025 alone, a 24 percent increase. The Big Five publishers shifted strategy away from aggressive consolidation toward portfolio refinement and niche category focus. E-books stagnated, declining 7.9 percent YoY in September 2025, squeezed by pricing disputes and reader fatigue.
one_sentence: Print stabilized, audio and indie authors exploded, and indie bookstores unexpectedly thrived, reshaping a market once written off for extinction.
major_players: Penguin Random House (Bertelsmann, $3.3 billion USD revenue 2024)
Hachette Livre ($3 billion revenue 2024)
HarperCollins (News Corp, $2.1 billion revenue FY 2024)
Simon & Schuster (2015-2022 Penguin random House, divested 2022)
Amazon (71% of reader purchases, 77% of direct book sales; Print-on-Demand revenue jumped 6 points to 30% in 2025)
Barnes & Noble (opening 60+ stores in 2026 after 67 store expansion in 2025)
Self-publishing platforms: Smashwords, Draft2Digital, IngramSpark
Seven Stories Press (acquired Two Dollar Radio in 2025)
Island Press (acquired by Princeton University Press, January 2026)
whats_growing: Audiobooks (9% growth to $2.43 billion in 2025, projected 26.56% CAGR through 2034 globally). Self-publishing (3.5 million ISBN-registered titles in 2025, 38.7% YoY growth, projected $6.16 billion by 2033). Indie bookstores (422 new openings in 2025, 70% growth in total number over five years). Print-on-demand and direct sales (Amazon POD revenue jumped from 24% to 30% of sales in one year). Romance and romantasy trade fiction (driving the 762 million print units sold in 2025).
whats_shrinking: E-books (-7.9% YoY in September 2025). Traditional trade book sales (offset by romance/romantasy niche strength). Established indie bookstore closures due to rent (56 closures in 2025, though offset by 422 openings). Textbook and academic publishing (rental and used markets continue to siphon new sales). Overall trade market share (Big Five consolidation paused, mid-tier publishers stable).
outlook: The 2026-2033 outlook is modest growth: books segment expected to grow 4.5% CAGR, broader publishing 2.4% CAGR. Audiobooks will continue rapid expansion fueled by AI production and smart-speaker adoption. Self-publishing will gain more share, reaching perhaps 30-40% of new title output by 2030 if current growth holds. E-books face structural headwinds: pricing disputes, reader fatigue, and saturation. Print stabilization is real but fragile—tariff threats on paper (Canada) and books (China) could spike costs in 2026-2027. Indie bookstores will keep opening but face rent risk; Barnes & Noble's 2025-2026 expansion signals the chain expects long-term physical retail demand. The Big Five will profit more per title with refined portfolios, though market share declines as indie and hybrid authors grab mindshare. AI will reshape the industry most: AI narration for audiobooks, AI-assisted covers/marketing for indie authors, and AI discovery tools competing with traditional marketing. The "book business" is becoming more granular—fewer blockbuster-dependent publishers, more focused catalog and direct-to-reader strategies.

title: Magazine & Periodical Publishing in the US
one_liner: A once-dominant print industry in managed decline, shifting toward digital subscriptions and niche audiences while print advertising collapses and costs rise.

key_stats.growth: -2.2% CAGR to $39.3 billion in 2026, with -3.8% decline in 2026 alone
key_stats.profit_margin: 7.5% projected (2027), down from 8.0% (2022)
key_stats.concentration: Low concentration; top players include Hearst, Condé Nast, Meredith, Axel Springer, Bauer Media

overview: The US magazine and periodical publishing industry is navigating a painful structural transition. Print still supplies the majority of current revenue but is shrinking steadily as advertisers and readers migrate online. Publishers have shifted to hybrid business models combining print and digital, with subscriptions now representing 35-40% of total revenue and growing toward 50-55% by 2034. Digital readership grew 19% from 2022 to 2025, yet digital advertising per subscriber remains far less lucrative than print, making the math fundamentally difficult. The industry is consolidating rapidly, with smaller and mid-tier titles vanishing and survivors focusing on niche, affluent audiences and direct subscriber relationships.
current_dynamics: Print advertising revenue has collapsed from $10 billion in 2017 to $4.3 billion in 2025, with projections falling to $3.2 billion by 2030. Publishers Clearing House, a major print circulation and subscription engine, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April 2025 due to rising paper and mailing costs combined with tanking customer response rates. Tariffs imposed in 2025 have driven up paper, pulp, and ink costs—Canada supplies 50% of US paper products, and faces a 25% tariff; China resources face 34% tariffs; and new 50% tariffs on Canadian imports arrived in August 2026. Major publishers like Condé Nast are shuttering underperforming titles (SELF, Glamour operations in Germany/Spain/Mexico, WIRED Italy) and concentrating investment on dominant brands like Vogue and The New Yorker. At the same time, AI-generated content is commoditizing generic coverage, making publishers compete on brand authority, deep expertise, and uniqueness rather than volume. The remaining competitive edge lies with publishers controlling direct subscriber relationships and first-party audience data.
one_sentence: US magazine publishing is contracting in print while pivoting to digital subscriptions and premium positioning, facing simultaneous headwinds from tariffs, AI content disruption, and collapsing print advertising.
how_it_makes_money: The industry traditionally relied on advertising (>50% of revenue) and subscription/single-copy sales. This balance has inverted: print advertising is in freefall while subscription revenue grows. In 2025, digital and print advertising streams crossed over, with digital becoming the larger source. Subscriptions now represent 35-40% of revenue and are the fastest-growing segment. Publishers supplement this with ancillary revenue: digital events, podcasts, newsletters, and AI-powered content tools. Bundled offerings (e.g., magazine plus news subscription) are emerging as a way to improve customer lifetime value.
cost_structure: Publishing is a fixed-cost business: research, writing, and design costs are incurred regardless of sales volume. Variable costs include printing and shipping, which scale with physical circulation. Digital distribution has much lower marginal cost, but revenue per digital user is still 30-40% below revenue per print subscriber. Paper and printing are the largest external cost drivers: recent tariffs have added 25-50% to input costs for major materials. Labor has been cut aggressively (employment down 3.96% CAGR from 2005-2022, further shrinkage projected), but remaining staff work on hybrid/digital workflows. Postage, which was critical for subscription delivery and Publishers Clearing House operations, remains a significant constraint on profitability.

whats_growing: Digital subscriptions and reader revenue from premium, direct-to-consumer models. Niche, specialized publications serving professional communities (finance, health, science) are outperforming general-interest titles because they rely more on subscriptions than ads. Digital magazine readership grew 19% between 2022 and 2025, driven by mobile access and bundling. Video and multimedia content created by magazine publishers for social distribution is expanding. AI-assisted editorial workflows are reducing production costs and enabling faster, more targeted content personalization.
whats_shrinking:
Print circulation and print advertising are in steep decline. Print magazine ad revenue fell from $10 billion in 2017 to $4.3 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $3.2 billion by 2030. Single-copy newsstand sales continue to erode. The number of magazine titles is contracting as publishers exit the industry or go digital-only. Print-dependent revenue models are unsustainable for all but the most premium titles serving loyal affluent audiences. General-interest magazines and celebrity/entertainment titles are losing readership and ad spend to social media and digital-native alternatives.</shrinking>
<parameter name="recent_developments">["April 2025: Publishers Clearing House files Chapter 11 bankruptcy after paper costs rose 31% (July 2020-July 2025) and customer response to mail offers collapsed; company's magazine/merchandise ad revenue fell from $879M (2018) to $181M (2024)", "2025: US magazine ad revenue totals $4.3 billion (down from $10B in 2017); Hearst CEO acknowledges difficult year for magazine advertising", "December 2024–2025: Condé Nast undergoes major restructuring, shuttering SELF magazine and winding down Glamour/WIRED operations in multiple countries; CEO Roger Lynch refocuses portfolio on dominant brands (Vogue, The New Yorker)", "February-August 2025-2026: Tariffs on paper products escalate—Canada paper faces 25% tariff, China 34%, with new 50% tariffs on Canadian imports imposed August 2026", "2025: Digital and print advertising revenue streams cross over; digital becomes larger revenue source for the industry", "2026: AI content tools move from editorial assist to autonomous workflows; publishers compete on brand authority and exclusivity as generic AI content commoditizes"]
outlook: The industry will continue shrinking at a measured pace (projected -1.0% to -2.2% CAGR through 2027 and beyond), stabilized by a core of affluent, loyal print subscribers and by growing digital subscription revenue. Publishers that own direct subscriber relationships and control first-party audience data will outcompete those dependent on advertising or legacy print distribution. Niche, specialized publications (professional, financial, health) will outperform general-interest titles. Print will remain a status symbol and niche market but will never return to historical revenue levels. Tariffs will continue to pressure profitability in 2026 and beyond unless they are rolled back. AI-generated content will commoditize generic coverage, raising the bar for editorial differentiation and quality. The number of traditional publishers will decline another 10-15% by 2030, with surviving players operating smaller, more focused portfolios. Bundled subscription offerings (magazine + news + audio) and international expansion into premium markets will be key growth levers.
themes: AI content disruption and brand differentiation

title: Newspaper Publishing in the US
one_liner: A shrinking print industry pivoting to subscriptions and AI automation as local news deserts spread and consolidation accelerates.
overview: In 2025-2026, US newspaper publishing is a declining but still substantial $29-30 billion industry shedding print editions, closing newsrooms, and desperately searching for digital revenue. The industry has lost roughly one-third of all newspapers since 2005, leaving vast communities without local journalism. Instead of traditional print recovery, major publishers are pushing paywalls (The New York Times crossed 11.6 million digital subscribers by Q1 2025), adopting AI for newsroom automation, and consolidating through deals like David Hoffmann's takeover of Lee Enterprises. Print advertising has collapsed 92% since 2000, while digital advertising remains volatile and insufficient to fill the gap. The industry faces a structural problem: what worked for 150 years—local monopolies on classified ads and classified information—has been permanently disrupted by free, global digital alternatives.

key_stats.businesses: 4,317 operating businesses in 2026; declined at -2.1% CAGR since 2021
key_stats.profit_margin: Tight and declining; advertising-dependent business model under pressure
key_stats.concentration: High consolidation among Gannett, Lee Enterprises, Alden Global Capital

current_dynamics: Print advertising revenue crashed from $73.2 billion in 2000 to $6 billion in 2023 to $407.7 million in 2024, a near-total collapse in what was historically the industry's lifeblood. Digital advertising, expected to replace print, has proved disappointing at just $315.1 million in 2024 and projected only $5.5 billion by 2028—far below print's former levels. Circulation revenue has stabilized slightly as major metros (New York Times, Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal) successfully monetize paywalls; NYT added 250,000 digital subscribers in Q1 2025 alone. But this success is limited to 10-15 national and large regional outlets with brand value; thousands of small-town and mid-size papers have no paywall strategy that works. The industry is simultaneously being pressured by rising newsprint costs (up to $580-670 per metric ton in 2025 from cheaper levels five years prior), tariff uncertainty on Canadian imports, and AI automation that's replacing reporting and copy-desk roles. Consolidation is the dominant survival strategy: Lee Enterprises is now controlled by billionaire Hoffmann (who injected $50 million in 2026), Gannett continues its dominance post-GateHouse, and Alden Global Capital's cost-cutting approach (72% newsroom cuts on some properties) exemplifies the "profit extraction" model. News Media Corporation abruptly shut down 14 papers across five states in August 2025. Meanwhile, nonprofit alternatives (American Journalism Project, local news initiatives) are growing with venture-philanthropy backing but remain tiny compared to legacy chains.
one_sentence: US newspapers face a structural decline from digital disruption, print advertising collapse, and consolidation, with only subscription-focused national outlets and nonprofit models showing viability.
whats_growing: Digital subscriptions for premium outlets (NYT model); nonprofit local news funded by philanthropy and membership; AI-driven newsroom automation for data/routine reporting; paywall strategies at papers with strong brand recognition.
whats_shrinking: Print advertising (down 92% since 2000); print circulation; local independent newspapers; newsroom headcount (especially copy editors, general assignment reporters); print edition frequency.

outlook: The industry will likely stabilize at a much smaller size (around $20-25 billion by 2030) dominated by 10-15 large national publishers with successful digital models, a handful of regional chains operating on razor-thin margins, and a growing network of nonprofit local news outlets. Print will persist in small volumes for niche/affluent readers but will no longer be the industry's center. Tariff shocks on Canadian newsprint could accelerate further closures. AI automation will eliminate more mid-tier jobs but won't solve the core problem: digital ads are worth a fraction of print ads because they're scattered across the open web. The real growth will come from subscription bundles (news plus entertainment/sports/games like NYT's model), membership models, and philanthropically-backed nonprofits. Communities without significant advertising markets (rural areas, small towns under 50,000) will likely see permanent loss of local news infrastructure unless subsidized by government or philanthropy.

title: Concert & Event Promotion in the US
one_liner: A mature market of 67,000+ event promoters charging record ticket prices to capacity crowds, now facing an antitrust breakup and consolidation of mid-market venues.
overview: The US concert and event promotion industry is at an inflection point in 2025-2026. Total market size reached $60.2 billion in 2026, up from $56 billion in 2024, driven by pent-up consumer demand and ticket price growth of 45% since 2019. Live Nation alone captured $25.2 billion in 2025 revenue, with its concerts business generating $20.9 billion and posting its best-ever profit margin of 3.3%. Yet fractures are spreading: a federal jury found Live Nation and Ticketmaster liable on every antitrust count in April 2026, potentially forcing divestiture and reshaping market structure for years; smaller independent venues continue closing at unprecedented rates due to high rents and operational costs; and consumer backlash over dynamic pricing and ticket fees is mounting pressure for regulatory change.

key_stats.concentration: Live Nation dominates with $25.2B revenue (2025); Ticketmaster controls 86% of primary ticketing at major venues (2026)
key_stats.profit_margin: 3.3% (Live Nation concerts segment, 2025); industry-wide estimated 3-5%

current_dynamics: Live Nation Entertainment reported record-breaking revenue of $25.2 billion in 2025, a 9% increase year-over-year, with 159 million fans attending 55,000 concerts globally. However, the landmark April 2026 antitrust verdict found Live Nation and Ticketmaster liable on all counts—monopolizing primary ticketing (86% market share at major venues), tying promotions to amphitheater access, and overcharging customers $1.72 per ticket. Damages could reach $450 million before trebling. Meanwhile, smaller venues are collapsing: NYC's Avant Gardner filed for bankruptcy owing $155 million in debt, Rockwood Music Hall closed in November 2024, The Music Hall of Williamsburg faces eviction at end of 2026, and UK grassroots venues are closing at a rate of one every two weeks. Concert ticket prices have soared to an average of $144 (2025), up 45% since 2019, driven by dynamic pricing algorithms—yet consumers are spending more, with 36% willing to spend $100-$499 and 17% willing to spend up to $1,000 per ticket in 2025. The industry is simultaneously consolidating via technology M&A (Cvent spent $700 million acquiring ON24 and Goldcast in December 2025; Eventbrite went private for $500 million) while facing new regulatory oversight including the FTC's junk-fees rule (May 2024) and mounting antitrust scrutiny.
one_sentence: The concert and event promotion industry is booming on paper—$60.2 billion in 2026, record attendance, and soaring ticket prices—but fracturing underneath as Live Nation faces forced breakup, independent venues collapse, and regulatory pressure mounts over monopoly ticketing practices.
how_it_makes_money: The industry generates revenue through: admission to live performing arts events (47.9% of industry revenue in 2022), including concerts (29.8%), theater, and festivals; admission to non-franchise sporting events (9.3%); contracted live performances at hotels and casinos (10.3%); media rights, licensing, and advertisement (7.3%); food, beverages, and merchandise sales (12.3%); and rental services (5.4%). Live Nation's segments are: Concerts ($20.9B, 2025), which handles artist management and venue booking; Ticketmaster ($3.1B, 2025), the primary ticketing platform; and Sponsorship & Advertising ($1.3B, 2025). Profitability depends heavily on ticket prices, merchandise sales, and ancillary services; dynamic pricing algorithms now drive pricing in real-time based on demand.

baseline_2022.growth: -8.6% annualized decline over 2016-2021 due to COVID-19; projected 14.5% growth 2021-2026 in 2022 report

whats_growing: Large arena and stadium shows. Live Nation reported its best-ever Q3 2025 revenue in the concerts segment; stadium ticket sales are up 80% year-over-year (2025), and stadium shows increased 60% in 2025. Music tourism is accelerating: concerts accounted for 52.55% of the music tourism market in 2025. Premium experiences command higher pricing: luxury field-level clubs and VIP hospitality zones are driving margins. International touring is rebounding despite higher visa and insurance costs. Sponsorship and advertising revenue grew 11% in 2025 ($1.3B). Hybrid and streamed events are becoming standard for mid-market promoters, supported by AI-powered personalization and virtual networking tools.
whats_shrinking: Independent mid-market venues and smaller promoters. Four in ten UK grassroots music venues operate at a loss; one closes every fortnight (2024 data). The US lost iconic independent venues like Rockwood Music Hall (NYC, November 2024) and Avant Gardner (NYC, 2025), while The Music Hall of Williamsburg faces eviction at end of 2026. TempleLive went out of business in September 2025. Rising rents, labor costs, and competition from Live Nation and AEG are blamed. The concert promotion segment outside Live Nation is consolidating under PE and tech platform ownership: Cvent and Eventbrite are buying up mid-market operators and technology. Small-scale independent promoters and nonemployer companies, which represent 89.3% of enterprises, are under acute pressure.

recent_developments: April 15, 2026: Federal jury found Live Nation and Ticketmaster liable on every antitrust count—monopolizing primary concert ticketing (86% share at major venues), illegal tying of promotions to amphitheater access, and overcharging $1.72 per ticket. Damages could exceed $450M if trebled; jury verdict dramatically strengthens states' position for forced divestiture or behavioral remedies in remedy phase.
December 2025: Cvent acquired ON24 for $400M and Goldcast for $300M; Eventbrite went private to Bending Spoons for $500M. Major consolidation in event tech and ticketing platforms.
November 2024: Rockwood Music Hall, iconic NYC independent music venue, closed after financial distress.
September 2025: Concert promotion company TempleLive went out of business, affecting multiple states.
2025: Average concert ticket price reached $144, a 45% increase from 2019 ($99); 80% of large venue shows for 2026 already booked at double-digit price increases.

May 2024: FTC junk-fees rule took effect, requiring all-in pricing for live event tickets (headline price includes all mandatory fees). Increased regulatory scrutiny of dynamic pricing and ticket markup practices.
themes: Consolidation of tech and mid-market operators
Ticket price inflation and dynamic pricing backlash
outlook: The 2026-2027 outlook is split into two worlds. For Live Nation and large promoters: strong near-term growth. Live Nation projects double-digit AOI growth in 2026, with 80% of large venue shows already booked and deferred revenue at $4B (up 21%). Stadium shows and premium experiences will command rising prices, and international touring will recover despite higher visa and insurance costs. However, the antitrust remedy phase will dominate 2026-2027. States are pushing for structural separation of Live Nation and Ticketmaster; even partial divestitures would fragment the market and create openings for competitors. Alternative ticketing platforms (Eventbrite, AXS, TicketX, Seatfun) will gain traction if behavioral remedies force open-access requirements. For independent venues: continued strain. Grassroots and mid-market promoters will face margin compression from rising rents, labor costs, and competition. Some will be acquired by PE or tech platforms; others will close. A two-tier market is solidifying: mega-promoters (Live Nation, AEG, Cvent-owned operators) handling stadium and arena tours, and fragmented independent/hybrid platforms serving clubs and local events. Consumer sentiment is deteriorating—backlash over dynamic pricing and junk fees is mounting—and regulators (FTC, DOJ, state AGs, and international bodies eyeing bans on dynamic pricing) are unlikely to relent. By end of 2027, the market structure will be materially different depending on antitrust remedy outcomes.

title: Live Performance Theaters
one_liner: The US live performance theaters industry—Broadway, regional theater, and touring productions—is facing a bottleneck: record box-office revenues but squeezed margins from labor demands, rising rents, and dynamic pricing backlash.
overview: The US live performance theaters industry stands at a paradox in 2025-2026. Broadway just notched its highest-grossing season ever in 2024-2025 ($1.89 billion, 14.7 million attendees) and maintained momentum in 2025-2026 ($1.91 billion, 14.6 million attendees), proving strong consumer demand for live entertainment. But the broader industry of theaters, opera houses, and live venues is contracting—the overall market fell 0.4% in 2025 to $8.6 billion. Labor costs are exploding after Broadway actors and musicians won tentative contracts with major wage increases. Rents and production costs have doubled since 2016. Dynamic pricing strategies—once a growth lever—now face public backlash and may be suppressing attendance in some segments.

key_stats.concentration: Low fragmentation; Broadway (three major operators: Shubert, Nederlander, Jujamcyn) = <15% of total revenue
key_stats.profit_margin: ~0.8–1.0% (historically low, down from 6.3% pre-pandemic in 2017)

current_dynamics: Broadway dominates mindshare but is only a fraction of the $8.6 billion total. The real story: a labor reckoning is forcing producers to choose between higher ticket prices and capped production. In October 2025, Broadway actors and musicians both authorized strikes over wages and healthcare contributions; tentative agreements were reached just before walkouts, raising costs industry-wide. Operating costs for major productions ($650,000–$800,000 weekly) are heavily weighted toward labor; rent in prime markets has doubled since 2016, outpacing ticket-price growth. Dynamic pricing—deployed to maximize per-seat revenue—sparked public fury in 2025 (Oasis, Springsteen, World Cup pricing) and is now associated with "funflation"; some venues are backing away to protect brand trust. Tourism recovery is uneven (US only at 97% of 2019 by 2024, down from Europe's 106%), limiting one major revenue stream. Off-Broadway and regional theater data is sparse, but the narrow profit margins and exit of smaller operators suggest consolidation pressure below Broadway's spotlight.
one_sentence:
Broadway's record-breaking revenues mask an industry fighting rising labor costs, rent inflation, and public backlash against dynamic pricing, with overall market growth stalled and profit margins razor-thin.</sentence>
<parameter name="whats_growing">Broadway box office and attendance remain robust, with 2025-2026 eclipsing 2024-2025 in total grosses. International tourism is recovering unevenly but steadily (Europe +6% vs. 2019 as of 2025). Live Nation (concert and tour promotion) and related entertainment sectors are expanding rapidly (concert/event promotion industry at $60+ billion in 2026, growing 11%+ annually), providing an adjacent-market expansion path for some operators.
whats_shrinking: The overall live performance theaters industry fell 0.4% in 2025 after a strong 2020–2025 recovery. Movie theater chains and some luxury cinema concepts (iPic, Alamo Drafthouse) filed bankruptcy in 2025–2026, signaling venue-level operator stress. Regional theater and off-Broadway segments are underfunded compared to Broadway's scale, with fewer data points but implied consolidation and closures. Federal funding for the creative arts has grown only 0.8% annually, failing to keep pace with inflation, particularly hurting nonprofit and community theaters.

Nederlander Organization (major Broadway operator)
Jujamcyn Theaters (Broadway)
Live Nation Entertainment (touring, ticketing, promotion)
WNET/Public Television (nonprofit, cultural infrastructure)
Regional theater networks (American Repertory Theater, Guthrie, etc.)
Disney Theatrical Productions (musicals licensing)
Sony Pictures / Alamo Drafthouse (acquired 2024)
recent_developments: October 2025: Broadway actors (Actors' Equity) and musicians (AFM Local 802) authorized strikes over wages and healthcare; tentative three-year contracts reached 6 AM Saturday, with meaningful wage increases and health benefit expansions.
2024–2025 Broadway Season: Record $1.89 billion, 14.7 million attendees; 2025–2026 Season: $1.91 billion, 14.6 million attendees (up 1% in grosses, down 0.6% in attendance on a strict 52-week basis).

2025–2026: Dynamic pricing backlash peaks (Oasis reunion, Bruce Springsteen, FIFA 2026 World Cup); 91% of UK survey respondents oppose surge pricing; organizers of LA 2028 Olympics and Euro 2028 pledge to avoid dynamic pricing.
February 2026: iPic Theaters files Chapter 11 bankruptcy; cites lagging attendance, rising labor and rent costs, high studio profit-share.
April 2025: Live Nation acquires Hayashi International Promotions (HIP), Japan's 2nd-largest concert promoter, signaling adjacent-market consolidation.
2025–2026: International tourism at 1.52 billion (2025) with uneven regional recovery (Europe +6% vs. 2019, Americas only 97%, Asia-Pacific 87%); projected to reach 1.58 billion in 2026.
outlook: Near-term (2026–2027): Labor cost inflation will force either ticket-price escalation (risking attendance) or production scaling-back (fewer shows, reduced cast/crew). Dynamic pricing will likely retreat as a consumer-facing lever, replaced by more opaque algorithmic allocation and membership models. Broadway will likely sustain its revenue near $1.9 billion, but smaller regional/community theaters will face margin compression and further consolidation. International tourism recovery will remain uneven, supporting premium audiences in major metros but not offsetting domestic leisure-time fragmentation (streaming, gaming). Longer-term (2027–2030): The industry will bifurcate—luxury Broadway venues and high-draw touring shows (Disney, concerts) will thrive; smaller, nonprofit, and regional theaters will consolidate or go digital-first. Federal funding for creative arts remains at risk, pressuring the nonprofit segment. Hybrid ticketing (in-person + livestream) will expand but will not fully offset venue-based economics. Profit margins will remain structurally low (1–2%) unless producers achieve meaningful automation in non-labor roles (marketing, ops) or venues shift to premium/membership models to reduce per-show dependency.

title: Colleges & Universities in the US
one_liner: Mature nonprofit higher education sector serving 19.4 million students, facing enrollment recovery headwinds, financial consolidation pressure, and AI-driven curriculum disruption.
one_sentence: The US college and university sector reached $605.1 billion in 2026 after contracting through the pandemic recovery, now stabilizing as domestic enrollment returns to growth but international student recruitment weakens and institutional failures accelerate.
overview: The US colleges and universities sector reached $605.1 billion in 2026 (2026), marking a 7.5% contraction from pandemic peaks but stabilizing as enrollment recovered to 19.4 million students (fall 2025, 2026). Domestic undergraduate enrollment has returned to growth for the first time in over a decade (1.2% increase fall 2025, 2026), though the composition has shifted dramatically—community colleges absorbed all gains while nonprofit private four-year institutions shrank. International student enrollment holds at an all-time high of 1.177 million in the 2024-25 academic year (2025), but new enrollments dropped a jarring 17% year-over-year in fall 2025 (2026), signaling fragility. The sector faces a structural squeeze: AI is outpacing curriculum development (37% of students doubt program relevance to AI futures; 2025), accreditation is under regulatory attack from the Trump administration (executive order April 2025), and 40+ private nonprofits merged or closed in 2024 alone, with over 100 institutions gone since 2020 (2026).

key_stats.growth: -7.5% CAGR (2021-2026); stabilizing with projected positive growth ahead
key_stats.profit_margin: Pressured by rising wage expenditures; endowment volatility constraining returns
key_stats.businesses: 2,483 institutions (2026); 40+ closures/mergers in 2024 alone; over 100 gone since 2020
key_stats.concentration: University of California largest player; low-to-moderate concentration with regional operators dominant

current_dynamics: Enrollment is reviving but its composition is fracturing along income and institutional lines. Community colleges grew 3.0% (fall 2025, 2026) while public four-year institutions grew 1.4% and nonprofit privates contracted, amplifying pressure on tuition-dependent schools with weak endowments. International graduate enrollment collapsed 12% (fall 2025, 2026) even as international undergraduates held steady, signaling that US graduate programs are losing their appeal. Endowments, which spiked 683.6% in 2021 on private-equity gains, have reversed sharply due to inflation and rising rates, forcing universities to cut programs and staff. The sector is undergoing forced consolidation—Elon acquired Queens in 2026, Russell Sage merged with Albany College, Ursuline entered Gannon, and Villanova absorbed Cabrini and Rosemont—driven by cascading enrollment losses at small privates. Federal policy is destabilizing: the Trump administration ended the SAVE income-driven repayment plan (2025), capped graduate PLUS loans (July 2026), and signaled it will approve lower-bar accreditors (April 2025 executive order), threatening regulatory leverage that has kept quality standards intact. AI is widening the relevance gap—only 51% of 2025 graduates felt prepared for AI-fluent jobs, and only 30% agreed their program felt current, creating liability for institutions that delay curriculum modernization.
how_it_makes_money: Nonprofit universities generate revenue from tuition (undergraduates and graduate), government appropriations (state and federal, roughly 40% each in 2022), private donations and endowment payouts, and research grants. Tuition varies by institution type: four-year public institutions raised tuition 1.5% annually (2015-2019), while nonprofit privates raised 2.5% annually, creating affordability pressure. Federal research funding supports graduate programs. Endowment spending has become volatile as markets swing; some institutions overspent endowment returns (2021-2022) and must rebuild. For-profit and online alternatives pull some price-sensitive students, but MOOCs have not destroyed residential demand because accreditation, in-person mentorship, and social experience remain irreplaceable. Cost structure is labor-intensive: faculty and staff wages consume most operational budgets. Revenue sources are also highly concentrated—endowment-rich schools (Ivy-adjacent, top state flagships) have margin; tuition-dependent regional privates do not.
whats_growing: Domestic undergraduate enrollment returned to growth (1.2% in fall 2025, 2026), led by community college surge (3.0% growth). Online and hybrid course enrollment continues to expand—exclusively distance undergraduates reached 3.7 million in 2024-25 (2025). International undergraduate enrollments grew 5% for new entrants (2024-25, 2025), though this reversed sharply in 2025-26. Graduate degree programs in AI, data science, and cybersecurity are rising as employers demand AI fluency. Online education platforms like Coursera (60M visits in Q1 2025), Duolingo (130.2M monthly active users Q1 2025, 2025), and Khan Academy (36.6M visits, 2025) are absorbing career-switchers and upskilling workers outside degree paths. Strategic mergers and consolidations are creating larger, financially stable entities, though at the cost of institutional autonomy.
whats_shrinking: Undergraduate enrollment at private nonprofit four-year institutions contracted 1.6% (fall 2025, 2026); for-profit sector contracted 2.0% (fall 2025, 2026). New international graduate enrollments plummeted 15% (2024-25, 2025) and declined further to -12% (fall 2025, 2026). Small tuition-dependent regional colleges are disappearing through closure or forced merger—40+ in 2024 alone, over 100 since 2020. International student recruitment faces headwinds from visa uncertainty, rising USD strength, and competition from Canada and UK. Faculty tenure-track positions are shrinking as institutions hire more contingent lecturers to cut costs. Traditional on-campus residential revenue is eroding as students shift to lower-cost community college start paths or online alternatives. Research funding uncertainty—particularly NSF discretionary grants—pressures graduate programs. Private giving declined in 2020-2021 (tied to recession) and remains below historical peaks relative to institutional ambition.

Harvard University and Ivy League (highest endowments; $50B+ each)
Stanford University (tech and research dominance)
MIT (research and graduate reputation)
University of Michigan (large public flagship)
UCLA and UC Berkeley (public flagship leaders)
NYU (urban private anchor)
Northwestern University (comprehensive private)
University of Chicago (research-intensive private)
Penn State (large public system)

September 2025: Elon University announced acquisition of Queens University of Charlotte; deal closed summer 2026, signaling wave of small-school forced mergers
