title: Home Care Providers in the US
one_liner: A rapidly growing but margin-squeezed home healthcare sector serving an aging population, pressured by reimbursement cuts, severe workforce shortages, and ongoing consolidation by private equity and large insurers.
overview: The US home care industry is expanding fast because 90% of seniors want to age at home, and Medicare and Medicaid prefer home care over costly hospitals. The market hit $191.6 billion in 2026, growing 3.9% that year after a 6.7% compound annual rate from 2021 to 2026. But the growth masks deep stress: Medicare slashed payments by 1.3% in 2026, the fourth consecutive year of cuts, and Medicaid reimbursement remains under pressure, squeezing profit margins to near zero in many agencies. Simultaneously, home care agencies are turning away up to 25% of patient requests due to staffing shortages so severe that 95% of providers report moderate-to-severe staff gaps, with caregiver turnover at 75% annually.

key_stats.employees: Over 2.4 million projected in 2026; 17% growth in home health aide positions projected 2024-2034
key_stats.businesses: 437,000+ establishments; highly fragmented; private equity owns ~41% of deal volume in 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: Near zero to negative in many agencies; strong performers target 15-20% SDE margins; 34% of agencies reported profit concerns in 2025-2026
key_stats.concentration: Low; top players include Kindred (Humana acquisition 2024), UnitedHealth/Optum, Aveanna, Enhabit; Medicare and Medicaid represent ~75% of revenue

current_dynamics: Medicare payment cuts hit home care providers for four straight years, with 2026 seeing a 1.3% aggregate reduction ($220 million) after a 6.4% cut was initially proposed. These cuts are driving a wave of agency closures in rural and underserved areas. Simultaneously, the industry faces a caregiver shortage crisis: 95% of agencies report moderate-to-severe staffing shortages, with agencies turning away up to 25% of patient requests. Caregiver wages rose from $13.07 per hour in 2014 to $16.77 in 2024, but turnover remains at 75% annually due to low pay relative to other healthcare roles. Private equity continues to acquire and consolidate the fragmented market, with 55 home health and hospice deals in the first half of 2026 alone, 41% PE-backed. Technology adoption is accelerating, with cloud-based EMRs and remote patient monitoring becoming mainstream, though integration remains incomplete and creates administrative burden. Value-based care models are shifting financial risk to lower-performing agencies through CMS rebalancing of quality scorecards.
one_sentence: The US home care industry is growing due to an aging population preferring care at home, but faces existential margin compression from stacked payment cuts, severe workforce shortages at 75% annual turnover, and regulatory complexity that is driving consolidation into larger platforms.
major_players: Kindred Healthcare (acquired by Humana, 2024; $7.2B revenue)
UnitedHealth/Optum (acquired LHC Group $5.4B and Amedisys $3.3B)
Aveanna Healthcare (PE-backed; $175.5M Family First Homecare acquisition 2026)
Enhabit (formerly Encompass; $263.6M Q3 2025 revenue)
TEAM Services Group (acquired by General Atlantic, $3B deal 2026)
whats_growing: Demand for home care driven by aging population (71.4 million Americans aged 65+ by 2029), preference for aging in place (90% of seniors), and cost advantage versus institutional care. Pediatric home care growing, with deal volume up 50% in 2025. Remote patient monitoring and cloud-based EMR adoption accelerating. Private equity deployment in home care hit record levels, with 32+ active PE rollup platforms in 2026.
whats_shrinking: Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates declining for fourth consecutive year (2026 down 1.3% nationally). Rural and underserved home health agencies shuttering due to payment cuts exceeding local cost growth. Traditional home healthcare as a revenue share of total industry (down from 55.2% in 2021). Independent single-agency operators being acquired into larger platforms; number of truly independent agencies declining.
recent_developments: CMS finalizes 2026 home health Medicare payment rule with 1.3% aggregate reduction (November 2025), down from 6.4% proposed cut
General Atlantic acquires TEAM Services Group for ~$3 billion (Q2 2026), largest home care deal on record
Kinderhook Industries acquires Enhabit for $1.1 billion take-private (Q1 2026)
Humana snaps up remaining stake in Kindred Healthcare for $5.7 billion to fully own the home care giant (2024)
Aveanna Healthcare announces $175.5M acquisition of Family First Homecare, targeting Ohio, West Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky expansion (March 2026)
CMS introduces stricter value-based purchasing rebalance: 40% OASIS outcomes, 40% claims-based, 20% patient experience (2026)
how_it_makes_money: Home care providers bill Medicare, Medicaid, commercial insurance, and out-of-pocket pay for skilled nursing, personal care, homemaker services, home hospice, physical/occupational therapy, and home infusion. Medicare and Medicaid represent ~75% of revenue. Home hospice (29% of revenue in 2021) and traditional home healthcare/nursing care (55%) are the largest segments. Smaller segments include homemaker services, therapy services, and specialty disease management programs.
cost_structure: Labor dominates: wage costs for nurses, aides, therapists, and administrative staff represent 50-60% of revenue. Per-hire recruitment costs run $2,600 to $5,000, with 75% annual turnover. Medicaid and Medicare reimbursement cuts compress per-patient margins. Compliance and technology costs rising: electronic visit verification (EVV), EMR systems, quality reporting, background screening. Transportation, equipment, and supplies make up 15-20% of costs. Overhead for managing complex payer contracts and regulatory requirements increasing.
outlook: The industry will keep growing through 2030+ on demographic tailwinds: 71.4 million seniors aged 65+ by 2029, with 70% needing care during their lifetime. However, profit growth will remain severely constrained. Medicare payment cuts are expected to continue as CMS seeks to control costs. Medicaid state budgets face pressure from work requirements (January 2027) and provider tax restrictions (FY 2027+) under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Workforce shortage will persist: the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 6.1 million job openings for home health aides over the next decade. Consolidation will accelerate as independent agencies lose viability and private equity acquires them at lower multiples (5.5x-10x EBITDA in 2026). Technology adoption will increase but will also raise compliance costs. Rural areas will see continued access loss. Large PE-backed and insurance-integrated platforms will survive and grow; small and mid-sized independents will struggle.

title: HMO Providers
one_liner: A mature, consolidating industry managing care for 35 million Medicare beneficiaries and millions of employer/individual plan holders, now facing profitability pressure from medical cost inflation, regulatory scrutiny, and insurer market exits.
overview: In 2025–2026, the US HMO Provider industry has become a tale of two markets: rapid decline in employer-sponsored HMO enrollment (down to 12% of covered workers in 2025) offset by Medicare Advantage dominance where HMOs account for over half of all MA plan offerings. Revenue surged after COVID, plunged with inflation and low-cost substitutes, then rebounded on subsidies—only to face new headwinds from tariffs and policy uncertainty. The industry is dominated by three mega-insurers: UnitedHealth Group (26% of MA enrollment, down from 29%), Humana (20%, up from 17%), and Anthem, who together control nearly half the market. Profitability has compressed dramatically: major carriers are working to restore margins to 3–5% targets, with many cutting supplemental benefits, exiting unprofitable markets, and tightening provider networks.

key_stats.businesses: 255 HMO providers (2026), down from expansion during ACA years
key_stats.concentration: High—UnitedHealth, Anthem, Humana dominate; Humana alone grew 1.3M MA enrollees in 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: 3–5% target (major insurers); compressed from historical 4.4%

current_dynamics: Medical loss ratios (MLRs) are the core crisis: 17% of MA contracts ran above 100% MLR in 2023, and another third sit in the 90–95% range with no margin cushion. Claims are growing faster than premiums—earned premiums rose 14.3% in 2025 but incurred claims grew 15.5%, meaning insurers are losing money on individual policies even after steep premium hikes. Prescription drugs, especially GLP-1s like Ozempic, are driving surprise costs. Meanwhile, Medicare Advantage itself is contracting for the first time in two decades: CMS expects enrollment to fall from 35 million in 2024 to around 34 million in 2025, and as many as 2.9 million seniors are being forced to switch plans because insurers exited unprofitable markets. Tariffs have added 2–3.6% to premium bills, and regional plans including Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare have ceased all lines of business except MA as of 2026. The industry faces simultaneous headwinds: CMS is launching aggressive audits for "upcoding" (falsely reporting patients as sicker to justify higher risk-adjusted payments), requiring new prior-authorization transparency, and enforcing tighter reimbursement validation. Consolidation continues: Cigna sold its MA business to Health Care Service Corp, and smaller regional plans are being absorbed by megacarriers.
one_sentence: HMO providers are a mature, consolidating sector where Medicare Advantage growth masks steep profitability declines, employer-market retreat, and emerging regulatory pressure on cost justification and network adequacy.

baseline_2022.market_size: $216.2 billion (2021, from IBISWorld report dated April 2021)

major_players: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (26% of MA enrollees, ~9.3M; Q2 2026: $5.48B profit, 4.9% margin)
Humana Inc. (20% of MA enrollees, ~7M; Q2 2026: $694M net income; largest MA growth 2025–2026)
Anthem Inc. / Elevance Health (major national player; competitor for market share)
CVS Health (via Aetna acquisition; restoring margins to 3–5% target; repricing half of MA products 2026)
whats_growing: Medicare Advantage enrollment itself is not growing—it's shrinking for the first time in ~20 years (2025–2026). What is growing within MA: Special Needs Plans (SNPs) now represent 23% of enrollees (2026) vs 21% (2025); HMO plan design focus (57% of all MA plans offered in 2026 are HMOs, emphasizing network control). Revenue per member is climbing due to 5.06% rate increases from CMS for 2026 and mandatory premium hikes of ~4.8–9% across employer plans. Humana gained 1.3M MA enrollees in 2026, gaining market share from UnitedHealth.
whats_shrinking: Employer-sponsored HMO enrollment: HMOs represent only 12% of covered workers in 2025, down from nearly 30% in the late 1990s. PPO and high-deductible plans (HDHP/SO, at 33%) now dominate. Total MA plan count: 3,373 plans available in 2026, down 9% from 2025. Geographic coverage: insurers exiting entire regional markets (e.g., Health Alliance, FirstCarolinaCare dropping all non-MA plans). Profit margins: major carriers targeting 3–5%, down from historical 4.4% baseline and far below break-even on many contracts. Supplemental benefits: being cut across the industry to restore margins.
recent_developments: May 22, 2025: CMS launches aggressive audit strategy to enhance and accelerate Medicare Advantage audits, targeting upcoding claims.
2025 (Q2–Q3): Multiple major insurers (UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Aetna, CVS) announce market exits and benefit reductions for 2026 MA plans.
March 2025: Cigna completes sale of Medicare business (MA, Part D, supplemental) to Health Care Service Corp.
January 1, 2026: Health Alliance and FirstCarolinaCare cease all operations except Medicare Advantage; hundreds of thousands of Medicaid/ACA enrollees forced to find new coverage.
April 2025: CMS releases final 2026 MA rule with new prior-authorization transparency requirements (list of services requiring PA, approval/denial metrics).
2026 (ongoing): Tariff-driven premium increases of 2–3.6% cited by multiple carriers; market-wide median requested increase ~15%, with 25%+ of insurers seeking 20%+ hikes.
outlook: The industry faces a profitability crisis masked by scale: Medicare Advantage enrollment peaked and is now declining, insurers are cutting plans and exiting regions to stanch losses, and regulatory pressure (CMS audits, prior-auth transparency, risk-adjustment validation) will make gaming reimbursement harder. The employer-sponsored HMO market continues its decades-long slide as workers shift to PPO and HDHP options. Consolidation will accelerate—smaller regional and Medicaid-focused plans cannot absorb the margin pressure and will be absorbed or will exit. UnitedHealth's loss of 647,000 MA enrollees to competitors like Humana signals that brand loyalty does not overcome network quality perception and benefit cuts. Profit margins will remain compressed at 3–5% unless medical cost inflation slows materially or CMS reimbursement grows faster than claims. Tariff exposure is real and will persist if trade policy remains contested. The next 12–24 months will likely see further consolidation, more regional MA plan closures, and pressure on the largest players to demonstrate they can make MA profitable without aggressively cutting enrollee benefits or triggering political backlash. The industry is structurally mature, consolidating, and squeezed between regulatory vigilance and medical cost inflation it cannot fully pass to consumers.
how_it_makes_money: HMO providers earn revenue from monthly premiums paid by employers, individuals, and government programs (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid). They control costs through closed provider networks (physicians and hospitals under contract) and gate access via primary care physicians who must approve specialist referrals. Profit comes from the spread between premiums collected and medical claims paid out (adjusted for risk scores that reflect enrollee health status). Supplemental benefits (dental, vision, hearing aids, fitness programs) attract higher-income seniors and can command premium prices. Government programs (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid) now drive growth, though Medicaid expansion is uncertain due to ongoing state-level rollbacks. Revenue volatility comes from enrollment swings, policy changes (subsidies, rate adjustments), and unpredictable medical cost trends.
cost_structure: Medical claims represent the bulk of costs (typically 80%–90% of premiums must be spent on medical care under the minimum medical loss ratio mandated by the ACA). Administrative costs (including claims processing, customer service, underwriting) absorb much of the remaining margin, further compressed by labor shortages and software investment in prior authorization, risk adjustment, and fraud detection. Provider reimbursement (salaries for employed physicians in staff models, capitated payments to provider groups, or FFS to independent physicians) is a major line item. Pharmacy costs have exploded due to high-cost drugs (especially GLP-1s). Marketing and enrollment costs spike during open enrollment periods. Real estate and IT infrastructure support the closed networks. Reinsurance is purchased to cover catastrophic claims. Regulatory compliance (audits, network adequacy, quality reporting) is increasingly expensive.
